title: One-dimensional quantum Gibbs states in constant circuit depth
summary: We prove that the Gibbs state of any spin chain can be exactly decomposed into a mixture of product states over contiguous blocks of qubits with bounded length, at any constant temperature. As a consequence, any such Gibbs state can be prepared by local unitary circuits of constant depth, with efficient classical preprocessing. We place strong limits on the spatial structure of thermal entanglement: both the entanglement depth and entanglement width (measures of multiparticle entanglement) are bounded by constants, while the localizable entanglement (the bipartite entanglement that can be generated with the aid of local measurements and classical communication) vanishes exactly beyond a constant threshold distance. Our result also has implications for quantum thermalization: for any translation-invariant spin-chain Hamiltonian with nondegenerate spectral gaps, typical low-complexity pure states drawn from a maximally entropic ensemble at any constant effective temperature become locally indistinguishable from the Gibbs state upon unitary evolution. Additionally, we obtain an analogous decomposition for fermionic systems: the Gibbs state of any 1D local fermionic Hamiltonian is exactly a mixture of constant-depth local fermionic circuits acting on Gaussian states.

AI.tldr: The Gibbs state of any 1D spin chain at constant temperature is exactly a mixture of product states on constant-length contiguous blocks, giving constant-depth local unitary preparation and strong limits on thermal entanglement structure.
AI.motivation: Thermal (Gibbs) states are central to quantum many-body physics, yet their spatial entanglement structure and preparation complexity at finite temperature are not fully understood. The paper aims to characterize the entanglement structure and circuit complexity of Gibbs states in 1D.
AI.method: Proves an exact decomposition of any spin-chain Gibbs state into a convex mixture of product states over contiguous qubit blocks of bounded length at any constant temperature. Derives consequences for constant-depth local unitary circuit preparation with efficient classical preprocessing and analyzes measures of thermal entanglement. Extends the decomposition to 1D local fermionic Hamiltonians using constant-depth local fermionic circuits acting on Gaussian states.
AI.result: Gibbs states can be prepared by constant-depth local unitary circuits with efficient classical preprocessing. Entanglement depth and entanglement width are bounded by constants, and localizable entanglement vanishes exactly beyond a constant threshold distance. For translation-invariant spin-chain Hamiltonians with nondegenerate spectral gaps, typical low-complexity pure states from a maximally entropic ensemble at constant effective temperature become locally indistinguishable from the Gibbs state under unitary evolution.
AI.conclusion: Thermal entanglement in 1D spin chains is fundamentally short-ranged and low-complexity at constant temperature, enabling constant-depth preparation and yielding implications for quantum thermalization, with a parallel fermionic result.

title: Deciding the Attainability of the Multiparameter Quantum Fisher Information is NP-Hard
summary: The quantum Fisher information (QFI) sets a fundamental bound on the attainable precision when estimating multiple parameters simultaneously. Incompatibility among the individually optimal measurements can, in some cases, imply that the precision limit set by the QFI is not attainable. In certain special cases, including pure states and full-rank states, the exact conditions for when the precision limit set by the QFI can be saturated are known. However, general conditions for the attainability of the QFI with measurements on individual copies of the quantum state have long been sought. Indeed, this was recently stated as one of the five problems in quantum information theory highlighted by [P. Horodecki et al, PRX Quantum 3, 010101 (2022)]. In this work we prove that exact attainability with individual measurements is NP-hard to decide, even for a restricted set of real, constant-rank quantum models. The source problem for our proof is the NP-hard problem of deciding whether a given bipartite density matrix is separable or not. Our result shows that the longstanding difficulty in obtaining general conditions for QFI attainability reflects a fundamental computational obstruction, rather than merely a limitation of existing mathematical techniques: unless P=NP, no efficiently computable necessary-and-sufficient criterion can exist in general.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that deciding whether the quantum Fisher information (QFI) precision limit is exactly attainable via measurements on individual copies of a quantum state is NP-hard, even for restricted real, constant-rank models, by reduction from the separability problem.
AI.motivation: The QFI bounds multiparameter estimation precision, but incompatibility among optimal measurements can make this bound unattainable. While exact attainability conditions are known for special cases (pure states, full-rank states), general conditions for attainability using individual-copy measurements have long been sought and were listed by Horodecki et al. (PRX Quantum 3, 010101, 2022) as one of five key open problems in quantum information theory.
AI.method: A computational-complexity reduction: the authors reduce from the NP-hard bipartite separability problem (deciding whether a given bipartite density matrix is separable) to the problem of deciding exact QFI attainability with individual measurements, using a restricted class of real, constant-rank quantum models.
AI.result: Exact attainability of the QFI with individual measurements is NP-hard to decide, even for the restricted set of real, constant-rank quantum models.
AI.conclusion: The longstanding difficulty in finding general QFI attainability conditions is a fundamental computational obstruction, not merely a limitation of existing mathematical techniques: unless P=NP, no efficiently computable necessary-and-sufficient criterion can exist in general.

title: Chern-number estimation: nearly optimal quantum algorithm and provable quantum speedup
summary: Topological phases of matter are characterized by global properties of quantum states beyond conventional local order parameters. The Chern number is a central invariant in this characterization, linking the geometry of quantum states to robust physical observables and making its determination key to understanding quantum matter. We construct a nearly optimal quantum algorithm for estimating the Chern number of a smooth Hamiltonian family over a two-dimensional parameter torus with a unique, gapped ground state, including interacting many-body systems. The algorithm transports and reuses two ground-state copies prepared at a single reference point and uses generalized quantum signal processing to coherently accumulate geometric phases. It achieves a Hamiltonian-oracle evolution time of $\tilde{O}(L_xL_y/Δ_{\min}^3)$, where $L_x,L_y$ bound the parameter derivatives of the Hamiltonian and $Δ_{\min}$ is a known spectral-gap lower bound. We prove a matching worst-case oracle lower bound, even when the Chern number is promised to be zero or one, establishing optimality up to polylogarithmic factors. For local Hamiltonian families with an inverse-polynomial gap and a supplied guiding state, exact Chern-number computation is in $\mathsf{FBQP}$ and is $\mathsf{BQP}$-hard, and merely deciding whether the Chern number is zero or one is already $\mathsf{BQP}$-complete. These results establish how efficiently quantum computers can estimate a quantized topological invariant and provide evidence for quantum advantage in characterizing topological phases.

AI.tldr: A nearly optimal quantum algorithm estimates the Chern number of a smooth (including interacting many-body) Hamiltonian family over a 2D parameter torus, with a matching worst-case oracle lower bound proving optimality up to polylog factors.
AI.motivation: The Chern number is a central topological invariant linking quantum-state geometry to robust observables, so determining it is key to understanding quantum matter. The paper aims to establish how efficiently quantum computers can estimate this quantized topological invariant.
AI.method: The algorithm transports and reuses two ground-state copies prepared at a single reference point and employs generalized quantum signal processing to coherently accumulate geometric phases. Its Hamiltonian-oracle evolution time is Õ(L_x L_y / Δ_min^3), where L_x, L_y bound parameter derivatives of the Hamiltonian and Δ_min is a spectral-gap lower bound. A matching worst-case oracle lower bound is proved. Complexity for local Hamiltonian families is also analyzed.

For local Hamiltonian families with inverse-polynomial gap and a supplied guiding state, exact Chern-number computation lies in FBQP and is BQP-hard; deciding whether it is 0 or 1 is BQP-complete.
AI.conclusion: The results delineate how efficiently quantum computers can estimate a quantized topological invariant and provide evidence for quantum advantage in characterizing topological phases.

title: Discrete Scale Invariance of Ising Mesons
summary: Discrete scale invariance often arises from resonant few-body or singular scale-invariant dynamics. We show that it can instead emerge in the internal motion of a composite excitation in an ordered quantum magnet. In the marginal $1/r^4$ transverse-field Ising chain, long-range bonds generate an asymptotic inverse-square attraction between dressed domain walls, with strength fixed by the spontaneous magnetization. The dressed two-kink threshold curvature sets the relative kinetic scale. Together, these independently accessible quantities determine the scale-anomaly exponent and hence the meson hierarchy. In the supercritical regime, the same exponent governs geometric binding-energy and size ratios, logarithmic level accumulation, and log-periodic threshold scattering. Full-spin exact diagonalization and a fourth-order weak-field Hamiltonian support the coupled energy--size scaling in the finite window between core and ring effects. This provides a microscopic many-body realization of quantum limit-cycle physics, with its universal scaling fixed by magnetic order and kink mobility.

AI.motivation: Discrete scale invariance typically originates from resonant few-body or singular scale-invariant dynamics. The authors aim to demonstrate that DSI can instead arise from collective many-body physics in an ordered quantum magnet, providing a microscopic realization of quantum limit-cycle behavior.
AI.method: The study analyzes the marginal 1/r^4 transverse-field Ising chain, where long-range bonds induce an asymptotic inverse-square attraction between dressed domain walls, with strength set by spontaneous magnetization. The relative kinetic scale is fixed by the dressed two-kink threshold curvature. These quantities determine the scale-anomaly exponent. Analysis employs full-spin exact diagonalization and a fourth-order weak-field Hamiltonian.
AI.result: The scale-anomaly exponent sets the meson hierarchy. In the supercritical regime, the same exponent governs geometric binding-energy and size ratios, logarithmic level accumulation, and log-periodic threshold scattering. Exact diagonalization and the weak-field Hamiltonian support the predicted coupled energy–size scaling within the finite window between core and ring effects.
AI.conclusion: DSI emerges microscopically in a many-body magnet, realizing quantum limit-cycle physics whose universal scaling is fixed by magnetic order and kink mobility.

title: Characterizing quantum precision enhancement for multiple currents in open quantum systems
summary: The kinetic uncertainty relation (KUR) constrains fluctuations of individual currents in classical nonequilibrium systems in terms of the dynamical activity, which quantifies the average number of transitions per unit of time. Here, we derive a multi-current KUR (MKUR) establishing the precision limit for multiple currents generated in classical stochastic processes in the nonequilibrium steady state. We then apply our theory to identify quantum devices whose correlated current fluctuations surpass this classical limit by comparing the quantum system to a classical emulator with the same average currents in the steady state. In this way, violations of the emulator's MKUR have a clear physical meaning, i.e., that the quantum-coherent evolution reduces joint current fluctuations below what is possible for a classical Markovian system with the same energy-level structure and incoherent resources. Since the MKUR incorporates correlations between currents, its violation pinpoints nonclassical fluctuations in parameter regimes where the single-current KUR is satisfied. We illustrate the essential and complementary role of these bounds for characterizing joint current precision with two examples: a coherently driven two-level system and an experimentally motivated model of a three-level heat engine subject to parasitic environmental couplings.

AI.tldr: The paper derives a multi-current kinetic uncertainty relation (MKUR) bounding the joint precision of multiple currents in classical nonequilibrium steady states, and uses it as a classical benchmark to certify nonclassical current fluctuations in quantum devices.
AI.motivation: The standard kinetic uncertainty relation (KUR) constrains single-current fluctuations via the dynamical activity, but many devices generate multiple correlated currents whose joint precision is not captured by single-current bounds. A classical limit on joint fluctuations is needed to meaningfully identify genuinely quantum-coherent reductions in noise.
AI.method: Derive a multi-current KUR for classical stochastic processes in the nonequilibrium steady state. Compare a quantum system to a classical emulator possessing the same average steady-state currents, and interpret violations of the emulator's MKUR as signatures of nonclassical fluctuations. Apply to a coherently driven two-level system and a three-level heat engine with parasitic environmental couplings.
AI.result: The MKUR establishes a precision limit for multiple currents and, by incorporating inter-current correlations, reveals violations in parameter regimes where the single-current KUR remains satisfied. Two examples demonstrate that quantum-coherent evolution can suppress joint current fluctuations below the classical Markovian bound.
AI.conclusion: The MKUR provides a classical benchmark for joint current precision, complementing the single-current KUR. Its violation pinpoints nonclassical fluctuations and offers a practical tool to identify quantum devices whose correlated transport surpasses classical limits.

title: Locking transition in coupled disordered systems
summary: When a system of many interacting constituents is extended across space, every region carries the same disordered landscape, and it is unclear whether distant regions settle into the same state. We study copies of the Random Energy Model (REM), sharing one disorder realization, coupled along a chain. A first-order transition separates a phase with short-range correlations, from a locked phase in which the entire chain occupies the lowest-energy state with probability one, even at positive temperature. No intermediate ordering lengths occur. In the Generalized REM the chain locks either to the lowest-energy state or to the lowest free-energy valley.

AI.tldr: Coupled copies of the Random Energy Model sharing one disorder realization on a chain exhibit a first-order transition between a short-range-correlated phase and a locked phase where the whole chain sits in the lowest-energy state with probability one, with no intermediate ordering lengths.
AI.motivation: When a many-body system with quenched disorder is extended across space, each region shares the same disordered landscape, raising the question of whether distant regions settle into the same state. The authors probe this by asking how spatial coupling selects among the many metastable states of a shared random landscape.
AI.method: They study copies of the Random Energy Model (REM) that share a single disorder realization, coupled along a one-dimensional chain. They then extend the analysis to the Generalized REM (GREM).
AI.result: A first-order transition separates a phase with short-range correlations from a locked phase in which the entire chain occupies the lowest-energy state with probability one, even at positive temperature. No intermediate ordering lengths appear. In the Generalized REM, the chain locks either to the lowest-energy state or to the lowest free-energy valley.
AI.conclusion: Spatially coupling replicas of a shared random landscape yields a sharp, first-order locking transition without intermediate length scales; the GREM case shows locking can target either the lowest-energy state or the lowest free-energy valley.

title: Asymptotically Optimal Mixed-State Cloning

AI.tldr: The paper determines the asymptotic optimal global fidelities for cloning generic mixed states with simple full-rank spectra at fixed dimension and gain γ>1, deriving a closed-form expression and showing a spectrum-independent cloner is minimax optimal; it also treats flat projector states and shows the proposed cloners beat purify-clone-trace (PCT).
AI.motivation: Asymptotic quantum cloning of mixed states is less understood than the pure-state case, especially when the input ensemble is generic with a nontrivial spectrum. The work aims to characterize the fundamental limits of cloning such states and to quantify the separate contributions of spectral and eigenbasis uncertainty.
AI.method: The authors construct cloning channels combining classical processing of Schur–Weyl labels with a covariant Cartan-sector channel. They prove converses via local asymptotic normality and a Gaussian fidelity bound valid against arbitrary channels. For flat projector states ρ=P/r they give a separate optimality proof, and they estimate the exact asymptotic fidelity of purify–clone–trace (PCT) for comparison.
AI.result: For a known simple full-rank spectrum p1>…>pd>0 with m_n/n→γ>1, the optimal root fidelity is F_orb(γ,p)=∏_{i<j}(√γ+√(q_ij(γ−1+q_ij)))/(γ+q_ij), q_ij=p_j/p_i. When the spectrum is unknown, a spectrum-independent cloner attains F_univ(γ,p)=((2√γ)/(1+γ))^{(d−1)/2} F_orb(γ,p) uniformly on compact subsets of the simple full-rank chamber and is minimax optimal. For flat projector states ρ=P/r, the optimum is γ^{−r(d−r)/2}. The proposed cloners strictly outperform PCT at every fixed gain for simple full-rank spectra and rank-r projector states with 1<r<d.
AI.conclusion: The asymptotic cloning limits for generic mixed states admit an explicit fidelity formula, decompose into spectral and eigenbasis uncertainty factors, and are achieved by a minimax-optimal universal cloner. The results extend to flat projector states and demonstrate a strict advantage over purify–clone–trace.

title: Collectivity limits quantum entanglement
summary: Understanding what limits many-body quantum entanglement is a central problem in physics. Spatial locality has long provided a fundamental mechanism: correlations between a region and its complement must be mediated through a small spatial interface, thereby constraining their entanglement. Here we show that universal constraints on entanglement can persist even when interactions are strongly nonlocal, through collectivity: many weak interactions suppress collective quantum fluctuations while retaining a finite overall interaction scale. We establish this mechanism rigorously for generic gapped Hamiltonians with Kac-normalized power-law interactions $r^{-α}$ on a $D$-dimensional lattice. For arbitrary bipartitions, we prove that the ground-state entanglement scales at most logarithmically with system size for $α<D/2$ and subextensively for $D/2<α<D$, due to suppressed collective fluctuations around individual sites. For spatially regular bipartitions with codimension-one boundaries, we show that collective suppression can be propagated to successively larger length scales through a renormalization-group construction. As a result, we prove that the entanglement bound improves to polylogarithmic scaling for $D/2<α<(D+1)/2$, and remains parametrically stronger than the arbitrary-bipartition bound for $(D+1)/2<α<D$. Together, these results reveal collectivity as a fundamental mechanism for constraining many-body entanglement alongside spatial locality.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that collective suppression of quantum fluctuations in systems with Kac-normalized power-law interactions $r^{-\alpha}$ constrains ground-state entanglement, yielding at most logarithmic scaling for $\alpha<D/2$, subextensive scaling for $D/2<\alpha<D$, and polylogarithmic scaling for regular bipartitions when $D/2<\alpha<(D+1)/2$.
AI.motivation: Spatial locality has traditionally been viewed as the fundamental mechanism limiting many-body entanglement, since correlations must be mediated through a small spatial interface. The authors ask whether universal entanglement constraints can persist even when interactions are strongly nonlocal, identifying collectivity as a candidate mechanism.
AI.method: They rigorously analyze generic gapped Hamiltonians with Kac-normalized power-law interactions $r^{-\alpha}$ on a $D$-dimensional lattice. For arbitrary bipartitions they exploit suppressed collective fluctuations around individual sites to bound ground-state entanglement. For spatially regular bipartitions with codimension-one boundaries, they use a renormalization-group construction to propagate the collective suppression to successively larger length scales.
AI.result: For arbitrary bipartitions, ground-state entanglement scales at most logarithmically with system size for $\alpha<D/2$ and subextensively for $D/2<\alpha<D$. For regular bipartitions, the bound improves to polylogarithmic scaling for $D/2<\alpha<(D+1)/2$ and remains parametrically stronger than the arbitrary-bipartition bound for $(D+1)/2<\alpha<D$.
AI.conclusion: Collectivity is established as a fundamental mechanism constraining many-body entanglement, operating alongside spatial locality. Many weak nonlocal interactions can suppress collective quantum fluctuations while retaining a finite overall interaction scale, yielding universal entanglement bounds even without locality.

title: Out-of-time-order Correlators in Volcano potentials
summary: The out-of-time-order correlator (OTOC) has emerged as an important diagnostic for quantum information scrambling and a key signature of quantum chaos. In this work, we discuss out-of-time-order correlators, analytically and numerically, for the so-called Volcano potentials. This family of potentials parametrically interpolates between bounded wells and confining walls, and includes Pöschl-Teller as a specific case. Through a combination of numerical diagonalization and semiclassical analysis, we investigate various regimes of the potential parameter regimes containing regions of both positive and negative curvatures. Moreover, we demonstrate in this case that short-time exponential growth of the OTOC does not necessarily signal global quantum chaos; instead, it correlates with the sampling of negative curvature regions by excited states.

AI.tldr: This work analyzes out-of-time-order correlators (OTOCs) for Volcano potentials—interpolating between bounded wells and confining walls, including Pöschl-Teller—via numerical diagonalization and semiclassical methods, showing that short-time exponential OTOC growth does not necessarily imply global quantum chaos but instead tracks excited-state sampling of negative-curvature regions.
AI.motivation: The OTOC is a key diagnostic for quantum information scrambling and quantum chaos, but its interpretation must be examined across realistic potentials with mixed curvature, where signatures like early exponential growth may not be reliable indicators of global chaos.
AI.method: Analytical and numerical study of OTOCs for Volcano potentials, a family parametrically interpolating between bounded wells and confining walls (subsuming Pöschl-Teller), using numerical diagonalization combined with semiclassical analysis across parameter regimes containing both positive- and negative-curvature regions.
AI.result: In the investigated regimes, short-time exponential growth of the OTOC does not necessarily signal global quantum chaos; instead, it correlates with the sampling of negative-curvature regions by excited states.
AI.conclusion: Early-time exponential OTOC growth can be a misleading criterion for global quantum chaos, as it may reflect local negative-curvature sampling rather than global chaotic dynamics, cautioning against overinterpreting short-time OTOC behavior.

title: Local autonomous inference machines for quantum LDPC codes
comment: 6 pages main text with 3 figures, comments welcome
summary: We introduce a local and distributed framework for decoding quantum LDPC codes. Built atop belief propagation (BP), the architecture combines strictly local processing of syndrome information, local feedback, autonomous operation, and highly parallelized decoding. We establish the framework at two complementary levels. First, we show that any code exhibiting a threshold under iterative BP decoding can be promoted to an autonomous local measurement-and-feedback dynamics while preserving that threshold. We then turn to codes for which naive BP does not itself exhibit threshold behavior. Our key observation is that BP can nevertheless provide sufficiently accurate \emph{local} marginal information: active syndrome defects use these local beliefs to \emph{move}, pair, and annihilate through asynchronous feedback. We demonstrate numerically that this construction exhibits threshold behavior in the point-like sectors of the two- and three-dimensional toric codes, where conventional BP decoding fails. Exploiting the graph-generality of BP, we then study the inference dynamics on the membrane-like sector of the three-dimensional toric code and in a family of bivariate-bicycle quantum LDPC codes.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a local, distributed, autonomous framework for decoding quantum LDPC codes built on belief propagation, showing threshold behavior even for codes where naive BP fails.
AI.motivation: Conventional BP decoding of quantum LDPC codes does not always exhibit threshold behavior, and there is a need for decoders that are local, autonomous, and highly parallelizable while still achieving good thresholds.
AI.method: The framework builds on BP with strictly local syndrome processing, local feedback, and autonomous parallel operation. It first promotes any BP-threshold code to an autonomous local measurement-and-feedback dynamics preserving the threshold. For codes without naive BP thresholds, it exploits BP's accurate local marginals so that active syndrome defects move, pair, and annihilate via asynchronous feedback.
AI.result: Numerically, the construction exhibits threshold behavior in the point-like sectors of the 2D and 3D toric codes, where conventional BP decoding fails. The inference dynamics are also studied on the membrane-like sector of the 3D toric code and on a family of bivariate-bicycle quantum LDPC codes.
AI.conclusion: BP-based local, autonomous, distributed decoding can achieve thresholds beyond the reach of conventional BP, and generalizes across different code families via graph-generality of BP.

title: Digital Quantum Algorithms for Generating and Utilizing Spin Squeezed States
summary: Spin squeezed states (SSSs) are conventionally viewed as analog resources for quantum metrology. Here we develop algorithms to efficiently generate and exploit SSSs on a digital quantum computer. We introduce an adaptive local-circuit protocol that prepares SSSs with squeezing parameter $ξ$ in depth $\mathrm{O}\left(\log{1/ξ}\right)$, yielding an exponential improvement over non-adaptive approaches. We prove that this depth is optimal for permutation symmetric SSSs by deriving a matching lower bound on entanglement entropy. We further leverage the squeezing paradigm to deterministically prepare the Dicke states using asymptotically fewer resources than prior methods. Remarkably, classical simulations of our preparation protocols under realistic noise models predicts a metrological gain of 4.2 dB beyond the standard quantum limit with 55 superconducting qubits in total including ancillae. Our work paves the way for performing quantum metrology on near-term digital quantum devices.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces adaptive local-circuit algorithms to efficiently generate and exploit spin squeezed states (SSSs) on digital quantum computers, achieving optimal depth and demonstrating metrological gain.
AI.motivation: Spin squeezed states are conventionally viewed as analog resources for quantum metrology. The authors aim to enable their generation and exploitation on digital quantum computers, paving the way for quantum metrology on near-term digital devices.
AI.method: An adaptive local-circuit protocol prepares SSSs with squeezing parameter ξ in depth O(log 1/ξ). The authors prove this depth is optimal for permutation symmetric SSSs via a matching lower bound on entanglement entropy. They also use the squeezing paradigm to deterministically prepare Dicke states with asymptotically fewer resources, and perform classical simulations of the protocols under realistic noise models.

AI.conclusion: The work enables performing quantum metrology on near-term digital quantum devices by efficiently generating and exploiting spin squeezed states.

title: Fast Hamiltonian engineering from cut polytope geometry
summary: Hamiltonian engineering (HE) simulates quantum dynamics under a target Hamiltonian using a native entangling system Hamiltonian and restricted control, with applications from quantum gate design to analog quantum simulation. Observing that, for many systems, formulating HE as a linear program only requires specific commutation relations between the control pulses and the system Hamiltonian, we provide a unified framework for broad classes of $2$-local qubit, qudit, and fermionic systems. We reformulate time-optimal HE as a complex $k$-cut polytope problem, with $k$ the number of distinct phases in these commutation relations, and prove it NP-complete for every finite $k$. We therefore relax the polytope to the elliptope and apply a Krivine-type rounding, yielding pulses informed by the system and target Hamiltonians, which we then use in a linear program. We derive how many informed pulses are necessary and sufficient for the linear program to be reliably feasible. Additionally mixing in uniformly sampled pulses guarantees a solution close to the relaxation value from $\mathrm{O}(m)$ pulses, with $m$ the number of interaction terms. Together with upper and lower bounds on the optimal quantum run time, this yields an $\mathrm{O}(\sqrt{m})$ approximation ratio. In benchmarks on a fully connected Ising model, a chiral clock model for qudits, and the fermionic Harper-Hofstadter model, our approach attains near-optimal quantum run times wherever the optimum is computable, reaches run times that saturate with the lattice size in the fermionic case, and outperforms state-of-the-art methods with $\mathrm{O}(m)$ pulses. This establishes a unified approach with provable guarantees to the automatic programming of analog quantum simulators.

AI.tldr: The paper provides a unified framework for Hamiltonian engineering (HE) by reformulating time-optimal HE as a complex k-cut polytope problem, proving NP-completeness, then relaxing to the elliptope with Krivine-type rounding to derive informed control pulses. This yields an O(√m) approximation ratio and near-optimal run times on Ising, qudit chiral clock, and fermionic Harper-Hofstadter benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Hamiltonian engineering simulates quantum dynamics under a target Hamiltonian using a native entangling Hamiltonian and restricted control, with applications from quantum gate design to analog quantum simulation. Existing methods lack a unified, provably guaranteed approach to automatically program analog quantum simulators. The authors observe that formulating HE as a linear program only requires specific commutation relations between control pulses and the system Hamiltonian, motivating a unified treatment across qubit, qudit, and fermionic systems.

They relax the polytope to the elliptope and apply Krivine-type rounding to obtain pulses informed by the system and target Hamiltonians, which are then used in a linear program. title: Entanglement spectrum and magic in higher-dimensional free fermionic systems
summary: We study fermionic non-local magic in higher-dimensional free-fermion systems through the lens of the entanglement spectrum. For translationally invariant Gaussian states in strip geometries, dimensional reduction maps the problem to independent lower-dimensional momentum sectors, leading in two dimensions to a multiplicative logarithmic violation of the boundary law analogous to Gioev-Klich-Widom scaling. We further show that the second Rényi fermionic non-local magic is bounded by the capacity of entanglement and introduce an entanglement-temperature deformation that probes the low-energy structure of the entanglement Hamiltonian. Applied to the matter-Majorana sector of the Kitaev model, this response is exponentially suppressed in the Abelian phase and algebraic in the non-Abelian phase, where its ratio with the capacity approaches a universal constant. Out of equilibrium, we extend the quasi-particle description to fermionic non-local magic in higher-dimensional quenches and show that random Gaussian circuits exhibit diffusive spreading in two spatial dimensions.

AI.tldr: Fermionic non-local magic in higher-dimensional free-fermion systems is studied via the entanglement spectrum, revealing Gioev-Klich-Widom-like scaling, an entanglement-temperature deformation bounded by entanglement capacity, phase-dependent responses in the Kitaev model, and diffusive spreading under random Gaussian circuits in 2D.
AI.motivation: Non-local magic—the non-stabilizerness generated by non-local operations—remains poorly understood in higher-dimensional free-fermion systems. The authors aim to characterize it through the entanglement spectrum, exploiting the tractability of Gaussian states to access universal scaling and phase-discriminating signatures.
AI.method: For translationally invariant Gaussian states in strip geometries, dimensional reduction maps the problem onto independent lower-dimensional momentum sectors. The second Rényi fermionic non-local magic is bounded by the capacity of entanglement, and an entanglement-temperature deformation is introduced to probe the low-energy structure of the entanglement Hamiltonian. This is applied to the matter-Majorana sector of the Kitaev model and extended out of equilibrium via a quasi-particle description of higher-dimensional quenches, including random Gaussian circuits.
AI.result: In two dimensions, the approach yields a multiplicative logarithmic violation of the boundary law analogous to Gioev-Klich-Widom scaling. The entanglement-temperature response is exponentially suppressed in the Abelian phase of the Kitaev model and algebraic in the non-Abelian phase, where its ratio to the capacity approaches a universal constant. Out of equilibrium, random Gaussian circuits exhibit diffusive spreading in two spatial dimensions.
AI.conclusion: Entanglement-spectrum methods provide a unified framework for fermionic non-local magic in higher-dimensional free-fermion systems, connecting it to entanglement capacity, distinguishing topological phases of the Kitaev model through universal response ratios, and revealing diffusive dynamics in random Gaussian circuits in 2D.

title: Is rapid mixing stable?
summary: Several physically interesting Lindbladians, such as those describing generic open quantum system models as well as engineered state preparation processes, are often rapidly mixing, that is, they relax to steady states in time scaling polylogarithmically with the system size. Owing to the short mixing times, it is physically expected that local perturbations do not substantially increase the mixing time. In this work we question this expectation and ask whether rapid mixing survives. We provide counterexamples showing that rapid mixing is not stable in general, even when the perturbation does not change the steady state. We also show that arbitrarily weak local Hamiltonian perturbations can destroy rapid mixing. Complementing these results, we develop an array of sufficient conditions which imply stable rapid mixing, including several classes of quasifree fermionic systems, commuting Lindbladians, and local spin systems. We also identify conditions under which modified logarithmic Sobolev inequalities (MLSIs), a stronger form of convergence, lead to stable rapid mixing. As a further implication of our results, we show that rapid mixing does not imply a positive MLSI constant.

AI.tldr: Rapid mixing of Lindbladians is shown to be unstable under local perturbations in general, though sufficient conditions and classes guaranteeing stable rapid mixing are identified.
AI.motivation: Many physically relevant Lindbladians (generic open quantum systems, engineered state preparation) mix rapidly, relaxing in polylogarithmic time. It is physically expected that local perturbations should not substantially increase mixing time. This work questions that expectation and asks whether rapid mixing survives perturbations.
AI.method: The authors construct counterexamples to test stability of rapid mixing, including cases where the perturbation preserves the steady state and cases of arbitrarily weak local Hamiltonian perturbations. They then develop sufficient conditions implying stable rapid mixing, covering quasifree fermionic systems, commuting Lindbladians, and local spin systems, and analyze conditions under which modified logarithmic Sobolev inequalities (MLSIs) yield stable rapid mixing.
AI.result: Rapid mixing is not stable in general; counterexamples show local perturbations, even steady-state-preserving ones, can destroy it, and arbitrarily weak local Hamiltonian perturbations can also destroy rapid mixing. Sufficient conditions for stable rapid mixing are established for several system classes. Additionally, rapid mixing is shown not to imply a positive MLSI constant.
AI.conclusion: Rapid mixing of Lindbladians is not robust under local perturbations in general. Stability requires additional structure, characterized by the sufficient conditions provided. Moreover, rapid mixing is weaker than a positive MLSI constant.

title: Independent density and coherence skin effects in adaptive fermion circuits
summary: Adaptive circuits use measurements and outcome-conditioned feedback to implement nonreciprocal dynamics without postselection. We show that fermion circuits host independently tunable density and coherence skin effects. The stationary state has an exact density tilt set only by measurement strength and feedback displacement: conditioned-gate details cancel, yielding an exponential one-particle profile and, at any filling, a tilted ensemble of configuration weights. Decaying coherences instead obey, in the bulk, an effective Hatano-Nelson generator controlled by the conditioned gates through a relative occupation phase. Tuning this phase drives a point-gap topological transition and reverses coherence localization at fixed density, allowing density and coherence to localize at opposite edges. We derive both exponents for conditioned $U(2)$ gates and propose a correlator-ratio probe using ensemble-averaged observables.

AI.tldr: Adaptive fermion circuits exhibit independently tunable density and coherence skin effects, governed by measurement strength, feedback displacement, and a relative occupation phase that drives a point-gap topological transition, allowing density and coherence localization at opposite edges.
AI.motivation: Adaptive circuits implement nonreciprocal dynamics via measurements and outcome-conditioned feedback without postselection, motivating a study of how such feedback shapes the stationary state and coherence structure in fermion circuits.
AI.method: The authors analyze conditioned U(2) gate circuits, deriving the stationary density profile and an effective Hatano-Nelson generator that governs bulk coherence decay, and propose a correlator-ratio probe using ensemble-averaged observables.
AI.result: The stationary state shows an exact exponential one-particle density tilt set only by measurement strength and feedback displacement (conditioned-gate details cancel), plus a tilted ensemble of configuration weights at any filling. Coherences obey a bulk effective Hatano-Nelson generator controlled by the relative occupation phase, whose tuning drives a point-gap topological transition and reverses coherence localization at fixed density. Both localization exponents are derived for conditioned U(2) gates.
AI.conclusion: Density and coherence skin effects in adaptive fermion circuits can be tuned independently, enabling density and coherence to localize at opposite edges, and are experimentally accessible via an ensemble-averaged correlator-ratio probe.

title: Out-of-Time-Ordered Correlators Beyond Lindblad
comment: Main and Supplemental Material, 18 pages, 4 figures
summary: Out-of-time-ordered correlators (OTOCs) provide a powerful probe of quantum chaos and scrambling. While the Lindblad formalism is often used to describe OTOCs in open systems, microscopic mechanisms that give rise to the Lindblad equation at the level of time-ordered correlation functions do not necessarily justify this approach at the level of OTOCs. Starting from a microscopic model of a subsystem coupled to a random bath, we show that the resulting OTOC dynamics contains an additional contribution compared to the standard Lindblad approach. This contribution, induced by correlations between different replicas, allows key properties of the underlying unitary dynamics such as long-time freeness to be retained and information scrambling to be captured more faithfully. As an application, we show that this extended formalism can be used to numerically study OTOCs in large closed systems by replacing part of the system with a dissipative boundary, offering a way to study operator spreading and higher-order correlations beyond directly accessible system sizes.

AI.tldr: OTOC dynamics in open systems cannot be captured by the standard Lindblad equation; an extra replica-correlation term is required, which preserves long-time freeness and improves scrambling descriptions, and enables numerical study of OTOCs in large closed systems via a dissipative boundary.
AI.motivation: The Lindblad formalism, though widely used for OTOCs in open systems, is only justified at the level of time-ordered correlation functions. Its validity for OTOCs is questionable, since OTOCs probe quantum chaos and scrambling in ways that time-ordered correlators do not.
AI.method: The authors start from a microscopic model of a subsystem coupled to a random bath and derive the resulting OTOC dynamics, comparing it to the standard Lindblad approach. They identify an additional contribution arising from correlations between different replicas.
AI.result: The OTOC dynamics contains an extra term beyond the Lindblad result, induced by inter-replica correlations. This term retains key features of the underlying unitary dynamics, such as long-time freeness, and captures information scrambling more faithfully.
AI.conclusion: The extended formalism can numerically study OTOCs in large closed systems by substituting part of the system with a dissipative boundary, providing access to operator spreading and higher-order correlations beyond directly simulable system sizes.

title: Quantum Estimation under Decoherence in Neutrino Oscillations: Quantum Resources, Flavor Accessibility, and Multiparameter Incompatibility
summary: Neutrino oscillations offer an interferometric setting for open-system dynamics, quantum resources, and parameter estimation. We distinguish two often-conflated statistical families: propagation-basis dephasing uses a survival factor $η_p$ to damp interference before flavor projection, changing flavor probabilities; effective flavor-mode dephasing suppresses only off-diagonal coherence of a single-particle, two-mode state while fixing its populations. For the two-flavor mode state, we derive exact concurrence, entanglement of formation, and local quantum uncertainty, and reduce one-sided projective discord to a one-parameter optimization. For $0<P<1$ and $0<η_m<1$, the QFIM in $(P,χ,η_m)$ is diagonal, with $\mathcal{H}^{\rm mode}_{χχ}=C_{η_m}^2$ and $\mathcal{H}^{\rm mode}_{ξ_mξ_m}=C_{η_m}^2/(1-η_m^2)$, where $ξ_m=-\lnη_m$. For propagation-basis dephasing, basis-matched QFI and flavor FI separate dynamical information loss from measurement inaccessibility for the mixing angle, mass-squared splitting, and dephasing rate. A monochromatic three-flavor benchmark evaluates the mixed-state QFIM, flavor FIM, and SLD incompatibility for $(θ_{23},δ_{\rm CP},ξ_{31},g)$ at DUNE-like, T2HK-like, and ESSnuSB-inspired points. At $Γ_0=10^{-23}\,\mathrm{GeV}$, the fixed-coordinate ratio $\mathcal{F}^{\rm flav}_{δδ}/\mathcal{H}_{δδ}$ is approximately $0.010$, $0.013$, and $0.105$, respectively; all three points show strong $θ_{23}$--$ξ_{31}$ incompatibility. A single-energy flavor measurement supplies only two independent probabilities, so its four-parameter FIM is rank deficient: these diagonal ratios are conditional diagnostics, not joint four-parameter sensitivities. These are state-level information-geometric benchmarks, not event-level sensitivity forecasts.

They compute the QFIM in (P, χ, η_m) with ξ_m = −ln η_m and establish its diagonal form. For propagation-basis dephasing, they separate basis-matched QFI from flavor FI. A monochromatic three-flavor benchmark evaluates the mixed-state QFIM, flavor FIM, and SLD incompatibility for (θ_23, δ_CP, ξ_31, g) at DUNE-like, T2HK-like, and ESSnuSB-inspired points.
AI.result: For 0<P<1 and 0<η_m<1, the QFIM in (P, χ, η_m) is diagonal with H^mode_χχ = C_ηm^2 and H^mode_ξmξm = C_ηm^2/(1−η_m^2).
