A single-energy flavor measurement yields only two independent probabilities, making its four-parameter FIM rank deficient.
AI.conclusion: The derived ratios are conditional diagnostics rather than joint four-parameter sensitivities, since the four-parameter FIM is rank deficient. These results are state-level information-geometric benchmarks, not event-level sensitivity forecasts.

title: From Projected Subspaces to Full-Space Implementations: Representation-Equivalence Audits for Open-Shell ADAPT-VQE
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables; 36-page supplementary material supplied as an ancillary PDF. Submitted to The Journal of Chemical Physics
summary: A variational state optimized in a symmetry-projected space need not be the state prepared by exponentiating the corresponding unprojected parent generators. For an orthogonal target-space projector $P$, $Q=I-P$, and an anti-Hermitian generator $A$, exact equivalence for all amplitudes requires target-space invariance, $QAP=0$. We formulate this condition as a representation-equivalence audit for open-shell ADAPT-VQE. For a canonical CAS(15e,9o) type-1 Cu(II) Hamiltonian, 274 of 323 bare Hartree--Fock-origin single, double, and triple excitations violate this condition. Projected-doublet ADAPT reaches 1.5719 m$E_h$ with 121 operators, whereas the same amplitudes in the corresponding full-space sequence give 464.730 m$E_h$ error, 0.07343 fidelity with the projected state, and 54.45\% quartet weight. Reoptimizing the same 121 parent generators in the same order under the hard constraint $p_D\ge0.999$ reduces the best converged error to 8.482 m$E_h$, showing that the catastrophic same-angle failure is primarily a representation/parameter-transfer failure but is not completely repaired by full-space reoptimization of the fixed sequence. An independent 12-qubit NO benchmark exhibits the same mechanism more mildly. A spin-preserving generalized full-space construction removes the representation ambiguity and reaches 1.493 and 1.181 m$E_h$ at 18 and 24 qubits. For the 18-qubit positive control, selectively refining only four Suzuki-2 factors and re-transpiling with a fixed compiler seed passes the predeclared circuit-equivalence gate at 19,660 controlled-X (CX) gates and depth 23,016. Circuit synthesis and final-energy measurement therefore constitute separate validation layers. The contribution is a validation framework, not a new spin-adapted ADAPT algorithm.

AI.tldr: A symmetry-projected variational state is not generally equivalent to exponentiating its unprojected parent generators; the target-space invariance condition QAP=0 exposes a representation/parameter-transfer failure in open-shell ADAPT-VQE, which is a validation issue distinct from spin adaptation.
AI.motivation: Symmetry-projected ADAPT-VQE assumes that exponentiating unprojected parent generators prepares the projected variational state, but this equivalence can fail. The paper aims to diagnose this mismatch as a representation-equivalence audit rather than proposing a new spin-adapted algorithm.
AI.method: For orthogonal projector P, Q=I-P, and anti-Hermitian generator A, exact equivalence for all amplitudes requires target-space invariance QAP=0. This is formulated as a representation-equivalence audit and tested on a canonical CAS(15e,9o) type-1 Cu(II) Hamiltonian and 12-, 18-, and 24-qubit NO benchmarks, comparing projected-doublet ADAPT, full-space reoptimization under the constraint p_D>=0.999, a spin-preserving generalized full-space construction, and selective Suzuki-2 factor refinement with fixed compiler seed against a circuit-equivalence gate.
AI.result: 274 of 323 bare Hartree-Fock-origin single, double, and triple excitations violate QAP=0. Projected-doublet ADAPT reaches 1.5719 mE_h with 121 operators, while the same amplitudes in the full-space sequence give 464.730 mE_h error, 0.07343 fidelity, and 54.45% quartet weight. Reoptimizing the same 121 generators under p_D>=0.999 reduces the error to 8.482 mE_h, showing the failure is primarily representation/parameter-transfer but not fully repaired by fixed-sequence reoptimization. The 12-qubit NO benchmark shows the same mechanism more mildly. The spin-preserving generalized full-space construction reaches 1.493 and 1.181 mE_h at 18 and 24 qubits. For the 18-qubit positive control, selective refinement of four Suzuki-2 factors passes the circuit-equivalence gate at 19,660 CX gates and depth 23,016.
AI.conclusion: Projected and unprojected generator representations are not interchangeable in open-shell ADAPT-VQE; target-space invariance is a necessary equivalence condition, and circuit synthesis and final-energy measurement are separate validation layers. The work provides a validation framework, not a new spin-adapted ADAPT algorithm.

title: Witness-based quantification of non-Markovianity without complete Choi state reconstruction
comment: 18 (double column)+3 (single column), 3 figures, comments are welcome
summary: Quantifying non-Markovianity is a fundamental problem in the theory of open quantum systems, as it is essential for exploiting environmental memory as a resource in quantum technologies. Existing resource-theoretic and operational quantifiers, however, generally require complete knowledge of the intermediate dynamical map and are therefore experimentally demanding. Here, we develop a witness-based framework for the quantification of non-Markovianity that bypasses complete reconstruction of the Choi state associated with the intermediate dynamical map. We first show that every non-Markovianity witness provides a certifiable lower bound on the geometric resource measure of non-Markovianity and identify the necessary and sufficient conditions under which this bound is tight. Motivated by the fact that non-positive-semidefinite witnesses are generally difficult to measure in real experimental scenario, we then focus on positive-semidefinite witnesses, which admit a natural implementation as positive operator valued measure (POVM) elements. We prove that every positive witness yields a certified lower bound on the Rivas--Huelga--Plenio (RHP) measure, thereby establishing a complete hierarchy connecting witness-based quantification, the RHP measure, and the geometric distance measure. Applying our framework to amplitude-damping and general Pauli dynamics, we find that the optimal positive witnesses reduce to simple Bell-parity projectors. Furthermore, we show that the resulting witness values can be obtained directly from a small number of experimentally accessible correlation measurements, thereby eliminating the need for complete Choi-state reconstruction and providing an efficient and experimentally feasible approach for the quantification of non-Markovianity in open quantum systems.

AI.tldr: A witness-based framework quantifies non-Markovianity without full Choi-state reconstruction, providing certified lower bounds on geometric and RHP measures, with optimal positive witnesses reducing to Bell-parity projectors implementable via few correlation measurements.
AI.motivation: Quantifying non-Markovianity is fundamental for exploiting environmental memory as a quantum resource, but existing resource-theoretic and operational quantifiers require complete knowledge of the intermediate dynamical map (full Choi-state reconstruction), making them experimentally demanding.
AI.method: The authors develop a witness-based quantification framework. They prove every non-Markovianity witness gives a certifiable lower bound on the geometric resource measure and derive necessary and sufficient tightness conditions; then specialize to positive-semidefinite witnesses (realizable as POVM elements), proving each yields a certified lower bound on the RHP measure, establishing a hierarchy linking witness-based quantification, RHP, and geometric distance measures. Applied to amplitude-damping and general Pauli dynamics.
AI.result: Every non-Markovianity witness certifies a lower bound on the geometric measure (with known tightness conditions); every positive witness certifies a lower bound on the RHP measure. For amplitude-damping and general Pauli dynamics, optimal positive witnesses reduce to simple Bell-parity projectors, and witness values are obtainable from a small number of experimentally accessible correlation measurements.
AI.conclusion: The framework unifies witness-based quantification with the RHP and geometric distance measures via a certified hierarchy, and eliminates the need for complete Choi-state reconstruction, offering an efficient and experimentally feasible route to quantifying non-Markovianity in open quantum systems.

title: Near-Optimal Parallel Unitary Process Tomography in Diamond Distance
summary: Unitary process tomography is the act of learning how an unknown unitary gate acts on a quantum system. It is an essential procedure for realizing a functioning quantum computer. As quantum technologies develop, it is important to understand the computational resources needed to conduct unitary process tomography using a variety of types of circuits. In particular, when measuring error in diamond distance, it is known how to achieve optimal query complexity using a sequential circuit architecture, but it had not been known whether a parallel circuit architecture could achieve the same optimal query complexity. In this work, we prove that unitary process tomography with near-optimal query complexity is indeed possible using a parallel circuit by introducing an explicit, novel parallel procedure. This closes the gap between sequential and parallel circuits up to a logarithmic factor, showing that parallel and sequential strategies are nearly equally capable for this task.

AI.tldr: This work proves that unitary process tomography with near-optimal query complexity is achievable using a parallel circuit architecture via an explicit novel procedure, closing the gap between sequential and parallel circuits up to a logarithmic factor.
AI.motivation: Unitary process tomography is essential for functioning quantum computers. While sequential circuits are known to achieve optimal query complexity for measuring error in diamond distance, it was unknown whether parallel circuits could achieve the same optimal query complexity.
AI.method: The authors introduce an explicit, novel parallel procedure for unitary process tomography that attains near-optimal query complexity under the diamond distance error metric.
AI.result: The proposed parallel procedure achieves near-optimal query complexity, matching the sequential architecture up to a logarithmic factor.
AI.conclusion: The gap between sequential and parallel circuits for unitary process tomography is closed up to a logarithmic factor, demonstrating that parallel and sequential strategies are nearly equally capable for this task.

title: From Classical to Quantum Channels: Achieving Positive Covert Rates
comment: 44 pages, 9 figures, single column, part of the results will be presented at the 2026 IEEE Information Theory Workshop
summary: In this paper, we study the conditions under which covert communication at positive rates is feasible over discrete memoryless classical, classical-quantum, and quantum channels. For classical point-to-point channels, we show that if the dimension of the channel input probability simplex exceeds that of the channel output probability simplex, equivalently, if the input alphabet has larger cardinality than the output alphabet, then positive covert rates are achievable for certain classes of Discrete Memoryless Channels (DMCs). We further show that allowing the innocent symbol (i.e., the symbol transmitted in the no-communication mode) to be chosen appropriately can enlarge the class of DMCs for which positive covert rates are achievable. We also study covert communication over classical Multiple-Access Channels (MACs), where the additional transmitter effectively enlarges the set of available channel input pairs, and we show that the conditions required to satisfy the covertness constraint are less restrictive for MACs than for point-to-point channels. We extend these results to classical-quantum DMCs by showing that if the dimension of the input probability simplex exceeds the affine dimension of the set of output states that can be induced at the channel output, then positive covert rates are achievable for certain classes of classical-quantum DMCs. Finally, for quantum channels, we show that if the innocent state (i.e., the state transmitted in the no-communication mode) is mixed, then the covertness constraint can always be satisfied by a non-trivial input ensemble. Consequently, positive covert rates are achievable whenever the legitimate receiver can distinguish at least two states in a suitable such ensemble.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes conditions for positive-rate covert communication over classical, classical-quantum, and quantum channels, showing feasibility when the input simplex dimension exceeds the output simplex/state affine dimension, and demonstrating that symbol/state choice and multiple-access settings relax covertness constraints.
AI.motivation: Prior work typically shows that covert communication at positive rates is infeasible (square-root law) over many channels. The paper seeks to identify structural conditions under which positive covert rates are actually achievable, and to understand how channel type (point-to-point vs. MAC, classical vs. quantum) and the choice of the innocent symbol/state affect feasibility.
AI.method: The authors analyze discrete memoryless classical, classical-quantum, and quantum channels, comparing the dimension of the channel input probability simplex with the dimension of the output probability simplex (or affine dimension of the induced output states). They examine the effect of appropriately choosing the innocent symbol, study classical multiple-access channels where the second transmitter enlarges the set of input pairs, and for quantum channels consider mixed innocent states.
AI.result: For classical point-to-point DMCs, positive covert rates are achievable for certain DMC classes when the input alphabet cardinality exceeds the output alphabet cardinality (input simplex dimension exceeds output simplex dimension). Appropriately choosing the innocent symbol enlarges the class of DMCs admitting positive covert rates. For MACs, covertness conditions are less restrictive than for point-to-point channels. For classical-quantum DMCs, positive rates are achievable when the input simplex dimension exceeds the affine dimension of the induced output states. For quantum channels with a mixed innocent state, the covertness constraint can always be satisfied by a non-trivial input ensemble, yielding positive covert rates whenever the receiver can distinguish at least two states in a suitable ensemble.
AI.conclusion: Positive-rate covert communication is feasible under identifiable dimensional conditions relating input and output (state) spaces, and feasibility is enhanced by judicious choice of the innocent symbol/state and by multi-user (MAC) settings; mixed innocent states guarantee non-trivial covert input ensembles for quantum channels.

title: Near-optimal quantum simulation of lattice Lindbladian dynamics
summary: We consider the problem of simulating dynamics under geometrically local Lindbladians acting on a lattice of qudits. We present an algorithm to approximate the time evolution under these Lindbladians for evolution time $t$ and on $N$ qudits to diamond norm error $\varepsilon$ using geometrically local circuits of depth $O(t \ \polylog(Nt/\varepsilon))$. Our results thus achieve a performance comparable to that of the Haah-Hastings-Kothari-Low (HHKL) algorithm for lattice Hamiltonian simulation.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an algorithm for simulating geometrically local Lindbladian dynamics on a lattice of qudits, achieving diamond norm error ε with geometrically local circuits of depth O(t·polylog(Nt/ε)), matching the performance of the HHKL algorithm for lattice Hamiltonian simulation.
AI.motivation: Dynamics under geometrically local Lindbladians on lattices are important for open quantum systems, but while efficient simulation algorithms exist for lattice Hamiltonians (e.g., HHKL), comparable circuit-depth results for Lindbladian (dissipative) evolution were lacking. This work aims to close that gap.
AI.method: The authors design an algorithm approximating the time evolution generated by geometrically local Lindbladians acting on N qudits, implemented using geometrically local quantum circuits.
AI.result: For evolution time t, the algorithm approximates the Lindbladian time evolution to diamond norm error ε using geometrically local circuits of depth O(t·polylog(Nt/ε)).
AI.conclusion: The proposed algorithm achieves performance comparable to the HHKL algorithm for lattice Hamiltonian simulation, extending efficient local-circuit simulation to geometrically local Lindbladian dynamics.

title: Bivariate Bicycle Codes over Group Algebras
summary: We study a weighted-shift formulation of bivariate bicycle group-algebra (BBGA) codes over finite group algebras. One binary shift acts by right multiplication and the other by left multiplication; associativity ensures that these shifts commute even for a nonabelian seed group. Bivariate polynomials in the shifts, including mixed monomials, therefore define CSS codes. We give explicit sparsity bounds and distinguish nonabelian seed groups from codes that are intrinsically inequivalent to abelian realizations. For $D_3$, a pair of weighted permutation shifts generates a regular $C_6\times C_{12}$ action and recovers the known $[[144,12,12]]$ and $[[144,14,14]]$ bivariate bicycle codes. We also present a computer-verified $[[144,16,12]]$ code over $A_4\times C_6$, with every check of weight eight. This example belongs to the established nonabelian two-block group-algebra family. Exhaustive low-weight enumeration and an intrinsic stabilizer-support invariant certify that it is inequivalent to any ordinary abelian BB or two-block group-algebra realization, even under qubit permutations combined with local Clifford operations. Finally, a nonuniform weighted-shift construction over $\mathbb{F}_2[C_3]$ yields a $[[18,4,3]]$ code with check weights six and eight. An exact enumeration of its minimum stabilizer supports rules out every ordinary binary 2BGA realization at that length, under the same equivalence. This establishes that the unrestricted weighted-shift formulation extends beyond the ordinary 2BGA class, even with an abelian seed group.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a weighted-shift formulation of bivariate bicycle group-algebra (BBGA) codes where one shift is a right multiplication and the other a left multiplication over a finite group algebra. It provides sparsity bounds, constructs new nonabelian codes, and proves that the weighted-shift class strictly extends the ordinary two-block group-algebra (2BGA) class.
AI.motivation: Ordinary bivariate bicycle (BB) and two-block group-algebra (2BGA) codes rely on commuting shifts that restrict the achievable code parameters and equivalence classes. The authors seek a more general construction that allows mixed monomials in noncommuting-looking shifts while preserving the CSS commutation condition, thereby accessing codes intrinsically inequivalent to abelian realizations.
AI.method: A weighted-shift BBGA formulation is defined: one binary shift acts by right multiplication and the other by left multiplication in a finite group algebra, with associativity guaranteeing commutation even for nonabelian seed groups. Bivariate polynomials in these shifts, including mixed monomials, define CSS codes. The authors derive explicit sparsity bounds, construct examples over D_3, A_4×C_6, and F_2[C_3], and apply exhaustive low-weight enumeration plus an intrinsic stabilizer-support invariant for equivalence certification.
AI.result: For D_3, weighted permutation shifts generate a regular C_6×C_12 action and recover the known [[144,12,12]] and [[144,14,14]] BB codes. A computer-verified [[144,16,12]] code over A_4×C_6 with all checks of weight eight is constructed in the nonabelian two-block group-algebra family; it is certified inequivalent to any ordinary abelian BB or 2BGA realization, even under qubit permutations combined with local Clifford operations. A nonuniform weighted-shift construction over F_2[C_3] yields an [[18,4,3]] code with check weights six and eight, and enumeration rules out every ordinary binary 2BGA realization at that length under the same equivalence.
AI.conclusion: The unrestricted weighted-shift formulation strictly extends the ordinary 2BGA class, even when the seed group is abelian, as demonstrated by the [[18,4,3]] code over F_2[C_3] having no ordinary 2BGA realization. The framework thus provides access to intrinsically new CSS codes beyond abelian bivariate bicycle constructions.

title: Quantifying Teleportation Overhead in Distributed Unitary Coupled-Cluster Ansätze
summary: Distributed quantum computing (DQC) has been proposed as a way to scale quantum algorithms for practical applications beyond monolithic quantum processor architectures. Among these applications, quantum chemistry is widely regarded as one of the most promising use cases for quantum computing. In this work, we estimate the distributed-resource requirements of unitary coupled-cluster (UCC) ansätze for quantum chemistry, focusing on unitary coupled-cluster singles and doubles (UCCSD), unitary pair coupled-cluster doubles (UpCCD), and unitary pair coupled-cluster with generalized singles and doubles (UpCCGSD) circuits for hydrogen chains. We focus on a teleportation-based approach to DQC, quantitatively comparing a naive distribution method to the output of the TeleSABRE algorithm. For both approaches, we estimate the cost of handling nonlocal two-qubit gates across a fixed midpoint or quarter-point partition, reporting Bell-pair/classical-communication costs in teleportation. Across Jordan-Wigner and Bravyi-Kitaev, we find that UpCCD with spin-blocked Jordan-Wigner ordering gives the most favorable scaling, while UCCSD incurs substantially larger distributed-resource requirements.

AI.tldr: This work estimates the distributed-resource requirements (Bell pairs, classical communication) of UCC-based quantum chemistry ansätze on hydrogen chains under a teleportation-based distributed quantum computing model, comparing naive distribution with TeleSABRE and different partitions and fermionic encodings.
AI.motivation: Distributed quantum computing (DQC) is a candidate route to scale quantum algorithms beyond monolithic processors, and quantum chemistry is among its most promising applications. However, the distributed-resource cost of chemistry ansätze—especially under practical circuit-distribution strategies—remains insufficiently quantified.
AI.method: Estimate distributed-resource requirements for UCC ansätze—UCCSD, UpCCD, and UpCCGSD circuits—for hydrogen chains. Adopt a teleportation-based DQC model, quantitatively comparing a naive distribution method against the TeleSABRE algorithm, for both fixed midpoint and quarter-point partitions. Report Bell-pair and classical-communication costs for handling nonlocal two-qubit gates, across Jordan-Wigner and Bravyi-Kitaev encodings.
AI.result: Across Jordan-Wigner and Bravyi-Kitaev encodings, UpCCD with spin-blocked Jordan-Wigner ordering exhibits the most favorable scaling, whereas UCCSD incurs substantially larger distributed-resource requirements.
AI.conclusion: The choice of ansatz, fermionic encoding/ordering, circuit-distribution algorithm, and partition scheme materially governs DQC resource costs, with UpCCD under spin-blocked Jordan-Wigner ordering being the most resource-efficient of the studied chemistry ansätze.

title: Puncturing for Adaptive Entanglement-Assisted Stabilizer Codes
summary: Quantum error-correcting codes are essential for reliable quantum communication. The achievable parameters can be improved by using entanglement-assisted stabilizers at the cost of consuming pre-shared Bell pairs. If the availability of such Bell pairs is intermittent, the ability to adapt the code to available resources is beneficial. That is, to pick a single mother code that can be adapted to different entanglement budgets. To achieve this, we extend an existing puncturing construction for standard/unassisted stabilizers to the entanglement-assisted setting through a three-step procedure: Interpreting the code as an unassisted stabilizer, puncturing a receiver-side qubit, and recovering an entanglement-assisted representation. This procedure reduces the number of required Bell pairs by one while preserving the number of transmitted and logical qubits. We derive a bound on the resulting distance loss and establish conditions for preserving the original code distance. Finally, we analyse distinct, randomly generated, entanglement-assisted stabilizers with five to eight transmitted qubits. Of these codes, 14.75% have a greater distance than their associated unassisted representations. Among this subset, 81.4% admit at least one puncturing choice that preserves the original entanglement-assisted distance. These results illustrate how puncturing can reduce entanglement requirements while maintaining code distance.

AI.tldr: This paper extends puncturing of stabilizer codes to the entanglement-assisted (EA) setting, enabling a single mother code to adapt to varying entanglement budgets by reducing the required Bell pairs by one while preserving transmitted and logical qubits, with bounds on distance loss and conditions for distance preservation.
AI.motivation: Quantum error-correcting codes are essential for reliable quantum communication, and entanglement-assisted stabilizers improve achievable parameters at the cost of consuming pre-shared Bell pairs. When Bell pair availability is intermittent, it is beneficial to adapt a single mother code to different entanglement budgets rather than being locked to a fixed consumption level.
AI.method: The authors extend an existing puncturing construction for standard (unassisted) stabilizers to the entanglement-assisted setting via a three-step procedure: (1) interpreting the EA code as an unassisted stabilizer, (2) puncturing a receiver-side qubit, and (3) recovering an entanglement-assisted representation. This reduces required Bell pairs by one while preserving the number of transmitted and logical qubits. They derive a bound on the resulting distance loss and establish conditions for preserving the original code distance.
AI.result: They analyse distinct, randomly generated entanglement-assisted stabilizers with five to eight transmitted qubits. 14.75% of these codes have a greater distance than their associated unassisted representations. Within this subset, 81.4% admit at least one puncturing choice that preserves the original entanglement-assisted distance.
AI.conclusion: Puncturing is an effective tool to reduce entanglement (Bell pair) requirements while maintaining code distance, illustrating how EA codes can be made adaptable to intermittent entanglement resources.

title: Conversable Quantum Fire in the Standard Model
summary:
Quantum fire consists of quantum states that can be efficiently functionally cloned but cannot be transmitted using one-way classical communication. Whereas all previous quantum-fire constructions with proven untelegraphability are relative to an oracle, ours, based on one-shot signatures, is in the standard model.
  Our construction achieves two further notions that we introduce: (a) keyless untelegraphability, a strengthening of untelegraphability; and (b) conversability, meaning that a flame, though not telegraphable via one-way classical communication, can be transmitted via classical interaction. Hence one-way and two-way classical communication differ qualitatively in their power to transmit this quantum fire.
  We use these two novel properties of quantum fire, along with its clonability, to give one of the first cryptographic applications of quantum fire. Keyless untelegraphability forces the distribution of serial numbers of valid flames to have high min-entropy, while conversability and clonability allow the corresponding flame to be cloned and transferred using only classical communication.
  We present two variants of our conversable quantum-fire construction. The first, based on one-shot signatures (instantiable from subexponential iO, subexponentially secure one-way functions, and LWE), supports polynomially many flames, and super-logarithmic min-entropy of the serial-number distribution. The second, under the stronger assumption of exponentially unforgeable one-shot signatures (instantiable relative to a classical oracle), supports exponentially many flames, and linear min-entropy.

AI.tldr: The paper constructs quantum fire in the standard model based on one-shot signatures, introducing keyless untelegraphability and conversability, and demonstrates a cryptographic application exploiting clonability combined with these properties.
AI.motivation: All prior quantum-fire constructions with proven untelegraphability were only relative to an oracle; the authors aim to achieve this in the standard model and to strengthen and broaden the notion for cryptographic use.
AI.method: Construct quantum fire from one-shot signatures, achieving keyless untelegraphability (a strengthening of untelegraphability) and conversability (classically transmittable via interaction though not via one-way classical communication); use these properties plus clonability for a cryptographic application, with two variants: one from one-shot signatures (subexponential iO, subexponentially secure OWFs, LWE) and one from exponentially unforgeable one-shot signatures (classical oracle).
AI.result: Standard-model quantum fire with proven untelegraphability, plus keyless untelegraphability and conversability; one cryptographic application where keyless untelegraphability forces high min-entropy of valid flame serial numbers while conversability and clonability permit cloning and transfer via classical communication; Variant 1 supports polynomially many flames and super-logarithmic min-entropy; Variant 2 supports exponentially many flames and linear min-entropy.
AI.conclusion: One-way and two-way classical communication differ qualitatively in their power to transmit quantum fire; the construction establishes standard-model quantum fire with stronger properties and a first cryptographic application.

title: Separability rigidity of Gaussian states under positive domination
summary: We prove a separability rigidity theorem for finite-mode Gaussian states. Let $ρ_G$ be Gaussian and let $\mathcal I$ be a fixed partition of the modes. If $ρ_G$ dominates a nonzero positive operator $T$ that is separable across $\mathcal I$, $0\neq T\preccurlyeq ρ_G$, then $ρ_G$ itself is separable across $\mathcal I$. The dominated operator is arbitrary and need not be Gaussian. As consequences, convex mixing among finitely many separability partitions creates no new Gaussian states: a Gaussian state belonging to such a convex class is already separable across one fixed partition. In particular, full inseparability and genuine multipartite entanglement coincide for finite-mode Gaussian states, and identical copies of a biseparable Gaussian state cannot activate genuine multipartite entanglement. We also show that the implication cannot be reversed by constructing a fully separable Gaussian state that dominates a positive multiple of a genuine multipartite entangled state.

AI.tldr: The paper proves a separability rigidity theorem: if a finite-mode Gaussian state dominates any nonzero operator separable across a fixed mode partition, the Gaussian state itself is separable across that partition. This yields strong structural results on Gaussian entanglement, including the coincidence of full inseparability and genuine multipartite entanglement.
AI.motivation: Understanding the separability structure of Gaussian states in continuous-variable systems is fundamental, but it is unclear whether weak witnesses of separability (dominated separable operators) can certify separability of the Gaussian state itself, and how partial separability behaves under convex mixing and tensor copies.
AI.method: The authors establish a separability rigidity theorem for finite-mode Gaussian states ρ_G relative to a fixed mode partition I: if 0 ≠ T ≼ ρ_G with T separable across I (T arbitrary, not necessarily Gaussian), then ρ_G is separable across I. They then derive corollaries on convex mixing among finitely many separability partitions, full inseparability versus genuine multipartite entanglement, and non-activation of genuine multipartite entanglement under identical copies. A counterexample constructs a fully separable Gaussian state dominating a positive multiple of a genuine multipartite entangled state.
AI.result: Gaussian states dominated by a separable operator (across a fixed partition) are themselves separable across that partition. Convex classes generated by finitely many separability partitions add no new Gaussian states: any such Gaussian state is already separable across one fixed partition. Full inseparability and genuine multipartite entanglement coincide for finite-mode Gaussian states, and identical copies of a biseparable Gaussian state cannot activate genuine multipartite entanglement. The forward implication is shown to be non-reversible.
AI.conclusion: Separability of Gaussian states exhibits a rigidity that sharply constrains mixed-state entanglement structure: weak, possibly non-Gaussian separable sub-states fully determine separability of the Gaussian host, ruling out convex-mixing-based entanglement activation and equating two key notions of multipartite entanglement in the finite-mode Gaussian setting.

title: Dynamical resource theory of time-reversal symmetry breaking
comment: 24 pages, 5 figures, 1 table. Comments are welcome
summary: Time-reversal symmetry and its violation (T-violation) are fundamental across diverse physics domains, from particle physics to fluctuation theorems and reciprocity. While time-reversal symmetry for isolated systems is simply determined by the Hamiltonian, quantifying the magnitude of T-violation, especially in noisy quantum processes, has been a subject of ongoing debate. Here, we propose an operationally meaningful framework to quantify the intrinsic T-violation of quantum channels. We integrate operationally defined time-reversal transformations into dynamical resource theory to formulate T-violation as a resource. T-violation decomposes into two distinct components: kinematic T-violation originating from antiunitary motion-reversal, and nonunitality driven purely by thermodynamics. This decomposition resolves the longstanding confusion between broken time-reversal symmetry and non-invertibility. Finally, we analyze the resulting resource theory of kinematic T-violation, showing that it is neither quality-like nor quantity-like, and proving the existence of a universal golden unit even within classical channels.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an operationally meaningful framework quantifying the intrinsic time-reversal violation (T-violation) of quantum channels by integrating time-reversal transformations into dynamical resource theory, decomposing T-violation into kinematic and nonunitality components.
AI.motivation: Time-reversal symmetry and its violation are fundamental across physics, but quantifying the magnitude of T-violation, particularly in noisy quantum processes, has been a subject of ongoing debate. Existing approaches lack an operationally meaningful measure, and there is longstanding confusion between broken time-reversal symmetry and non-invertibility.
AI.method: The authors integrate operationally defined time-reversal transformations into dynamical resource theory, formulating T-violation as a resource. They decompose T-violation into two components: kinematic T-violation (from antiunitary motion-reversal) and nonunitality (driven purely by thermodynamics). They then analyze the resulting resource theory of kinematic T-violation.
AI.result: T-violation decomposes into kinematic T-violation and nonunitality, resolving the confusion between broken time-reversal symmetry and non-invertibility. The resource theory of kinematic T-violation is shown to be neither quality-like nor quantity-like, and a universal golden unit is proven to exist even within classical channels.
AI.conclusion: The proposed operational framework provides a principled quantification of intrinsic T-violation in quantum channels, with a clean decomposition that disentangles kinematic effects from thermodynamic nonunitality, and establishes structural properties of the associated resource theory including a universal golden unit.

title: Transverse momentum as the counter-diabatic generator in bent waveguide couplers
summary: Bending the axis of a mode-evolution coupler suppresses the nonadiabatic coupling between its supermodes, and bent couplers of this kind were recently shown to realize the counter-diabatic (CD) protocol. Here we identify the operator responsible. Rigid lateral displacement of a waveguide structure is generated by the transverse momentum $\hat p_x$, whose diagonal matrix elements vanish in a real supermode basis and whose off-diagonal element is purely imaginary; in a two-mode system such an operator is proportional to $\sy$. The CD term of a two-waveguide coupler is itself proportional to $\sy$, while the detuning and the coupling, the two parameters set by the waveguide widths and spacing, lie in the $σ_z$--$σ_x$ plane and cannot produce it. The transverse momentum is therefore the CD generator of the bent coupler, by necessity rather than by design. Equating the term it supplies to the nonadiabatic coupling gives the axis slope in closed form as a ratio of two matrix elements of the unperturbed supermodes at a single cross section, which a commutator identity recasts in coupled-mode variables as $\dot{\xo}=\dotθ/(γ\dbeta^{2})$. The expression agrees with the numerical offset search to $0.3\%$ and requires no search. Beam propagation simulations confirm the design and compare it, for the first time, with the CD protocol realized by unitary transformation in a straight coupler built from the same reference structure. The two devices reach $0.994$ and $1.000$ supermode fidelity where the untreated coupler reaches $0.886$, and agree in bandwidth and fabrication tolerance, while their internal trajectories differ by exactly the frame transformation that relates them.

AI.tldr: The transverse momentum operator is identified as the counter-diabatic generator of bent mode-evolution couplers, yielding a closed-form axis slope and high-fidelity supermode transfer.
AI.motivation: Bending a mode-evolution coupler's axis suppresses nonadiabatic coupling between supermodes and was recently shown to realize the counter-diabatic (CD) protocol, but the underlying operator responsible for this effect remained unidentified.
AI.method: The authors analyze the bent waveguide structure via rigid lateral displacement generated by transverse momentum $\hat p_x$, whose diagonal matrix elements vanish in the real supermode basis and which is proportional to $\sigma_y$ in a two-mode system. They equate the operator's contribution to the nonadiabatic coupling to derive the axis slope in closed form as a ratio of unperturbed supermode matrix elements, recast via a commutator identity into coupled-mode variables as $\dot{x}=\dot\theta/(\gamma\Delta\beta^2)$. Beam propagation simulations validate the design against a straight-coupler implementation of the CD protocol via unitary transformation.
AI.result: The closed-form slope expression agrees with numerical offset search to 0.3% without requiring any search. Beam propagation simulations confirm the design: the bent coupler and the unitary-transformation straight coupler reach 0.994 and 1.000 supermode fidelity respectively, versus 0.886 for the untreated coupler, with matching bandwidth and fabrication tolerance; internal trajectories differ by exactly the frame transformation relating the two.
AI.conclusion: The transverse momentum is the CD generator of the bent coupler by necessity rather than design, providing a search-free closed-form design rule and establishing equivalence (up to a frame transformation) with the unitary-transformation CD protocol.

title: Degree Balance as a Fine-Grained Complexity Boundary for Quantum SAT
summary:
The local Hamiltonian problem is the canonical $\mathsf{QMA}$-complete problem, and $O(2^n)$ time classical algorithms and $O(2^{n/2})$ time quantum algorithms are known to solve the problem in the worst case. It is not clear how to improve these brute force strategies for a broad class of the problem because ground states are highly entangled in general, and we cannot directly apply known strategies for classical CSPs.
  In this work, we present exponentially faster classical and quantum algorithms under two mild assumptions: (1) the Hamiltonian is frustration-free on YES instances, and (2) it is approximately regular, meaning that every qubit is acted upon by approximately the same number of constraints.
  We complement these upper bounds by showing that, assuming (Q)SETH, quantum 5-SAT admits no non-trivial worst-case speedup. Our lower bound further demonstrates that the dependence of our algorithms on regularity is in some sense nearly optimal. Specifically, quantum 5-SAT remains (Q)SETH-hard even for Hamiltonians in which all but $O(\sqrt{n})$ qubits participate in only constantly many constraints, while the remaining $O(\sqrt{n})$ qubits each participate in $O(\sqrt{n})$ constraints. By contrast, if either the size of this high-degree subset or the degrees of its qubits is reduced by a factor of $n^δ$, for any $δ>0$, our algorithm solves the problem in time $O(2^{(1- \varepsilon)n})$ for some $\varepsilon>0$.
  Together, our upper and lower bounds establish a fine-grained complexity dichotomy for quantum satisfiability.

AI.tldr: This work gives exponentially faster classical and quantum algorithms for the local Hamiltonian problem under frustration-freeness and approximate regularity, and proves matching (Q)SETH-based lower bounds that establish a fine-grained complexity dichotomy for quantum satisfiability.
AI.motivation: The local Hamiltonian problem is QMA-complete, and the best known worst-case algorithms are brute-force: O(2^n) classical and O(2^{n/2}) quantum. These brute-force strategies are hard to improve broadly because ground states are highly entangled and classical CSP techniques do not directly apply. The authors seek conditions under which exponential speedups are possible.
AI.method: The authors design classical and quantum algorithms exploiting two assumptions: (1) frustration-freeness on YES instances, and (2) approximate regularity, where every qubit is acted on by roughly the same number of constraints. They complement these algorithms with (Q)SETH-based lower bounds for quantum 5-SAT, analyzing Hamiltonians with a small high-degree subset of qubits.
AI.result: Under the two assumptions, they obtain exponentially faster classical and quantum algorithms. They also show that, assuming (Q)SETH, quantum 5-SAT admits no non-trivial worst-case speedup: it remains (Q)SETH-hard even when all but O(√n) qubits have constant degree while the remaining O(√n) qubits each have O(√n) degree. If either the high-degree subset size or its qubits' degrees is reduced by a factor n^δ (δ>0), the algorithm runs in O(2^{(1-ε)n}) for some ε>0.
AI.conclusion: The upper and lower bounds together yield a fine-grained complexity dichotomy for quantum satisfiability, and show the regularity dependence of the algorithms is nearly optimal.

title: Quantum Computing for Network Security Classification: Near-Term Classification and Long-Term Memory Efficiency
summary: Quantum computing has already been explored in several network-security applications. However, how quantum computing may contribute to network-security classification in both the near term and the longer term has not been systematically discussed. This paper studies this question through two complementary experiments. First, we evaluate near-term quantum-kernel support vector machines (SVMs) on practical network-security classification tasks and compare them with classical SVM baselines on KDD Cup 1999, CICIDS2017, and BoT-IoT. Across these runs, quantum kernels are competitive. They can match or improve classical baselines in some settings, while classical RBF kernels remain stronger in others. This suggests that near-term quantum-kernel methods should be evaluated as practical, dataset-dependent alternatives to classical kernels rather than as uniformly superior replacements. Second, we use quantum oracle sketching (QOS) to study a longer-term memory advantage for classification with streaming classical samples. In QOS, samples are processed online and used to incrementally construct an approximate quantum oracle, which provides coherent query access for downstream quantum algorithms without retaining the entire dataset. Under the QOS-inspired machine-size estimate, comparable accuracy corresponds to a substantially smaller effective memory-size proxy than explicit sparse/QRAM-style storage. Compared with a simple streaming proxy, the result is more nuanced because aggressive feature filtering can make the streaming dimension small. This suggests that the long-term value of quantum computing for network-security classification may lie in memory-efficient data access rather than immediate runtime speedup. Together, these experiments show how quantum computing may contribute to network-security classification from near-term classification performance and longer-term memory efficiency.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how quantum computing can contribute to network-security classification through two experiments: (1) near-term quantum-kernel SVMs compared to classical SVM baselines on three datasets, and (2) a longer-term quantum oracle sketching (QOS) approach for memory-efficient streaming classification.
AI.motivation: Quantum computing has been explored in network security, but its role in network-security classification across near-term and long-term horizons has not been systematically discussed. The paper aims to clarify whether and how quantum methods offer practical advantages.
AI.method: Two complementary experiments: (1) evaluating near-term quantum-kernel support vector machines (SVMs) on practical network-security classification tasks and comparing them with classical SVM baselines on KDD Cup 1999, CICIDS2017, and BoT-IoT; (2) using quantum oracle sketching (QOS) to study a longer-term memory advantage, where streaming classical samples are processed online to incrementally construct an approximate quantum oracle providing coherent query access without retaining the entire dataset.
AI.result: Quantum kernels are competitive: they can match or improve classical baselines in some settings, while classical RBF kernels remain stronger in others. Under the QOS-inspired machine-size estimate, comparable accuracy corresponds to a substantially smaller effective memory-size proxy than explicit sparse/QRAM-style storage; however, compared with a simple streaming proxy, the result is more nuanced because aggressive feature filtering can make the streaming dimension small.
AI.conclusion: Near-term quantum-kernel methods should be evaluated as practical, dataset-dependent alternatives to classical kernels rather than uniformly superior replacements. The long-term value of quantum computing for network-security classification may lie in memory-efficient data access rather than immediate runtime speedup.

title: Improved Quantum Algorithms for Black-Box Abelian Group Decomposition
summary:
Decomposing finite Abelian black-box groups into cyclic factors is a basic problem in quantum computation. We give a quantum algorithm for decomposing finite Abelian black-box groups by adapting the quantum sampling and classical lattice-reduction method of Regev's factoring algorithm. The algorithm computes an invariant-factor decomposition and corresponding cyclic generators with high probability. For a group G of order at most 2^n with unique encodings and reversible group-operation cost T_op = Omega(sqrt(n)), our algorithm uses O(sqrt(n)) quantum circuits, each with O~(n T_op) gates and executed at most O(n) times.
  For comparison, we consider the Cheung-Mosca algorithm, which decomposes the Sylow p-subgroups separately. We also consider the common-modulus implementation of the extended Cheung-Mosca algorithm. Our algorithm reduces the sum of the circuit gate counts from O~(n^2 T_op) to O~(n^(3/2) T_op). The total quantum time bound decreases from O~(n^3 T_op) to O~(n^(5/2) T_op), and the quantum space bound decreases from O(n^2) to O(n) qubits. The classical computation uses polynomially many bit operations and group-operation queries.
  These improvements rely on two technical ingredients. We prove that the integer relation lattices used in our algorithm admit, with high probability, integral bases whose vectors have Euclidean norm at most exp(O(sqrt(n))). We preserve the circuit-size advantage of Regev's algorithm for group decomposition by incorporating all O(n) sampled generators while keeping the lattice-reduction dimension at O(sqrt(n)).

AI.tldr: A quantum algorithm decomposes finite Abelian black-box groups into invariant factors by adapting Regev's sampling and lattice-reduction method, achieving reduced circuit gate counts, quantum time, and space versus Cheung-Mosca algorithms.
AI.motivation: Decomposing finite Abelian black-box groups into cyclic factors is a fundamental problem in quantum computation, motivating more efficient algorithms than existing approaches such as the Cheung-Mosca algorithm.
AI.method: The algorithm adapts the quantum sampling and classical lattice-reduction technique from Regev's factoring algorithm. It computes an invariant-factor decomposition with corresponding cyclic generators, incorporating all O(n) sampled generators while keeping the lattice-reduction dimension at O(sqrt(n)). It also proves that the integer relation lattices admit integral bases with vectors of Euclidean norm at most exp(O(sqrt(n))) with high probability.
AI.result: For a group of order at most 2^n with unique encodings and reversible operation cost T_op = Omega(sqrt(n)), the algorithm uses O(sqrt(n)) quantum circuits, each with O~(n T_op) gates, executed at most O(n) times. Compared to the Cheung-Mosca and extended Cheung-Mosca algorithms, it reduces the sum of circuit gate counts from O~(n^2 T_op) to O~(n^(3/2) T_op), total quantum time from O~(n^3 T_op) to O~(n^(5/2) T_op), and quantum space from O(n^2) to O(n) qubits. Classical computation uses polynomially many bit operations and group-operation queries.
AI.conclusion: The proposed algorithm improves efficiency over prior methods by reducing gate counts, quantum time, and space, while preserving Regev's circuit-size advantage through lattice-basis and dimension control techniques.

title: Affine spin-pencil factorization of generalized driven anisotropic Rabi--Stark Hamiltonians in an inhomogeneous orthosymplectic superalgebra
summary: We construct a supersymmetric factorization for generalized driven anisotropic Rabi--Stark Hamiltonians using an affine factor $\hat{A}=\hat{C}+\hat{a}\hat{D}$ in an inhomogeneous orthosymplectic superalgebra, with two real invertible spin matrices $\hat{C}$ and $\hat{D}$. The six real pencil parameters constrain nine Hamiltonian frequencies and one energy offset up to an overall frequency scale. The normal product $\hat{A}^{\dagger}\hat{A}$ has an exact zero-energy ground doublet and, with its antinormal partner $\hat{A}\hat{A}^{\dagger}$, gives a Witten index of two. For distinct pencil roots with finite baseline slopes, coherent gauges define a Bargmann hierarchy and endpoint conditions for exceptional finite-polynomial states. The spin grading organizes four limiting cases, comprising two driven-oscillator families with every baseline exact and the constrained anisotropic-Rabi and Rabi--Stark sheets, which meet at the degenerate-qubit isotropic Rabi model. An aligned interior example adds direct and longitudinal drives, Stark deformation, and intensity-dependent coupling while retaining the factorization.

AI.tldr: The paper builds a supersymmetric factorization of generalized driven anisotropic Rabi–Stark Hamiltonians via an affine supercharge in an inhomogeneous orthosymplectic superalgebra, yielding an exact zero-energy ground doublet, Witten index two, and a classification of limiting cases.
AI.motivation: Generalized driven anisotropic Rabi–Stark models are physically relevant but lack a unified algebraic treatment; the authors seek a supersymmetric (SUSY) factorization framework that organizes their spectra, ground states, and limiting cases systematically.
AI.method: An affine factorization operator A = C + aD with two real invertible spin matrices C, D is introduced in an inhomogeneous orthosymplectic superalgebra. Six real pencil parameters fix nine Hamiltonian frequencies and one energy offset up to an overall frequency scale. Normal and antinormal products (A†A, AA†) define the SUSY partner Hamiltonians, and coherent gauges yield a Bargmann hierarchy with endpoint conditions for exceptional finite-polynomial states.
AI.result: A†A possesses an exact zero-energy ground doublet, and together with AA† gives a Witten index of two. For distinct pencil roots with finite baseline slopes, the Bargmann hierarchy and endpoint conditions characterize the exceptional finite-polynomial states. Spin grading organizes four limiting cases: two driven-oscillator families with exact baselines and the constrained anisotropic-Rabi and Rabi–Stark sheets, all intersecting at the degenerate-qubit isotropic Rabi model. An aligned interior example retains the factorization while adding direct and longitudinal drives, Stark deformation, and intensity-dependent coupling.
AI.conclusion: The affine orthosymplectic SUSY factorization provides a unified description of generalized driven anisotropic Rabi–Stark Hamiltonians, tying ground-state degeneracy, Witten index, exceptional states, and limiting-case structure to a small set of pencil parameters.

title: Exponential Advantage of Quantum over Classical References in Leakage Detection
summary: Leakage from a known encoding subspace can be detected by projection. However, the corresponding projector is unavailable when the encoding subspace is not classically specified. Here we show how independent quantum references prepared by the same encoder enable leakage detection without a classical description of the encoding. A coherent measurement on the references and a single message leaves every state within the two-dimensional encoding subspace, including its entanglement with a remote system, exactly unchanged. We derive the exact detection law for $M$ ideal references and prove optimality among tests with zero false alarm for every encoding. For orthogonal leakage, the miss probability is asymptotic to $4/M$, independent of the ambient dimension $d$. Measuring all references first, even collectively, gives zero detection at every finite budget under the same zero-false-alarm requirement. For a fixed detection target between zero and one, the optimal measurement-first cost is $Θ(d/ε)$ at sufficiently small tolerance $ε$ on normal false alarm and conditional disturbance; a dimension-independent coherent budget suffices. For one logical qubit encoded in three physical qubits, seven coherent references achieve at least $50\%$ orthogonal-leakage detection, whereas any measurement-first receiver needs at least $588$ under the same $1\%$ normal tolerances. Quantum references thus support leakage checks without classical reconstruction, with a sample advantage exponential in the number of physical qubits.

AI.tldr: Independent quantum references from the same encoder enable leakage detection from a quantum encoding without a classical description, achieving an exponential-in-physical-qubits sample advantage over measurement-first strategies.
AI.motivation: Leakage from a known encoding subspace is detectable by projection, but the required projector is unavailable when the encoding subspace is not classically specified. Classical reconstruction of the encoding is a costly alternative that this work aims to circumvent.
AI.method: The authors use independent quantum references prepared by the same encoder and a coherent measurement jointly over the references and a single message, designed to leave every state in the two-dimensional encoding subspace—including entanglement with a remote system—exactly unchanged. They derive the exact detection law for M ideal references and prove optimality among tests with zero false alarm for every encoding, then compare against measurement-first protocols.
AI.result: For orthogonal leakage the miss probability is asymptotically 4/M, independent of ambient dimension d. Measuring all references first, even collectively, gives zero detection at every finite budget under zero false alarm. For a fixed detection target in (0,1), the optimal measurement-first cost is Θ(d/ε) at small tolerance ε, while a dimension-independent coherent budget suffices. For one logical qubit in three physical qubits, seven coherent references reach ≥50% orthogonal-leakage detection, versus at least 588 measurement-first references at 1% normal tolerances.
AI.conclusion: Quantum references support leakage checks without classical reconstruction, providing a sample advantage exponential in the number of physical qubits.

title: Factorization dynamics between quantum Fisher information and quantum coherence
summary: Quantum Fisher information (QFI) quantifies the sensitivity of a quantum state to a parameter change and plays a key role in quantum metrology. Meanwhile, quantum coherence is a crucial resource for quantum information processing. However, despite extensive studies on various aspects of quantum metrology, the interplay between the dynamics of the QFI and quantum coherence remains unexplored. Here, we explore the factorization relationship between the QFI and quantum coherence, both theoretically and experimentally. We prepare pure states in qubit and qutrit systems and apply unitary evolution to investigate this relationship. Our results confirm the factorization law, offering strong evidence for this relationship. Furthermore, we establish a lower bound on the variance of the estimated parameter that does not require the final state information. This approach reveals a deep connection between the QFI and quantum coherence, providing insights into quantum parameter estimation. These findings have potential applications in quantum sensing and quantum metrology.

AI.tldr: This work theoretically and experimentally investigates the factorization relationship between quantum Fisher information (QFI) and quantum coherence under unitary evolution, confirming a factorization law in qubit and qutrit systems and deriving a final-state-independent lower bound on the estimated parameter variance.
AI.motivation: QFI quantifies a quantum state's sensitivity to parameter changes and is central to quantum metrology, while quantum coherence is a key resource for quantum information processing. Despite extensive work on quantum metrology, the interplay between QFI dynamics and quantum coherence had remained unexplored.
AI.method: Pure states were prepared in qubit and qutrit systems and subjected to unitary evolution to study the QFI–coherence relationship, combining theoretical derivation with experiment.
AI.result: The experiments confirm the factorization law, providing strong evidence for the QFI–coherence relationship. A lower bound on the variance of the estimated parameter is established that does not require final state information.
AI.conclusion: The results reveal a deep connection between QFI and quantum coherence, offering insights into quantum parameter estimation with potential applications in quantum sensing and quantum metrology.

title: Shared Phase Arithmetic for Parallel Quantum Rotations
summary: A layer of diagonal quantum gates can be specified by an integer-valued function on computational basis states. This description suggests implementing the layer by evaluating that function reversibly and translating its value into a phase using a shared quantum register. We develop this viewpoint for parallel phase kickback (PPK): the weighted sum of several rotation parameters is computed coherently, added once to a phase-gradient state, and then uncomputed. The construction separates the cost of representing a phase function from the cost of applying it. We prove correctness, give explicit error bounds, and analyze logical gate counts for general weights, pairs of rotations, and weights with disjoint binary support. With Clifford-only encoding, a batch uses at most $4(b-1)$ T gates at $b$-bit phase resolution, excluding initialization. The first phase reference is prepared with independent rotations synthesized by Gridsynth; additional phase-gradient states then follow from the disjoint-support construction with $O(b)$ T gates each. The resulting bounds identify when shared phase arithmetic reduces amortized rotation cost and when encoding overhead limits that advantage.

AI.tldr: Diagonal quantum gates can be implemented via a reversible integer-valued phase function; the authors formalize "parallel phase kickback" (PPK), which coherently sums rotation weights, adds them once to a phase-gradient state, then uncomputes, separating encoding cost from application cost and yielding explicit T-count bounds.
AI.motivation: A layer of diagonal quantum gates is characterized by an integer-valued function on computational basis states, which naturally suggests a reversible evaluation-plus-phase-translation implementation using a shared quantum register. The paper aims to exploit this structure to amortize the cost of applying many rotation parameters.
AI.method: The PPK construction computes the weighted sum of several rotation parameters coherently, adds it once to a phase-gradient state, and then uncomputes. Correctness proofs and explicit error bounds are provided, with logical gate-count analysis for general weights, pairs of rotations, and weights with disjoint binary support. Phase references use Clifford-only encoding, with the first reference synthesized via Gridsynth and subsequent phase-gradient states produced by the disjoint-support construction.
AI.result: A batch uses at most 4(b-1) T gates at b-bit phase resolution (excluding initialization) under Clifford-only encoding. Additional phase-gradient states each cost O(b) T gates via the disjoint-support construction.
AI.conclusion: The derived bounds delineate when shared phase arithmetic reduces amortized rotation cost and when encoding overhead negates that advantage.

title: Root-system structure of sloppiness in passive Gaussian metrology
summary: Passive transformations of an $n$-mode squeezed probe become locally unidentifiable when the quantum Fisher matrix loses rank. For pure zero-mean Gaussian probes, we show that the $C_{n}$ restricted-root system of $\mathrm{Sp}(2n,\mathbb{R})/\mathrm{U}(n)$ governs this exact sloppiness. For squeezing magnitudes $r_{1},\ldots,r_{n}$ in the canonical basis, the roots $2r_{j}$ and $r_{j}\pm r_{k}$ label the local phase rotations and two beam-splitter quadratures, and their vanishing identifies every Fisher-null direction. The associated Fisher weights quantify the approach to each singular wall. At fixed positive mean photon number, we solve the E-optimal probe-design problem of maximizing the smallest passive Fisher eigenvalue in two explicit generator normalizations. In the canonical phase and beam-splitter angle convention, the unique optimum in the fundamental Weyl chamber is an arithmetic progression approaching the consecutive-odd-integer dual-Weyl direction at large resource. With an invariant generator norm, the smallest eigenvalue is independent of the passive frame and the optimum lies exactly on that ray at every resource. Uniform squeezing instead minimizes the local-phase A-optimal cost while leaving one beam-splitter quadrature unidentifiable for every mode pair. Finally, the two quadratures of each identifiable mode pair saturate the quantum-geometric incompatibility bound, and the largest compatible passive submodel has $n(n+1)/2$ parameters at a regular spectrum. The resulting classification separates local identifiability, sensitivity optimization, and simultaneous attainability.

AI.tldr: The paper links the loss of local identifiability of passive transformations on an n-mode squeezed Gaussian probe to the C_n restricted-root system of Sp(2n,R)/U(n): vanishing roots 2r_j and r_j±r_k exactly characterize Fisher-null directions. It then solves E-optimal and A-optimal passive probe-design problems at fixed mean photon number, showing the unique E-optimum is an arithmetic progression approaching the dual-Weyl ray (exactly on it under invariant generator norm), while uniform squeezing minimizes the local-phase A-optimal cost but leaves one beam-splitter quadrature unidentifiable per mode pair.
AI.motivation: Estimating passive (photon-number-conserving) transformations with squeezed Gaussian probes is fundamental to quantum metrology, yet local identifiability of such parameters can fail when the quantum Fisher matrix becomes rank-deficient. The paper aims to explain this "sloppiness" geometrically and to determine optimal squeezing resources that maximize the smallest estimable (passive Fisher) eigenvalue at fixed mean photon number.
AI.method: Restrict to pure zero-mean Gaussian probes and use the symmetric space Sp(2n,R)/U(n) with its C_n restricted-root system. Formulate and solve the E-optimal design (maximize smallest passive Fisher eigenvalue) in two generator normalizations (canonical phase/beam-splitter angle convention and invariant generator norm), and analyze the A-optimal cost for local phases.

In canonical normalization, the unique E-optimum in the fundamental Weyl chamber is an arithmetic progression of squeezing magnitudes approaching the consecutive-odd-integer dual-Weyl direction at large resource. Under the invariant generator norm, the smallest eigenvalue is frame-independent and the optimum lies exactly on that dual-Weyl ray at all resource levels. Uniform squeezing minimizes the local-phase A-optimal cost but leaves one beam-splitter quadrature unidentifiable for each mode pair. Each identifiable mode pair's two quadratures saturate the quantum-geometric incompatibility bound, and the largest compatible passive submodel has n(n+1)/2 parameters at a regular spectrum.
AI.conclusion: The C_n root-system framework gives a clean classification that separates local identifiability, sensitivity optimization, and simultaneous attainability for passive transformations probed by n-mode squeezed Gaussian states, with explicit optimal squeezing spectra (arithmetic progression / dual-Weyl ray) and quantified identifiability limits.

title: Synchronized Quantum Devices in Lossy Channels
summary: Due to their tight temporal coupling, entangled photon pairs produced by spontaneous parametric down-conversion offer a new route to improved network synchronization among quantum-enabled devices. In the emerging space-based quantum internet, such synchronization will be pivotal to operational success. Here, we propose and experimentally demonstrate a new polarization-assisted protocol that allows quantum-enabled devices to remain synchronized under the high loss conditions anticipated for satellite-to-ground quantum channels. Our experimental results show that polarization assistance extends reliable synchronization acquisition to higher channel losses and an increase of up to 40$\%$ in satellite-to-ground distance. Supporting Monte Carlo simulations show that this performance improvement extends over a wide range of photon-starved conditions. Collectively, these results not only provide a proof of concept for polarization-assisted network synchronization but also demonstrate its pragmatic importance in significantly extending the range under which quantum-enabled devices forming the backbone of the quantum internet can remain highly synchronized.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes and experimentally demonstrates a polarization-assisted synchronization protocol for entangled-photon-pair-based quantum networks, extending reliable synchronization acquisition to higher channel losses and increasing satellite-to-ground distance by up to 40%.
AI.motivation: Entangled photon pairs from spontaneous parametric down-conversion enable improved network synchronization among quantum-enabled devices due to their tight temporal coupling. In space-based quantum internet scenarios, synchronization is pivotal, but high-loss satellite-to-ground channels degrade reliable synchronization—motivating a loss-tolerant approach.
AI.method: A new polarization-assisted protocol is proposed and experimentally demonstrated. Polarization information is exploited alongside temporal correlations to maintain synchronization under high-loss conditions. Monte Carlo simulations are performed to assess performance across photon-starved regimes.
AI.result: Polarization assistance extends reliable synchronization acquisition to higher channel losses and yields up to a 40% increase in satellite-to-ground distance. Simulations confirm the improvement generalizes over a wide range of photon-starved conditions.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a proof of concept for polarization-assisted network synchronization and demonstrates its practical importance in significantly extending the range over which quantum-enabled devices forming the quantum internet backbone can remain highly synchronized.

title: Optimized Randomized Hamiltonian Simulation via Average-Error Analysis
summary: Hamiltonian simulation is a central application of quantum computing. Randomized Hamiltonian simulation approximates the target dynamics by sampling quantum circuits and often allows simpler circuit implementations. We develop a framework for randomized Hamiltonian simulation in which Hamiltonian terms are sampled with arbitrary probabilities and the corresponding short-time evolutions are implemented sequentially. The leading channel error relative to ideal time evolution is governed by the variance of the sampled generators. Minimizing the variance-based upper bound on the worst-case error recovers qDRIFT, a leading randomized Hamiltonian simulation algorithm that samples terms in proportion to their operator norms. For typical input states, however, this sampling distribution need not be optimal. Minimizing Haar-averaged error bounds instead yields sampling probabilities proportional to the Hilbert-Schmidt norms of the terms. This choice can provide smaller average-error bounds than conventional qDRIFT. For Hamiltonians expressed as sums of Pauli strings, we combine this framework with commuting Pauli grouping to obtain smaller error bounds than conventional qDRIFT at fixed $R_z$ depth. Numerical benchmarks for the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev model show error-bound improvement factors consistent with linear scaling in the number of qubits. For the 108-qubit FeMoco Hamiltonian, the error bounds are reduced by a factor of about 5.65. These results establish average-error optimization as a practical design principle for randomized Hamiltonian simulation.

AI.tldr: A framework for randomized Hamiltonian simulation samples terms with arbitrary probabilities; minimizing worst-case error recovers qDRIFT, while minimizing Haar-averaged error yields Hilbert-Schmidt-norm sampling that improves error bounds in Pauli and molecular benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Randomized Hamiltonian simulation enables simpler circuits, and qDRIFT is a leading method but its norm-proportional sampling is optimized for worst-case error, which need not be optimal for typical input states. The paper seeks a principled framework to optimize sampling distributions for average-case error and improve practical performance.
AI.method: The authors formulate randomized Hamiltonian simulation where Hamiltonian terms are sampled with arbitrary probabilities and their short-time evolutions are applied sequentially. The leading channel error versus ideal evolution is characterized by the variance of sampled generators. They minimize worst-case variance bounds to recover qDRIFT, and minimize Haar-averaged error bounds to derive probabilities proportional to Hilbert-Schmidt norms. For Pauli-string Hamiltonians, they combine this with commuting Pauli grouping.
AI.result: Hilbert-Schmidt-norm sampling yields smaller average-error bounds than conventional qDRIFT, and with commuting Pauli grouping gives smaller bounds at fixed Rz depth. Numerical benchmarks: error-bound improvements consistent with linear scaling in qubit number for the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev model, and a factor of about 5.65 reduction for the 108-qubit FeMoco Hamiltonian.
AI.conclusion: Average-error optimization is established as a practical design principle for randomized Hamiltonian simulation, generalizing qDRIFT and delivering meaningful error-bound reductions in realistic benchmarks.

title: Quantum Fidelity Landscape-Guided Prior Calibration for Single-Circuit QGAN Image Generation
summary: Quantum Generative Adversarial Networks (QGANs) have emerged as representative generative models in the Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) era and have attracted increasing attention in quantum machine learning. However, most existing QGAN methods rely on patch-based decomposition strategies, which weaken the global consistency of generated images and increase quantum resource overhead. In this work, we investigate a simpler approach: pixel-level, end-to-end image generation using a single-quantum-circuit QGAN. By analyzing the structural matching relationship between the quantum prior and the target data distribution in Hilbert space, we provide a new theoretical perspective for understanding the training behavior of naive end-to-end QGANs. Specifically, we introduce the Quantum Fidelity Landscape (QFL), defined as the pairwise-fidelity structure induced by an ensemble of quantum states and preserved under shared unitary transformations of the quantum generation process. We show that, under a fixed Lipschitz readout, this invariant imposes a one-sided bound on decoded sample separation, motivating calibration of the prior-induced QFL before adversarial training. To validate this theoretical insight, we propose BasicQGAN, a QGAN framework incorporating quantum prior calibration. Before adversarial optimization, BasicQGAN aligns the prior-induced QFL with the data-induced QFL. Experimental results on small-scale grayscale image datasets show that BasicQGAN achieves stable and effective end-to-end pixel-level image generation while requiring fewer qubits and trainable parameters than representative patch-based quantum generators. Furthermore, experiments with different initial quantum-state ensembles show that QFL-calibrated ensembles achieve better generative performance.

The authors seek a simpler end-to-end, pixel-level approach but note that naive end-to-end QGANs exhibit unclear training behavior, motivating a theoretical understanding of the structural matching between quantum prior and target data distribution in Hilbert space.

They show that, under a fixed Lipschitz readout, this invariant imposes a one-sided bound on decoded sample separation, motivating calibration of the prior-induced QFL before adversarial training. They then propose BasicQGAN, a QGAN framework that aligns the prior-induced QFL with the data-induced QFL before adversarial optimization.
