Additionally, experiments with different initial quantum-state ensembles show that QFL-calibrated ensembles achieve better generative performance.
AI.conclusion: The QFL framework offers a new theoretical perspective for understanding naive end-to-end QGAN training, and prior calibration via QFL alignment enables simpler, resource-efficient, and stable pixel-level quantum image generation, validating the theoretical insight empirically.

title: A Divide-and-Conquer Quantum-Selected Configuration Interaction for Evaluating $π$-$π$ Stacking Interaction Energies in the Benzene Dimer
summary: Accurate evaluation of $π$--$π$ stacking interactions requires a description of electron correlation on a small energy scale. Direct variational quantum calculations of the benzene dimer with CAS(28e,20o) require 40 qubits and deep circuits. Here, we propose Divide-and-Conquer Quantum-Selected Configuration Interaction (Deep QSCI), combining the divide-and-conquer idea of Deep VQE with QSCI, and apply it to the sandwich benzene dimer. We perform QSCI for one monomer and construct a reduced local basis by applying particle-number-conserving one-electron excitations to its ground state. Using this basis and the intermonomer interaction Hamiltonian, we build and diagonalize an effective Hamiltonian of the dimer. Since the monomers have the same structure, the QSCI result is reused for both monomers and across intermolecular distances, reducing the required quantum register from 40 to 20 qubits for the monomer CAS(14e,10o). With 6-31G**, the model gives an attractive minimum of -0.91 kcal/mol at 4.0 $Å$, compared with the counterpoise-corrected CCSD(T) value of -1.14 kcal/mol. With cc-pVDZ, a large cancellation appears between the product-state interaction energy and the energy lowering by diagonalization. This may reflect insufficient consistency of the active orbitals and reduced local bases between monomers. Orbital consistency, reduced-space convergence across basis sets, and charge transfer remain key issues for quantitative accuracy. Deep QSCI thus provides a resource-efficient approach to constructing model interaction curves without repeating monomer quantum calculations at each separation.

AI.tldr: Deep QSCI combines the divide-and-conquer idea of Deep VQE with quantum-selected configuration interaction to compute the sandwich benzene dimer interaction curve, reusing a single monomer QSCI result across both monomers and all separations, cutting the quantum register from 40 to 20 qubits.
AI.motivation: Accurate description of pi-pi stacking requires capturing electron correlation on a small energy scale. A direct variational quantum treatment of the benzene dimer at CAS(28e,20o) demands 40 qubits and deep circuits, which is resource-intensive and must normally be repeated at every intermolecular separation.
AI.method: Divide-and-Conquer Quantum-Selected Configuration Interaction (Deep QSCI) merges Deep VQE's divide-and-conquer strategy with QSCI. QSCI is run on a single monomer CAS(14e,10o), and a reduced local basis is built by applying particle-number-conserving one-electron excitations to its ground state. This basis, together with the intermonomer interaction Hamiltonian, defines an effective dimer Hamiltonian that is constructed and diagonalized. Because both monomers are structurally identical, the monomer QSCI result is reused for both fragments and across all intermolecular distances.
AI.result: Using 6-31G**, the model yields an attractive minimum of -0.91 kcal/mol at 4.0 Å, versus a counterpoise-corrected CCSD(T) reference of -1.14 kcal/mol. With cc-pVDZ, large cancellation occurs between the product-state interaction energy and the diagonalization energy lowering, likely indicating insufficient consistency of active orbitals and reduced local bases between monomers.
AI.conclusion: Deep QSCI offers a resource-efficient route to model interaction curves without repeating monomer quantum calculations at each separation. Orbital consistency, reduced-space convergence across basis sets, and charge transfer remain key open issues for achieving quantitative accuracy.

title: Block-Wise Variational Quantum Algorithms for PDEs with Interface Penalty Constraints
summary:
Global variational quantum algorithm (VQA) frameworks for solving partial differential equations (PDEs) often rely on a single expressive ansatz over a uniform grid, which becomes structurally inefficient when solutions exhibit spatially heterogeneous complexity such as localized singularities or thin boundary layers. A localized nonsmooth feature can degrade the convergence of the entire global quantum representation, imposing unnecessary circuit depth and amplifying the risk of vanishing gradients in barren plateaus.
  To overcome this limitation, we propose a block-wise VQA framework for PDEs characterized by spatially heterogeneous solution complexity. The computational domain is decomposed into locally represented quantum subproblems, where grid budgets and ansatz families are dynamically assigned based on a computable difficulty indicator. Artificial block interfaces are coupled through unified jump penalties for state values, derivatives, and physical fluxes, while adaptive reblocking tracks moving rough regions to maintain local accuracy without excessive global qubit overhead. The error analysis rigorously separates spatial discretization, ansatz expressivity, optimization convergence, finite-shot sampling noise, transfer errors from reblocking, and interface-coupling contributions. Reproducible residual-based simulations on representative elliptic, advection--diffusion, and Burgers problems demonstrate lower approximation errors and reduced peak local circuit width compared to global VQA approaches. These results substantiate block-wise quantum resource localization, confirming that high-fidelity PDE solutions can be achieved on near-term quantum devices without requiring a single globally expressive ansatz.

AI.tldr: A block-wise VQA framework is proposed for PDEs with spatially heterogeneous solution complexity, decomposing the domain into locally represented quantum subproblems with dynamic grid/ansatz assignment and unified interface penalties, achieving lower errors and reduced circuit width than global VQA.
AI.motivation: Global VQA frameworks for PDEs rely on a single expressive ansatz over a uniform grid, which becomes structurally inefficient when solutions exhibit spatially heterogeneous complexity such as localized singularities or thin boundary layers. A localized nonsmooth feature can degrade convergence of the entire global quantum representation, imposing unnecessary circuit depth and amplifying the risk of vanishing gradients in barren plateaus.

Artificial block interfaces are coupled through unified jump penalties for state values, derivatives, and physical fluxes, while adaptive reblocking tracks moving rough regions to maintain local accuracy without excessive global qubit overhead. The error analysis rigorously separates spatial discretization, ansatz expressivity, optimization convergence, finite-shot sampling noise, transfer errors from reblocking, and interface-coupling contributions.

title: Quantum States and Spectra of Small Cylindrical and Toroidal Lattices
summary: We examine the spectrum and quantum states of small lattices with cylindrical and toroidal topology subject to a scalar gauge potential that introduces a position dependent phase in the inter-site coupling. Equivalency of gauges assumed in infinite lattices is generally lost due to the periodic boundary conditions, and conditions that restore it are identified. We trace the impact of various system parameters including gauge choice, boundary conditions and inter-site coupling strengths, and an additional axial field. We find gauge dependent appearance of avoided crossings and persistent degeneracies, and we show their impact on the associated eigenstates. Smaller lattices develop prominent gaps in spectral lines associated with edge states, which are suppressed in the thermodynamic limit. Toroidal lattices have counterparts of most of the features observed in cylindrical lattices, but notably they display a transition from localization to delocalization determined by the relation between the field parameter and the number of lattice sites.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes the spectrum and quantum states of small cylindrical and toroidal lattices under a scalar gauge potential producing a position-dependent phase in inter-site coupling. Gauge equivalence valid for infinite lattices breaks down under periodic boundary conditions; restoration conditions are identified. Spectral features—avoided crossings, persistent degeneracies, edge-state gaps, and a localization-to-delocalization transition—depend on gauge choice, boundary conditions, coupling strengths, axial field, and lattice size.
AI.motivation: Gauge equivalence is well-established for infinite lattices, but periodic boundary conditions (finite cylindrical/toroidal geometries) can invalidate it. The paper is motivated by the need to determine when gauge equivalence is restored in finite lattices and to understand how gauge choice, boundary conditions, and system parameters affect the spectrum and eigenstates of small lattice systems.
AI.method: The study examines the spectrum and quantum states of small lattices with cylindrical and toroidal topology subject to a scalar gauge potential that introduces a position-dependent phase in the inter-site coupling. It systematically traces the impact of system parameters including gauge choice, boundary conditions, inter-site coupling strengths, and an additional axial field, and identifies conditions restoring gauge equivalence.
AI.result: Gauge-dependent avoided crossings and persistent degeneracies are found, along with their effects on the associated eigenstates. Smaller lattices exhibit prominent gaps in spectral lines associated with edge states, which are suppressed in the thermodynamic limit. Toroidal lattices reproduce most features of cylindrical lattices but additionally show a transition from localization to delocalization governed by the relation between the field parameter and the number of lattice sites.
AI.conclusion: Gauge equivalence assumed for infinite lattices is generally lost under periodic boundary conditions, though conditions restoring it can be identified. Spectral and eigenstate properties depend on gauge choice, boundary conditions, coupling strengths, and axial field, with finite-size effects (edge-state gaps) vanishing in the thermodynamic limit. Notably, toroidal geometry exhibits a field-parameter- and site-number-dependent localization-to-delocalization transition absent in the cylindrical case.

title: Ordering controlled by the measurement-feedback interval in quantum Boltzmann samplers
summary: We show that the measurement--feedback interval alone can induce ordering in a quantum Boltzmann sampler with fixed programmed couplings and a fixed local dissipative rule. At zero environmental dephasing, repeated projective measurements remove transverse coherence regenerated during relaxation, thereby enhancing the local longitudinal response. We derive the exact finite-interval Markov kernel for successive measurement records and obtain the ordering threshold in the Curie--Weiss limit. For couplings below the equilibrium Curie--Weiss threshold, shortening the readout interval drives a continuous transition to an ordered stationary state even though the programmed Boltzmann distribution remains disordered. The stationary response and equation of state map exactly onto those of a continuously interacting model with dephasing, while the linear relaxation rates remain distinct at matched static response. Exact finite-size stationary calculations reveal the transition through bimodal magnetization distributions and mean-field critical scaling.

AI.tldr: Measurement-feedback interval alone can induce ordering in a quantum Boltzmann sampler with fixed couplings and a fixed local dissipative rule; shortening the readout interval drives a continuous transition to an ordered stationary state even when the programmed Boltzmann distribution is disordered.
AI.motivation: The paper investigates whether the measurement-feedback interval, independent of couplings and the dissipative rule, can act as a control knob for ordering in a quantum Boltzmann sampler, and whether measurement-induced ordering can occur where the programmed equilibrium distribution remains disordered.
AI.method: The authors analyze a quantum Boltzmann sampler with fixed programmed couplings and a fixed local dissipative rule at zero environmental dephasing. Repeated projective measurements remove transverse coherence regenerated during relaxation, enhancing the local longitudinal response. They derive the exact finite-interval Markov kernel for successive measurement records and obtain the ordering threshold in the Curie-Weiss limit, supported by exact finite-size stationary calculations.
AI.result: Below the equilibrium Curie-Weiss threshold, shortening the readout interval drives a continuous transition to an ordered stationary state despite the programmed Boltzmann distribution remaining disordered. The stationary response and equation of state map exactly onto those of a continuously interacting model with dephasing, while the linear relaxation rates remain distinct at matched static response. Finite-size calculations reveal the transition via bimodal magnetization distributions and mean-field critical scaling.
AI.conclusion: The measurement-feedback interval is an independent control parameter capable of inducing ordering in a quantum Boltzmann sampler, producing a measurement-induced phase transition whose static properties coincide with a dephased interacting model but whose dynamics (relaxation rates) differ. This demonstrates that non-equilibrium measurement protocols can generate order not present in the programmed equilibrium distribution.

title: Exact Trotterization in the Degenerate Quantum Rabi Model
summary: Digital quantum simulation of the quantum Rabi model in the deep strong coupling regime motivates the need for an exact characterization of Trotterization errors, so far known only through qualitative bounds. Here we derive such a characterization in the exactly solvable degenerate limit, valid for arbitrary coupling strength. The first-order Trotter operator admits a closed expression, showing that the generated phase-space trajectory lies exactly on a circle that is rescaled and rigidly rotated with respect to the exact one, rather than merely approximating it. This geometric renormalization yields a closed form for the state fidelity, structurally identical to the physical survival probability governing revivals in the deep strong coupling regime: both are the same geometric question -- the distinguishability of a displaced Fock state -- applied to two different pairs of points in phase space. We further show that this geometric error is exactly correctable by promoting the Trotter-step coupling to a complex amplitude, at no additional circuit cost. These results, obtained in the exactly solvable degenerate limit, provide a benchmark for Trotterization errors in the general Rabi model.

AI.tldr: The paper derives an exact characterization of first-order Trotterization errors for the quantum Rabi model in the exactly solvable degenerate limit, valid at arbitrary coupling. The Trotter operator yields a closed-form phase-space trajectory lying on a rescaled, rigidly rotated circle, giving a closed-form fidelity that is structurally identical to the physical revival survival probability. The error is exactly correctable by making the Trotter-step coupling complex at no extra circuit cost.
AI.motivation: Digital quantum simulation of the quantum Rabi model in the deep strong coupling regime requires an exact characterization of Trotterization errors, which were previously known only through qualitative bounds. The work is motivated by the need for a quantitative benchmark for Trotter errors in the general Rabi model.
AI.method: The authors work in the exactly solvable degenerate limit and derive a closed expression for the first-order Trotter operator, valid for arbitrary coupling strength. They analyze the generated phase-space trajectory geometrically, showing it lies exactly on a circle that is rescaled and rigidly rotated relative to the exact trajectory. They then derive a closed-form state fidelity and show the geometric error can be corrected by promoting the Trotter-step coupling to a complex amplitude.
AI.result: The first-order Trotter operator admits a closed expression whose phase-space trajectory lies exactly on a rescaled and rigidly rotated circle rather than approximating the exact one. This geometric renormalization yields a closed-form state fidelity structurally identical to the survival probability governing revivals in the deep strong coupling regime; both reduce to the same geometric question of distinguishability of a displaced Fock state applied to two pairs of phase-space points. The geometric error is exactly correctable by making the Trotter-step coupling complex, with no additional circuit cost.
AI.conclusion: The results, obtained in the exactly solvable degenerate limit, provide an exact benchmark for Trotterization errors in the general quantum Rabi model and reveal a unifying geometric interpretation linking Trotter errors and physical revivals.

title: Closing a single-copy gap to the Holevo bound with two-copy measurements
summary: The Holevo Cramér-Rao bound sets the asymptotically attainable precision of quantum multiparameter estimation, but its attainability with finite quantum state copies remains unresolved in general. While a gap between the single-copy optimum and the Holevo bound persists at any finite copy number for two-parameter estimation models, the higher-parameter case has remained open. Here we disprove universal finite-copy gap persistence beyond two parameters by constructing a three-parameter rank-two model whose Holevo bound is unattainable with one copy but attained exactly with two. We further prove finite-copy persistence for full-rank models with any number of parameters. We then experimentally implement the two-copy collective measurement for the constructed model using superconducting qubits. We observe a two-copy estimation error below the single-copy and separate-measurement bounds determined from state tomography. By introducing controlled depolarization, we show that this precision advantage persists over a finite noise range. Our results connect the attainability of ultimate quantum precision to the structure of the multiparameter estimation model and the resources available for collective measurements.

AI.tldr: A three-parameter rank-two model shows a single-copy Holevo-bound gap that vanishes exactly at two copies, disproving universal finite-copy gap persistence beyond two parameters, while full-rank models persist at any finite copy number, and the two-copy collective measurement advantage is verified on superconducting qubits.
AI.motivation: The Holevo Cramér-Rao bound gives the asymptotically attainable precision in quantum multiparameter estimation, but whether it is attainable with finite copies of the quantum state is unresolved in general. A single-copy-versus-Holevo gap was known to persist at every finite copy number for two-parameter models, leaving the higher-parameter case open.
AI.method: Construction of a three-parameter rank-two estimation model whose Holevo bound is unattainable with one copy but attained exactly with two; a proof of finite-copy gap persistence for full-rank models with arbitrary parameter number; and an experimental implementation of the two-copy collective measurement in the constructed model using superconducting qubits, including state tomography to establish single-copy and separate-measurement bounds and controlled depolarization to probe robustness.
AI.result: The constructed three-parameter rank-two model violates universal finite-copy gap persistence: the Holevo bound is not attainable with one copy yet is attained exactly with two. Finite-copy persistence is proven to hold for full-rank models with any number of parameters. Experimentally, the two-copy estimation error falls below both the single-copy and separate-measurement bounds, and the precision advantage survives over a finite noise range under controlled depolarization.
AI.conclusion: Attainability of the ultimate quantum precision depends jointly on the structure of the multiparameter estimation model and on the resources available for collective measurements; gap persistence is not universal beyond two parameters, being absent for certain rank-deficient models yet retained by full-rank models.

title: Digital Twin Modeling of Quantum Dynamical Systems: Dissipative Quantum Reservoir Computing
summary:
Modeling the response of driven many-body quantum systems from input--output data is difficult: the dynamics are nonlinear, history dependent, and expensive to simulate as system size grows. A paradigmatic case is High-Harmonic Generation~(HHG), where a strong field drives a medium to emit radiation that is highly sensitive to the drive and encodes long-range temporal correlations. We introduce a dissipative quantum reservoir computing~(DQRC) framework that builds a digital twin of such a system, learning its input--output map directly from data while the reservoir---itself a small open quantum system---stays fixed and only a classical readout is trained. We show that a minimal single-qubit reservoir reproduces the HHG response of a substantially larger Ising spin chain, and on a representative benchmark matches and on several metrics surpasses previously reported temporal convolutional and Kolmogorov--Arnold-network models, while using a simpler, physically realizable system. A single fixed reservoir further generalizes across a broad range of drives, indicating that it learns a shared physical response structure rather than memorizing trajectories. These results establish dissipative quantum reservoirs as compact, physically grounded digital twins for nonlinear, memory-dependent quantum dynamics.
  Code is available at \href{https://github.com/AI-and-Quantum-Computing/DQuRC}{https://github.com/AI-and-Quantum-Computing/DQuRC}.

AI.tldr: A dissipative quantum reservoir computing framework builds a compact digital twin of driven many-body quantum systems, using a single-qubit open reservoir to reproduce and even surpass larger models on High-Harmonic Generation benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Modeling driven many-body quantum systems from input-output data is hard: dynamics are nonlinear, history dependent, and simulation cost scales with system size. High-Harmonic Generation is a paradigmatic case, as it is highly sensitive to the drive and encodes long-range temporal correlations.
AI.method: The authors introduce a dissipative quantum reservoir computing (DQRC) framework that learns the input-output map directly from data. The reservoir is a small open quantum system kept fixed, with only a classical readout trained.
AI.result: A minimal single-qubit reservoir reproduces the HHG response of a substantially larger Ising spin chain. On a representative benchmark it matches and on several metrics surpasses prior temporal convolutional and Kolmogorov-Arnold-network models, while using a simpler physically realizable system. A single fixed reservoir also generalizes across a broad range of drives.
AI.conclusion: Dissipative quantum reservoirs serve as compact, physically grounded digital twins for nonlinear, memory-dependent quantum dynamics, learning a shared physical response structure rather than memorizing trajectories.

title: Device-independent quantification of steerability in tripartite scenario
summary: Quantum steering captures the ability of one party, through local measurements on a shared entangled state, to affect the conditional states held by distant parties in a way that admits no local explanation. Its device-independent (DI) quantification -- requiring no characterization of any state or measurement -- has been developed in the bipartite setting, notably through the framework of assemblage moment matrices (AMMs) [Phys. Rev. Lett. 116, 240401 (2016)], but has remained largely unexplored beyond it. Here, we extend the AMM framework to tripartite steering, covering both the scenario in which two parties jointly steer a third one (2-steer-1) and that in which a single party steers the remaining two (1-steer-2). For each scheme, we construct a semidefinite program that, from the observed correlations -- or merely from the violation of a Bell inequality -- yields lower bounds on the steering robustness of the underlying assemblage. As a by-product, our bounds also certify, in a DI manner, the incompatibility of the measurements performed by the steering parties.

AI.tldr: This work extends the assemblage moment matrix (AMM) framework for device-independent quantum steering from the bipartite to the tripartite setting, covering both 2-steer-1 and 1-steer-2 scenarios via semidefinite programs that yield lower bounds on steering robustness and certify measurement incompatibility.
AI.motivation: Device-independent quantification of quantum steering has been developed mainly for bipartite settings through the AMM framework, but remains largely unexplored beyond it. Tripartite steering, where either two parties jointly steer a third or one party steers the remaining two, lacks a device-independent characterization and quantification method.
AI.method: The authors extend the assemblage moment matrix (AMM) framework to tripartite steering, treating both the 2-steer-1 and 1-steer-2 scenarios. For each scheme, they construct a semidefinite program (SDP) that, given the observed correlations or merely the violation of a Bell inequality, produces lower bounds on the steering robustness of the underlying assemblage.
AI.result: The proposed SDPs yield lower bounds on the steering robustness of the underlying assemblage in both tripartite steering schemes. As a by-product, the bounds also certify, in a device-independent manner, the incompatibility of the measurements performed by the steering parties.
AI.conclusion: The AMM framework can be successfully generalized to tripartite quantum steering, providing device-independent quantification of steering robustness and, additionally, a device-independent certification of measurement incompatibility in both the 2-steer-1 and 1-steer-2 scenarios.

title: Exact quantum algorithm for searching of multiple sets intersection
summary: Grover's algorithm achieves a quadratic speedup for unstructured search when a global oracle for the target set is available. However, its success probability is generally below $100\%$. To overcome this issue, Long presented a modified version of Grover's search algorithm by introducing a phase-matching condition, which can search for the target set with zero theoretical failure rate. Nevertheless, in many applications, the target set is determined by the intersection of multiple constrained sets. Most existing Grover-based methods are limited to the intersection of only two sets and are not always successful in searching for the target set. In this work, based on Long's method, we propose an algorithm for exactly searching the intersection of multiple sets. We derive and prove a phase-matching condition for searching the intersection exactly. Furthermore, we present a quantum circuit that implements exact intersection search. Finally, we support our theoretical results with numerical simulations.

AI.tldr: This work proposes a Grover-based quantum algorithm that exactly finds the intersection of multiple constrained sets, deriving a phase-matching condition and providing a quantum circuit with numerical validation.
AI.motivation: Grover's algorithm offers a quadratic speedup for unstructured search with a global oracle, but its success probability is below 100%. Long's modified version introduces a phase-matching condition to achieve zero theoretical failure rate, but existing Grover-based methods mostly handle only the intersection of two sets and are not always successful. Many applications require searching the intersection of multiple constrained sets, motivating an exact multi-set intersection search method.
AI.method: Building on Long's method, the authors propose an algorithm for exactly searching the intersection of multiple sets. They derive and prove a phase-matching condition that guarantees exact intersection search, and design a quantum circuit implementing this exact intersection search.
AI.result: The derived phase-matching condition enables exact search of the intersection of multiple sets, and the proposed quantum circuit realizes this exact intersection search. Numerical simulations support the theoretical results.
AI.conclusion: The paper extends Long's phase-matching approach from a single target set to the exact search of the intersection of multiple constrained sets, providing a proven phase-matching condition, an implementing quantum circuit, and numerical evidence validating the theoretical findings.

title: Universal Inductive Inference of Quantum States
summary: Solomonoff's universal inductive inference [Inf. Control. 1964] is one of the most general frameworks for learning from sequential data and predicting future observations. It provides prediction guarantees for any computable stochastic source. We ask whether an analogous universal theory of induction can be developed for quantum systems. To this end, we introduce universal quantum inductive inference, a framework for learning and predicting quantum sources that may exhibit arbitrary correlations and entanglement across time. Given the outcomes of past measurements and the corresponding post-measurement quantum systems, the learner produces a joint state that predicts the next measurement outcome and post-measurement system while preserving correlations with the past systems. We model a quantum source as a multipartite quantum state whose description is generated by an unknown $s$-bit program within a given time bound. The learner is required to produce a state that is $ε$-close in trace distance to the target with probability at least $1-δ$. We establish an information-theoretic inference algorithm with round complexity $O(sε^{-2}δ^{-1})$. We further prove a matching lower bound in the relevant parameter regime, even for classical sources. As a second result, we construct a non-i.i.d. state tomography algorithm that outputs a classical description of the conditional state of the next system given past measurement outcomes. Our information-theoretic tomography algorithm achieves round complexity $O(s\min\{2^s,2^n\}ε^{-2}δ^{-1})$, where $n$ is the number of qubits received in each round. Finally, we investigate the computational hardness of universal quantum inductive inference under quantum cryptographic assumptions.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces universal quantum inductive inference, a framework extending Solomonoff's inductive inference to quantum systems with arbitrary temporal correlations and entanglement, establishing an information-theoretic algorithm with O(sε^{-2}δ^{-1}) round complexity, a matching lower bound, a non-i.i.d. state tomography algorithm, and computational hardness results under quantum cryptographic assumptions.
AI.motivation: Solomonoff's universal inductive inference provides prediction guarantees for any computable stochastic source, but no analogous universal theory of induction exists for quantum systems. The paper aims to develop such a framework for learning and predicting quantum sources that may exhibit arbitrary correlations and entanglement across time.
AI.method: The authors model a quantum source as a multipartite quantum state described by an unknown s-bit program within a given time bound. Given past measurement outcomes and corresponding post-measurement quantum systems, the learner produces a joint state predicting the next measurement outcome and post-measurement system while preserving correlations with past systems. The learner must output a state ε-close in trace distance to the target with probability at least 1-δ. They establish an information-theoretic inference algorithm and a non-i.i.d. state tomography algorithm, and analyze computational hardness under quantum cryptographic assumptions.
AI.result: The paper establishes an information-theoretic inference algorithm with round complexity O(sε^{-2}δ^{-1}) and proves a matching lower bound in the relevant parameter regime, even for classical sources. It constructs a non-i.i.d. state tomography algorithm achieving round complexity O(s min{2^s, 2^n} ε^{-2}δ^{-1}), where n is the number of qubits received per round. Finally, it investigates the computational hardness of universal quantum inductive inference under quantum cryptographic assumptions.
AI.conclusion: A universal theory of quantum inductive inference can be developed, paralleling Solomonoff's classical framework, with an information-theoretically optimal algorithm whose round complexity matches a proven lower bound even classically. The framework extends to non-i.i.d. state tomography, and the computational hardness results indicate that efficient universal quantum inductive inference is unlikely under quantum cryptographic assumptions.

title: Towards Scalable Quantum Unit Commitment in Power Systems: Encoding and Complexity Reduction Techniques
summary: This paper develops a Quantum optimisation Unit Commitment (UC) framework that benefits from Pauli Correlation Encoding (PCE) as a qubit reduction preprocessing technique and Sample-based Quantum Diagonalisation (SQD) as a hybrid post-processing refinement method. The UC problem is formulated in binary form, then transformed into a QUBO problem and mapped onto an Ising representation suitable for adiabatic quantum evolution within the Qibo framework. This study analyses how PCE and SQD techniques affect qubit scalability, computational effort, feasibility, and probability of recovering the optimal solution as the number of generators increases. The results show that PCE reduces the effective size of the encoded problem, SQD improves the concentration of probability on feasible and optimal solutions, and their combined application provides the best overall behaviour in several scalable case studies, achieving more reliable solutions with lower effective computational cost than the unreduced formulation. The repository is available open source in Github (link is not yet available until work is published. However, if requested by the reviewers, we can make it open for a scific time window, if requested).

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a quantum optimization framework for the Unit Commitment (UC) problem, combining Pauli Correlation Encoding (PCE) for qubit reduction and Sample-based Quantum Diagonalisation (SQD) as a hybrid post-processing refinement, evaluated within the Qibo framework.
AI.motivation: The UC problem grows combinatorially with the number of generators, making it hard for quantum hardware due to qubit scalability, computational effort, and the difficulty of recovering feasible and optimal solutions.
AI.method: The UC problem is formulated in binary form, transformed into a QUBO problem, and mapped onto an Ising representation suitable for adiabatic quantum evolution within Qibo. PCE is used as a qubit reduction preprocessing technique, and SQD is applied as a hybrid post-processing refinement method.
AI.result: PCE reduces the effective size of the encoded problem, and SQD improves the concentration of probability on feasible and optimal solutions. Their combined application yields the best overall behaviour across scalable case studies, achieving more reliable solutions with lower effective computational cost than the unreduced formulation.
AI.conclusion: The combined PCE and SQD approach enhances qubit scalability, feasibility, and optimal-solution recovery for quantum UC as the number of generators increases, outperforming the unreduced formulation. The implementation is available as an open-source repository on GitHub.

title: Quantum Query Lower Bounds for Triangle-Listing and Spanners
summary: This paper gives quantum query lower bounds for two relational graph problems, triangle listing and explicit multiplicative spanner construction, in the general graph query model, where quantum adjacency, degree and neighborhood queries are all available in arbitrary superposition. Both results are obtained by reductions via intermediate multi-block search problems. We extend the quantum query recording framework by Zhandry (CRYPTO 2019) and Hamoudi and Magniez (ToCT 2023) to handle a recording architecture for bidirectional oracles and give a generic blockwise soundness framework, which for arbitrary families of local accepting projectors, gives an exact operator-norm characterization of their maximum overlap with the subspace of bounded weight records. Using the intermediate search problems, we exhibit a family of $n$-vertex graphs with $Θ(n)$ triangles on which listing any constant fraction of the triangles requires $Ω(n^{3/2-o(1)})$ quantum queries. This is the first nontrivial quantum lower bound for triangle listing, a question raised by Jiang and Peng (ICML 2026). Further, we show that, for every fixed $k\ge 7$, constructing a multiplicative $k$-spanner requires $Ω(n^{1+\frac{1}{2μ_k}})$ quantum queries, where $μ_k=k/3+O(1)$. For $k\in\{7,8\}$ the bound is $Ω(n^{5/4})$, which matches what would be implied by an unproven instance of the Erdős girth conjecture, and for large $k$ the exponent $1+\frac{3}{2k}$ exceeds the $1+\frac{4}{3k}$ implied by the provable high girth dense graphs due to Lazebnik, Ustimenko and Woldar, 1995.

AI.tldr: This paper proves quantum query lower bounds for triangle listing and explicit multiplicative spanner construction in the general graph query model, using reductions via intermediate multi-block search problems and an extended quantum query recording framework.
AI.motivation: Triangle listing lower bounds were an open question raised by Jiang and Peng (ICML 2026), and spanner construction lacked tight quantum query lower bounds. The paper addresses these gaps by extending existing recording frameworks to handle bidirectional oracles and arbitrary local accepting projectors.
AI.method: The authors extend the quantum query recording framework of Zhandry (CRYPTO 2019) and Hamoudi and Magniez (ToCT 2023) to support a recording architecture for bidirectional oracles. They develop a generic blockwise soundness framework that, for arbitrary families of local accepting projectors, provides an exact operator-norm characterization of their maximum overlap with the subspace of bounded weight records. Both results are obtained via reductions through intermediate multi-block search problems.
AI.result: For triangle listing, the authors exhibit a family of n-vertex graphs with Θ(n) triangles on which listing any constant fraction requires Ω(n^{3/2-o(1)}) quantum queries — the first nontrivial quantum lower bound. For spanner construction, for every fixed k≥7, constructing a multiplicative k-spanner requires Ω(n^{1+1/(2μ_k)}) quantum queries, where μ_k=k/3+O(1). For k∈{7,8}, the bound is Ω(n^{5/4}), matching an unproven instance of the Erdős girth conjecture; for large k, the exponent 1+3/(2k) exceeds the 1+4/(3k) implied by provable high-girth dense graphs of Lazebnik, Ustimenko and Woldar (1995).
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes the first nontrivial quantum lower bound for triangle listing and strong quantum query lower bounds for multiplicative spanner construction. The extended recording framework and blockwise soundness characterization serve as general tools applicable to other relational graph problems in the general graph query model.

title: A quantum double-bracket algorithm for imaginary-time evolution with exponentially shorter depth
summary: Imaginary-time evolution (ITE) is a widely used technique for preparing the ground state of a target Hamiltonian. Building on the recently proposed framework of Double-Bracket quantum ITE (DB-QITE), we introduce a probabilistic variant (PDBQITE) that achieves an exponential reduction in circuit depth. Our algorithm requires only a single ancilla qubit and a quantum circuit that consists of one controlled real-time evolution and one mid-circuit measurement per iteration. The trade-off is an exponential decay of the total success probability with the number of iterations, for which we derive an analytical lower bound that is independent of system size. Our numerical simulations show that the per-step success probability remains close to unity, making it realistic to execute many iterations, thus providing a substantial improvement over prior constructions. We show that PDBQITE outperforms the near-term probabilistic algorithm PITE for ground-state preparation of molecular Hamiltonians, and that a hybrid QAOA-PDBQITE scheme achieves higher approximation ratios than QAOA at the same circuit depth on random regular graphs for the MaxCut problem.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces PDBQITE, a probabilistic variant of Double-Bracket quantum imaginary-time evolution that exponentially reduces circuit depth using one ancilla qubit, one controlled real-time evolution, and one mid-circuit measurement per iteration, with an analytically bounded success probability.
AI.motivation: Preparing ground states of target Hamiltonians is a central task in quantum computing, and imaginary-time evolution (ITE) is a standard technique for it. Existing approaches, including the recently proposed Double-Bracket quantum ITE (DB-QITE), face large circuit depth requirements, which limits practical execution, especially in the near term. There is a need for a method that reduces circuit depth while retaining effectiveness for ground-state preparation.
AI.method: The authors propose PDBQITE, a probabilistic variant of DB-QITE. Each iteration uses only one ancilla qubit, a circuit consisting of one controlled real-time evolution and one mid-circuit measurement. The algorithm succeeds probabilistically, with an analytical lower bound on total success probability derived to be independent of system size. The scheme is also combined with QAOA into a hybrid QAOA-PDBQITE approach.
AI.result: The total success probability decays exponentially with the number of iterations, but the derived lower bound is system-size independent, and numerical simulations show the per-step success probability stays close to unity, enabling many iterations. PDBQITE outperforms the near-term probabilistic algorithm PITE for ground-state preparation of molecular Hamiltonians, and hybrid QAOA-PDBQITE achieves higher approximation ratios than QAOA at equal circuit depth on random regular graphs for MaxCut.
AI.conclusion: PDBQITE achieves an exponential reduction in circuit depth for ground-state preparation with a practical per-step success probability, providing a substantial improvement over prior constructions. It outperforms PITE on molecular Hamiltonians and enhances QAOA on MaxCut, demonstrating its usefulness for both near-term and hybrid quantum algorithms.

title: Minimal building blocks for molecular quantum circuits with exact spin symmetry
comment: 72 pages, 7 figures; includes 25 pages of Supplementary Information. Data and code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22230014
summary: Preserving particle number and spin helps quantum circuits target molecular electronic states, but does not guarantee access to every state with the required quantum numbers. We determine which additional operations, combined with spin-independent orbital rotations connecting all spatial orbitals, generate every real state-space rotation within each complete subspace of fixed particle number $N$, total spin $S$, and spin projection $M_S$. We consider spin-free molecular calculations in real orbitals, without an additional spatial-symmetry restriction, and continuously tunable operations that preserve particle number, full spin symmetry, and real amplitudes. Below the maximal-spin limits set by the electron and hole numbers, repeated singlet-pair transfer between any two fixed spatial orbitals is sufficient. On nontrivial maximal-spin boundaries, pair transfer vanishes, and an additional generator built from one- and two-electron terms is sufficient exactly when its action in the target subspace is not a linear combination of orbital-rotation generators. The minimum number of spatial orbitals needed by one additional generator is two in the interior and three on nontrivial boundaries, even when terms involving more than two electrons are allowed. Both minima are attained using only one- and two-electron terms. The three-orbital optimum rotates two orbitals according to the occupation of a third, and its unitary factors exactly into eight commuting Pauli rotations. Molecular benchmarks show that this operation removes the observed boundary energy-error plateaus, while sparse interior constructions attain the prescribed energy accuracy with fewer compiled CNOT gates in selected fixed-orbital comparisons.

AI.tldr: A pair-transfer generator between two orbitals suffices to reach all real states in fixed (N, S, M_S) subspaces in the interior; on maximal-spin boundaries one extra one-/two-electron generator is needed, with minima of two (interior) and three (boundaries) orbitals, the latter factoring into eight commuting Pauli rotations.
AI.motivation: Preserving particle number and spin lets quantum circuits target the right symmetry sector, but does not by itself guarantee that every state in a fixed (N, S, M_S) subspace is reachable. The paper identifies the minimal additional generators that complete the reachable state space under spin-free, real-orbital, real-amplitude operations.
AI.method: The authors analyze Lie-algebra/generator constructions for real, spin-independent orbital rotations plus continuously tunable number- and spin-symmetry-preserving operations. They determine which generators span the full real rotation group of each complete fixed-(N, S, M_S) subspace, derive minimal orbital counts for the required extra generator, and construct/benchmark explicit ansätze using only one- and two-electron terms.
AI.result: Repeated singlet-pair transfer between any two fixed spatial orbitals is sufficient below the maximal-spin limits. On nontrivial maximal-spin boundaries pair transfer vanishes, and one additional generator suffices exactly when its target-subspace action is not a linear combination of orbital-rotation generators. The minimum number of spatial orbitals is two in the interior and three on boundaries, even allowing higher-than-two-electron terms; both minima use only one- and two-electron terms. The three-orbital optimum rotates two orbitals conditioned on a third's occupation and factors exactly into eight commuting Pauli rotations.
AI.conclusion: Particle-number and spin preservation plus orbital rotations is incomplete; the missing generators are identified and shown to be minimal and efficiently implementable. Molecular benchmarks confirm that the boundary generator eliminates energy-error plateaus, while sparse interior constructions reach target accuracy with fewer compiled CNOTs in selected fixed-orbital comparisons.

title: SQUARE: Structured Quantum Representation Adapters as Compact Quadratic Feature Maps for Frozen Language Models
summary: Frozen language models (LMs) are increasingly used as fixed feature extractors for downstream reranking, scoring, and preference modeling, raising a practical question: how should a compact module represent interactions among features in a fixed low-dimensional bottleneck? Common linear and low-rank adapters remain linear at the adaptation module itself, whereas explicit second-order alternatives introduce pairwise interactions through direct parameterization or predefined factorizations. We propose SQUARE, a Structured QUAntum REpresentation adapter that amplitude-encodes the bottleneck vector, applies a parameterized quantum circuit, and measures the resulting state. We show that each basis-probability feature is exactly a normalized quadratic form in the bottleneck coordinates, while the additional Pauli-$Z$ readouts are signed linear combinations of these probabilities. The measured map can therefore parameterize interactions over $O(d^2)$ coordinate pairs through a small set of shared circuit parameters, where $d$ is the bottleneck dimension. It provides a structured parameterization within, rather than beyond, the classical normalized-quadratic feature class. In a disjoint same-pipeline evaluation over eight GLUE-derived controlled interaction tasks and five shared seeds, SQUARE achieves an average test accuracy of $0.7565$, compared with $0.7355$ for an affine normalized-quadratic predictor, $0.7271$ for the evaluated parameter-matched Givens mixing model, $0.6817$ for an MLP, and $0.6155$ for a frozen-circuit control. Under reduced supervision, it also shows consistent gains over the strongest evaluated classical comparator, with the same qualitative pattern across multiple frozen LM backbones. All circuit experiments use simulation, while the learned feature map can be evaluated exactly in batched PyTorch without quantum hardware.

AI.tldr: SQUARE is a quantum-inspired adapter that amplitude-encodes a frozen LM's bottleneck vector into a parameterized quantum circuit, yielding readouts that are exactly normalized quadratic forms, giving a structured second-order feature class that outperforms classical adapters on controlled interaction tasks.
AI.motivation: Frozen LMs are widely used as fixed feature extractors for downstream reranking, scoring, and preference modeling, so a compact adapter must represent feature interactions within a fixed low-dimensional bottleneck. Existing linear and low-rank adapters stay linear at the adaptation module, while explicit second-order alternatives rely on direct parameterization or predefined factorizations, motivating a more structured way to parameterize pairwise interactions.
AI.method: SQUARE amplitude-encodes the bottleneck vector, applies a parameterized quantum circuit, and measures the resulting state. The authors show each basis-probability feature is exactly a normalized quadratic form in the bottleneck coordinates, while Pauli-Z readouts are signed linear combinations of these probabilities. This measured map parameterizes interactions over O(d^2) coordinate pairs using a small set of shared circuit parameters for bottleneck dimension d, placing it within the classical normalized-quadratic feature class. All circuit experiments use simulation; the learned feature map is evaluated exactly in batched PyTorch without quantum hardware.
AI.result: In a disjoint same-pipeline evaluation over eight GLUE-derived controlled interaction tasks and five shared seeds, SQUARE reaches average test accuracy of 0.7565, versus 0.7355 for an affine normalized-quadratic predictor, 0.7271 for a parameter-matched Givens mixing model, 0.6817 for an MLP, and 0.6155 for a frozen-circuit control. Under reduced supervision it also shows consistent gains over the strongest classical comparator, with the same qualitative pattern across multiple frozen LM backbones.
AI.conclusion: SQUARE provides a structured parameterization within, not beyond, the classical normalized-quadratic feature class, using a small number of shared quantum-circuit parameters to capture O(d^2) pairwise interactions. It consistently outperforms evaluated classical adapters across tasks, seeds, supervision levels, and frozen LM backbones, while remaining simulatable and exactly computable in batched PyTorch without quantum hardware.

title: Arbitrary high-dimensional entanglement purification with the superposition of paths
summary: High-dimensional quantum entanglement offers significant advantages over its two-dimensional counterparts in various quantum information processing tasks. We propose a scalable method for implementing an arbitrary high-dimensional entanglement purification protocol (HDEPP) using path superposition. By selecting appropriate single-qudit gates, qudit-flip errors and phase-flip errors can be purified. Counterintuitively, the HDEPP becomes more robust for higher-dimensional systems and exhibits enhanced purification fidelity as the dimension increases. Our HDEPP not only requires fewer operational resources but also in principle can achieve unity fidelity through multiple rounds of iteration. Furthermore, we develop feasible optical schemes to purify the frequency degree of freedom of photons suffering from qudit-flip and phase-flip errors using hyperentanglement. This work paves the way toward high-dimensional quantum communication and quantum networks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a scalable high-dimensional entanglement purification protocol (HDEPP) via path superposition, showing that purification becomes more robust and resource-efficient as qudit dimension increases, and provides optical schemes for photon frequency purification using hyperentanglement.
AI.motivation: High-dimensional entanglement outperforms two-dimensional counterparts in quantum information processing, but practical high-dimensional quantum communication requires overcoming decoherence. Existing purification methods for high-dimensional systems are limited, motivating a scalable HDEPP that efficiently corrects qudit-flip and phase-flip errors.
AI.method: The authors implement an arbitrary HDEPP using path superposition by selecting appropriate single-qudit gates to purify qudit-flip and phase-flip errors. They also develop feasible optical schemes to purify the frequency degree of freedom of photons affected by these errors using hyperentanglement.
AI.result: Counterintuitively, the HDEPP becomes more robust for higher-dimensional systems, with purification fidelity increasing as dimension grows. It requires fewer operational resources and in principle can achieve unity fidelity through multiple rounds of iteration.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a scalable approach to high-dimensional entanglement purification, enabling high-fidelity purification of photon frequency states and paving the way toward high-dimensional quantum communication and quantum networks.

title: Margenau-Hill distribution as a Necessary and Sufficient Signature of Measurement Incompatibility
summary: Measurement incompatibility and the negativity of quasi-probability distributions both demonstrate the signature of nonclassicality. However, their relations largely remained qualitative, and no explicit operational connection has been established. We provide an operational link between measurement incompatibility and the Margenau-Hill(MH) quasi-probability distribution associated with two dichotomic observables. { We first derive the joint measurability (measurement compatibility) condition for any pair of dichotomic observables in arbitrary finite dimension $d$.} We then rigorously prove that for any pair of unsharp dichotomic measurements in dimension $d$, the positivity of the MH distribution is equivalent to joint measurability \emph{i.e.}, the MH distribution is positive \emph{if and only if} the measurements are jointly measurable. We further introduce the MH-like quasi-probability distribution for $n$ dichotomic unsharp observables in arbitrary finite dimension and derive a sufficient condition of joint-measurability when the observables are mutually anticommuting. Finally, we propose an interferometric setup, inspired by quantum-switch architectures, that directly reconstructs MH quasi-probability which in turn provides a test of incompatibility.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes an operational link between measurement incompatibility and the negativity of the Margenau-Hill (MH) quasi-probability distribution for dichotomic observables.
AI.motivation: Measurement incompatibility and negativity of quasi-probability distributions both signify nonclassicality, but their relationship has remained largely qualitative with no explicit operational connection established.
AI.method: The authors derive the joint measurability condition for any pair of dichotomic observables in arbitrary finite dimension d. They prove that for any pair of unsharp dichotomic measurements, positivity of the MH distribution is equivalent to joint measurability. They introduce an MH-like quasi-probability distribution for n dichotomic unsharp observables and derive a sufficient condition for joint measurability under mutual anticommutation. An interferometric setup inspired by quantum-switch architectures is proposed to reconstruct the MH quasi-probability.
AI.result: For any pair of unsharp dichotomic measurements in dimension d, the MH distribution is positive if and only if the measurements are jointly measurable. A sufficient condition for joint measurability is obtained for mutually anticommuting observables via the MH-like distribution. The interferometric setup directly reconstructs the MH quasi-probability, providing a test of incompatibility.
AI.conclusion: The MH quasi-probability distribution serves as an operational witness of measurement incompatibility, and the proposed interferometric scheme enables its direct reconstruction, offering an experimental test of incompatibility.

title: A quantum thermal machine surpassing the classical thermodynamic limit on precision
summary: Precision in nonequilibrium processes comes at a thermodynamic cost: suppressing fluctuations generally requires increased dissipation. Thermodynamic uncertainty relations (TURs) make this trade-off quantitative by linking current fluctuations to entropy production in classical stochastic dynamics. In the decade since its discovery, the canonical steady-state TUR and its finite-time generalizations have become a cornerstone of non-equilibrium thermodynamics, constraining the performance of molecular machines and allowing heat dissipation to be inferred from observable fluctuations. Whether the canonical TUR can be violated in a controlled quantum device remains an outstanding experimental question, in part because doing so requires resolving extremely small steady-state currents as well as their fluctuations. Here we experimentally show that steady-state quantum transport can surpass the precision permitted by the canonical TUR. We observe this violation in a superconducting quantum thermal machine coupled to a microwave waveguide acting as a cold bath and to a classical noise source providing an effective infinite-temperature bath. We observe a TUR ratio $Q = 1.71 \pm 0.17$, in violation of the classical bound $Q \geq 2$. Our results demonstrate a fundamental distinction between classical and quantum thermodynamics, paving the way for quantum thermal devices that achieve enhanced precision at reduced energy cost.

AI.tldr: A superconducting quantum thermal machine violates the canonical thermodynamic uncertainty relation, achieving a TUR ratio Q = 1.71 ± 0.17 below the classical bound of 2, demonstrating quantum transport can surpass the precision permitted in classical stochastic thermodynamics.
AI.motivation: The canonical thermodynamic uncertainty relation (TUR) links current fluctuations to entropy production in classical stochastic dynamics, quantifying the trade-off between precision and dissipation. Whether this classical bound can be violated in a controlled quantum device remained an open experimental question, partly because it requires resolving extremely small steady-state currents and their fluctuations.
AI.method: The authors experimentally realized steady-state quantum transport in a superconducting quantum thermal machine. The device was coupled to a microwave waveguide acting as a cold bath and to a classical noise source providing an effective infinite-temperature bath, allowing measurement of the steady-state current and its fluctuations.
AI.result: A TUR ratio of Q = 1.71 ± 0.17 was observed, violating the classical bound Q ≥ 2 and showing that steady-state quantum transport can surpass the precision permitted by the canonical TUR.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate a fundamental distinction between classical and quantum thermodynamics and pave the way for quantum thermal devices attaining enhanced precision at reduced energy cost.

title: Non-Canonical Quantum Otto Engine
summary: The fast-developing quantum technology is propelling thermal machine, which lies at the heart of thermodynamics, into a new golden era. Being stochastic because of the non-negligible thermal and quantum fluctuations, the efficiency and power of a finite-time quantum heat engine exhibit a trade-off, preventing the simultaneous achievement of high power and high efficiency. Conventional studies treat the statistics of a heat engine by assuming canonical thermalization, which is valid only under weak-coupling conditions. We here investigate the noncanonical effect on the statistics of the efficiency and power for a finite-time quantum Otto cycle. It is revealed that their average values and variances are highly controllable by engineering the energy spectrum structure of the composite system consisting of the working substance and the bath. Near the quantum critical point induced by the formation of a bound state in the energy spectrum, the average efficiency and power can be boosted simultaneously, meanwhile, both of their variances are decreased. Deepening our understanding of the usefulness of quantum reservoir engineering in thermodynamics, our result lays the foundation for the realization of efficient and stable quantum energy devices.

AI.tldr: Noncanonical thermalization in a finite-time quantum Otto cycle allows simultaneous enhancement of average efficiency and power while reducing their variances, controllable via engineering the composite system's energy spectrum near a bound-state-induced quantum critical point.
AI.motivation: Conventional studies of quantum heat engine statistics assume canonical thermalization, valid only under weak-coupling conditions. The trade-off between power and efficiency in finite-time quantum heat engines (due to thermal and quantum fluctuations) prevents achieving high power and high efficiency simultaneously. This work addresses the overlooked noncanonical effect on efficiency and power statistics.
AI.method: The authors investigate the noncanonical effect on the statistics (average values and variances) of efficiency and power for a finite-time quantum Otto cycle, focusing on engineering the energy spectrum structure of the composite system (working substance plus bath).
AI.result: The average values and variances of efficiency and power are highly controllable by engineering the composite system's energy spectrum. Near the quantum critical point induced by bound-state formation, average efficiency and power are boosted simultaneously, while both variances are decreased.
AI.conclusion: The results deepen understanding of quantum reservoir engineering in thermodynamics and lay the foundation for realizing efficient and stable quantum energy devices.

title: Encoding universal quantum computation into quantized Berry phases: Hardness results and classical algorithms
summary: The Berry phase is a fundamental geometric quantity for characterizing the geometry and topology of quantum many-body systems. Previous work established a super-polynomial quantum advantage in Berry phase estimation at inverse-polynomial precision, given an ansatz state approximating the initial ground state. However, whether this hardness persists for Berry phases quantized by symmetry, which can be distinguished at constant precision, remained open. In this work, we characterize the computational complexity of quantized Berry phase estimation. First, we prove that deciding whether the Berry phase is exactly $0$ or $π$ is $\mathsf{BQP}$-complete when the spectral gap is inverse-polynomially small. This result implies that distinguishing the quantized Berry phase still has a super-polynomial quantum advantage, assuming $\mathsf{BPP}\neq \mathsf{BQP}$. To prove this result, we introduce an encoding that maps the output of any quantum computation to a Berry phase that is exactly $0$ or $π$. Second, we extend this hardness to physically motivated Hamiltonians on a 2D square lattice, including Heisenberg and XY interactions. Third, we provide a classical polynomial-time algorithm for geometrically local Hamiltonians on fixed-dimensional lattices with constant spectral gaps. Therefore we identify that the spectral gap is a key resource for the classical tractability, rather than precision. These results establish a super-polynomial quantum advantage for computing a quantized topological invariant that is unchanged under symmetry- and gap-preserving deformations, and provide new steps towards practical quantum advantage in quantum physics.

AI.tldr: This work fully characterizes the computational complexity of quantized Berry phase estimation, proving it is BQP-complete under inverse-polynomial spectral gaps and identifying spectral gap rather than precision as the key resource for classical tractability.
AI.motivation: Prior work showed super-polynomial quantum advantage in Berry phase estimation at inverse-polynomial precision, but it was open whether the hardness persists for symmetry-quantized Berry phases, which can in principle be distinguished at constant precision. The authors aim to determine whether quantized Berry phases retain super-polynomial quantum advantage and to understand what resource governs classical tractability.
AI.method: The authors characterize the computational complexity of quantized Berry phase estimation by proving that deciding whether the Berry phase is exactly 0 or π is BQP-complete when the spectral gap is inverse-polynomially small, using a new encoding that maps the output of any quantum computation to a Berry phase exactly 0 or π. They extend this hardness to physically motivated Hamiltonians on a 2D square lattice, including Heisenberg and XY interactions, and construct a classical polynomial-time algorithm for geometrically local Hamiltonians on fixed-dimensional lattices with constant spectral gaps.
AI.result: (1) Deciding whether the Berry phase is exactly 0 or π is BQP-complete when the spectral gap is inverse-polynomially small, implying a super-polynomial quantum advantage for distinguishing quantized Berry phases assuming BPP ≠ BQP. (2) This hardness extends to physically motivated 2D square-lattice Hamiltonians including Heisenberg and XY interactions. (3) A classical polynomial-time algorithm exists for geometrically local Hamiltonians on fixed-dimensional lattices with constant spectral gaps.
AI.conclusion: The spectral gap, rather than precision, is identified as the key resource for classical tractability of quantized Berry phase estimation. These results establish a super-polynomial quantum advantage for computing a quantized topological invariant unchanged under symmetry- and gap-preserving deformations, providing new steps toward practical quantum advantage in quantum physics.

title: Optimal Entanglement Routing in Quantum Repeater Chains: Beyond Fixed Operation Order and Purification Schedule
summary: Entanglement routing establishes entangled pairs between distant nodes of a quantum network by purifying and swapping pairs generated on elementary links. Existing methods typically restrict the decision space along two axes: the operation order, often fixed to purify-then-swap (PtS), and the purification schedule of each link, often restricted to pumping. Focusing on linear repeater chains with finite link capacities, we relax both restrictions and study the maximization of the expected end-to-end throughput subject to a fidelity threshold under two quantum-noise models. We develop a unified capacity-aware optimization framework comprising an exact mixed-integer linear program (MILP) under PtS, instantiated with either pumping or general tree purification schedules, and an exact dynamic program (DP) over arbitrary operation orders. Under symmetric Pauli noise, we prove that pumping converges to a fidelity strictly below unity, imposing a capacity-independent feasibility bound and a maximum chain length on every pumping-based PtS method, whereas general tree schedules yield a capacity-dependent bound. We further prove that post-swap purification never increases the throughput, so a free operation order can only increase feasibility. Numerical evaluations confirm the bounds: tree schedules serve over 90\% of the requests that pumping cannot at moderate fidelity thresholds; within the pumping class, a free operation order recovers much of this advantage; but once links use tree schedules, the tree-based MILP and the order-exact DP serve identical request sets throughout. Operation order and purification schedule are thus substitutes, with the purification schedule the dominant factor governing feasibility under symmetric Pauli noise.

title: Near-Optimal Quantum Algorithm and Complexity Analysis for Riccati Problems
summary: We develop quantum algorithms that construct block-encodings of solution matrices for continuous- and discrete-time algebraic Riccati equations (CAREs and DAREs), differential Riccati equations (DREs), and finite Riccati recursions. The Quantum Weighted Riesz Method, unifying four kinds of Riccati problems, constructs projectors onto the solution graphs using weighted Riesz branching operators and recovers the solution matrices. Under the stated access and normalization assumptions, our algorithms for CAREs and DAREs have near-optimal query complexity $Θ(\mathcal Rα)$ up to logarithmic factors, with the generalized singularity factor $\mathcal R$ that reflects spectral separation, and the output normalization $α$. For DREs and finite-horizon problems, the query complexity has an additional initialization conditioning factor $κ_{\rm init}$. We establish product query lower bounds for specified input-oracle families, demonstrating necessary joint dependence on spectral separation and initialization or output scale. We also prove that selected-value promise problems are BQP-complete on explicit circuit-generated families of single-control discrete-time algebraic and zero-terminal differential Riccati equations. Applications include classical feedback evaluation for linear-quadratic control, a query-complexity comparison for stable random-phase approximation Riccati equations in quantum chemistry, and heated boundary control with numerical validation.

AI.tldr: This paper develops quantum algorithms that construct block-encodings of solution matrices for continuous- and discrete-time algebraic Riccati equations (CAREs, DAREs), differential Riccati equations (DREs), and finite Riccati recursions via a unified Quantum Weighted Riesz Method, achieving near-optimal query complexity and proving BQP-completeness for selected-value promise problems.
AI.motivation: Riccati equations are central to linear-quadratic control, quantum chemistry, and boundary control, but solving them classically is costly. There is a need for quantum algorithms that efficiently produce block-encodings of their solution matrices, with rigorous complexity analysis and lower bounds justifying the dependence on spectral separation and scaling factors.

The approach assumes stated access and normalization conditions, and provides query-complexity analyses plus product query lower bounds for specified input-oracle families.

For DREs and finite-horizon problems, complexity includes an additional initialization conditioning factor κ_init. title: Encoding and Node Choices in Transversal Fault-Tolerant Distributed Quantum Computations: An Initial Study
summary: We compare and study different Bivariate-Bicycle (BB) encodings and node choices for distributed quantum operations such as transversal non-local CNOTs. We observe that while some encodings have more physical qubits requiring more ebits for a distributed computation, reducing ebit consumption alone might not be the best criterion for selecting an encoding for the logical qubits, if the goal is to reduce the logical error rate of the distributed computation; for example, one should also consider encodings with a larger distance, which using more physical qubits can provide. We consider distributed, or non-local, CNOTs and computation of the global gate (GCZ) over distributed logical qubits as examples. The choice of encoding enables particular concurrent operations; e.g., we show that a transversal physical GCZ on a self-dual $[[120,8,12]] BB$ code can realize eight concurrent logical GCZ operations after accounting for the logical permutation induced by transversal Hadamard.

AI.tldr: This work compares Bivariate-Bicycle (BB) code encodings and node choices for distributed quantum operations (non-local CNOTs, global GCZ), showing that minimizing ebit consumption alone is not optimal; larger-distance encodings using more physical qubits can reduce logical error rates, and self-dual BB codes enable concurrent logical operations.
AI.motivation: Distributed quantum computation requires selecting encodings and node layouts for logical qubits, but the trade-offs among physical qubit count, ebit consumption, and logical error rate are not well understood. The paper aims to clarify which criteria should guide encoding selection when the true goal is minimizing logical error rate.
AI.method: The authors systematically compare and study different Bivariate-Bicycle (BB) encodings and node choices for distributed/non-local operations. They use distributed (non-local) CNOTs and distributed logical global gate (GCZ) computations as benchmark examples, analyzing how encoding choices affect ebit requirements, physical qubit overhead, distance, and the concurrency of logical operations, including permutations induced by transversal Hadamard on self-dual codes.
AI.result: Some encodings need more physical qubits and thus more ebits for distributed computation, yet reducing ebit consumption alone may not be the best selection criterion if the objective is lowering the logical error rate; larger-distance encodings using more physical qubits can be preferable. A transversal physical GCZ on a self-dual [[120,8,12]] BB code can realize eight concurrent logical GCZ operations after accounting for the logical permutation induced by transversal Hadamard.
AI.conclusion: Encoding selection for distributed quantum computation should not be optimized solely for ebit consumption; distance and resulting logical error rate must also be considered. Certain BB encodings additionally enable beneficial concurrent logical operations, as exemplified by the self-dual [[120,8,12]] code supporting eight concurrent logical GCZ operations.

title: Ultra-high-distance quantum memories from amplified qLDPC codes
summary: A large code distance does not by itself guarantee a well-protected quantum memory, as faults during syndrome extraction can propagate into correlated data errors. Certifying circuit distance becomes demanding as circuits grow. In this work, we introduce distance amplifiers, a modular approach to increasing both code distance and certified circuit-level protection in quantum low-density parity-check codes. The construction tensors a base code with an amplifier, adapting their syndrome-extraction circuits to the amplified code. To certify the resulting memory, we develop a fault-response certificate that yields rigorous lower bounds on circuit distance. Suitable gate ordering and flag qubits control correlated errors, allowing us to establish explicit conditions under which the amplified circuit distance equals the product of the constituent circuit distances. We prove this multiplicative relation for three types of amplifiers: the flagged $[[4,2,2]]$, hypergraph-product, and rotated surface codes. The certificate extends recursively, so the circuit distance multiplies exactly at every amplification step. For example, four successive applications of the flagged $[[4,2,2]]$ amplifier to a $[[18,4,4]]$ seed yield a $[[13320,64,64]]$ code with the circuit distance $d_{\mathrm{circ}} \geq 48$ and check weights $w \leq 14$. We further show how individual logical qubits can be tracked explicitly through amplification. By enabling high-distance quantum memories to be built and certified from smaller building blocks, our framework offers a systematic route toward scalable fault-tolerant quantum computing.

A recursive fault-response certificate gives rigorous lower bounds on circuit distance, and explicit gate ordering and flag qubits yield a multiplicative circuit-distance relation for three amplifier types.

Certifying circuit distance is also computationally demanding as circuits grow, so a scalable, certifiable route to high-distance memories is needed.
AI.method: The authors define distance amplifiers by tensoring a base code with an amplifier and adapting their syndrome-extraction circuits to the amplified code. They develop a fault-response certificate providing rigorous lower bounds on circuit distance, and use suitable gate ordering plus flag qubits to control correlated errors. The certificate is applied recursively across amplification steps.
