AI.conclusion: By enabling high-distance quantum memories to be built and certified from smaller building blocks, the framework offers a systematic route toward scalable fault-tolerant quantum computing.

title: Approximate majorization and high-order capacity of quantum depolarizing channels
summary: A central challenge in quantum information theory is to determine whether entanglement provides an advantage for information processing when coherent operations across multiple channel uses are allowed. For depolarizing channels, King's proof of the additivity of the minimum output entropy rules out such an advantage for classical communication at leading asymptotic order, while leaving open the possibility of an advantage for higher orders. In this work, we conjecture a majorization relation for the outputs of depolarizing channels and prove an approximate version of this conjecture. Our proof combines an exact ordering of shifted log-determinants with an anti-concentration bound for the spectrum of the product-state output, refining King's analysis based on Schatten norms. As a direct application, we obtain a tight third-order expansion for the classical capacity of quantum depolarizing channels. Consequently, entangled codewords and collective decoding can improve the message size over the product-coding strategy by at most $O(\log \log n)$ bits, sharpening our understanding of the role of entanglement in the finite-blocklength regime.

AI.tldr: The paper conjectures a majorization relation for depolarizing channel outputs and proves an approximate version, yielding a tight third-order expansion of the classical capacity and showing entanglement gives at most an O(log log n)-bit advantage over product coding.
AI.motivation: In quantum information theory it is central to determine whether entanglement offers an advantage when coherent operations across multiple channel uses are permitted. For depolarizing channels, King's additivity of minimum output entropy rules out any leading-order advantage for classical communication but leaves open possible gains at higher orders, motivating a finer finite-blocklength characterization.
AI.method: The authors conjecture a majorization relation for outputs of depolarizing channels and prove an approximate version. The proof combines an exact ordering of shifted log-determinants with an anti-concentration bound for the spectrum of the product-state output, refining King's Schatten-norm-based analysis.
AI.result: A tight third-order expansion for the classical capacity of quantum depolarizing channels is obtained. Entangled codewords with collective decoding improve the message size over product coding by at most O(log log n) bits.
AI.conclusion: The approximate majorization result sharpens understanding of entanglement's role in the finite-blocklength regime, showing its advantage for depolarizing-channel classical communication is limited to at most O(log log n) bits beyond product coding.

title: L-band single-photon generation from a cavity-coupled silicon C-center
summary: Monolithic integration of single-photon sources into silicon photonics offers a compelling solution for realizing scalable quantum telecommunication architectures. Among the candidate silicon color centers, the C-center features a zero-phonon emission in the telecom L-band, corresponding to the spectral window of minimum transmission loss in optical fibers. Despite this advantage, isolating single C-centers has remained an unrealized challenge in solid-state quantum optics. In this work, we report the isolation of a single silicon C-center. We enhance the spontaneous emission rate of the zero-phonon line by coupling the single emitter to a nanophotonic crystal cavity, observing a fivefold reduction in the excited-state lifetime compared to bulk conditions, which corresponds to a Purcell factor lower bound of 33. Second-order autocorrelation measurements confirm single-photon emission from the investigated defect, obtaining an optical purity of $g^{(2)}(0) = 0.23$ without background correction. Our results establish a native telecom L-band quantum light source in silicon, laying the foundation for ultra-low-loss and long-distance quantum applications.

AI.motivation: Monolithic integration of single-photon sources into silicon photonics is desirable for scalable quantum telecommunication. The silicon C-center is attractive because its zero-phonon emission lies in the telecom L-band, the spectral window of minimum fiber transmission loss. However, isolating single C-centers had remained an unrealized challenge in solid-state quantum optics.
AI.method: The authors isolate a single silicon C-center and couple this single emitter to a nanophotonic crystal cavity to enhance its zero-phonon line spontaneous emission rate. They characterize the emission via excited-state lifetime measurements and second-order autocorrelation measurements.
AI.result: The excited-state lifetime is reduced fivefold relative to bulk, corresponding to a Purcell factor lower bound of 33. Second-order autocorrelation confirms single-photon emission with an optical purity of g(2)(0) = 0.23 without background correction.
AI.conclusion: The findings establish a native telecom L-band quantum light source in silicon, providing a foundation for ultra-low-loss and long-distance quantum applications.

title: Directional transfer from coherence to longitudinal polarization and algebraic storage in a transmon with Markovian dephasing and a glassy environment: A non-Markovian fractional renewal model
comment: 38 pages (main text and appendices), 10 figures. Submitted to Physical Review A on the 28th of September 2026
summary: We develop a completely positive and trace-preserving non-Markovian transmon model with longitudinal Markovian dephasing and transverse renewal events motivated by a glassy two-level-system environment. A microscopic Hamiltonian identifies coupling subspaces; a normalized Prabhakar waiting-time law phenomenologically coarse grains slow defect reconfigurations. Forward chronological renewal histories yield an exact map-level Volterra equation, a noncommuting kernel--resolvent master equation, and an equivalent drift-conjugated Caputo-type representation with its required initial-value term. Without energy relaxation, Pauli-space dynamics splits into two one-dimensional subspaces and a coupled $(σ_y,σ_z)$ subspace supporting directional transfer between coherence and longitudinal polarization; $σ_x$ polarization is renewal-insensitive. For heavy-tailed waiting times with $0<α<1$, branch-cut analysis gives a generic $t^{-α}$ storage tail in longitudinal polarization generated from initial coherence and $O(t^{-1-α})$ reverse transfer; constant-rate Poisson renewal yields pole-generated exponential decay. Independent zero-temperature relaxation at finite $T_1$ exponentially cuts off these tails when its rate is below twice the pure-dephasing rate. We compare independent inverse-Laplace reconstructions of the waiting-time density, memory kernel, and selected qubit-response components to assess numerical accuracy. For the studied parameters, Prabhakar renewal gives larger forward-transfer magnitudes at the prescribed readout than both a scale-matched constant-rate Poisson reference and an inhomogeneous Poisson reference matching the full expected-count profile, including finite-$T_1$ tests. Both Poisson references yield larger evaluated finite-window peaks. Disorder-motivated renewal memory reshapes transmon decoherence selectively by state and direction.

AI.motivation: Motivated by a glassy two-level-system environment, the authors seek a physically consistent non-Markovian transmon decoherence model that captures slow defect reconfigurations through renewal (waiting-time) statistics while remaining completely positive and trace-preserving.
AI.method: A microscopic Hamiltonian identifies coupling subspaces; slow defect reconfigurations are coarse-grained by a normalized Prabhakar waiting-time law. title: Quantum Leakage Resilience of Shamir Secret Sharing
summary:
We initiate the study of quantum leakage resilience of unmodified Shamir secret sharing over prime fields. A well-studied leakage model for Shamir's secret sharing classically is single-bit local leakage from each share. We consider its quantum analogue where, for each party, a local leakage channel takes as input the party's share and outputs a leaked qubit. Without preshared entanglement, we show that the distinguishing advantage is $2^{-Ω(n)}$ when the threshold rate $t/n=τ$ exceeds $τ_\star\approx0.73339$ by a fixed positive margin.
  More generally, we allow disjoint entangled blocks of any fixed maximum size where there is no entanglement between different blocks or with the adversary, and each block emits at most a fixed number of qubits. Security holds when the threshold rate is high enough (sufficiently close to one). We then allow a specified set of devices to share entanglement with the adversary. We show that security holds even when a linear number of devices ($αn$ for small $α>0$) share entanglement with each other and with the adversary for a large enough threshold rate.
  As a complementary negative result, we also show that even classical single-bit leakage makes Shamir scheme insecure if we allow arbitrarily large entanglement between the leakage devices. A GHZ state shared by exactly $t$ leakage devices makes even classical one-bit leakage insecure, without any entanglement with the adversary. In this attack, each participating device emits only one classical bit, and their joint parity distinguishes any chosen pair of secrets with a constant advantage. Thus, for fixed threshold rates above $τ_\star$, the maximum number of devices that may share arbitrary entanglement with one another and with the adversary while preserving security is linear in $n$ up to constant factors, although the optimal support fraction remains open.

AI.tldr: The paper initiates the study of quantum leakage resilience of unmodified Shamir secret sharing over prime fields, analyzing single-qubit local leakage channels and entangled leakage devices, showing security for high threshold rates and a complementary negative result for arbitrarily large entanglement.
AI.motivation: Classical single-bit local leakage from each share is a well-studied model for Shamir's secret sharing, but its quantum analogue—where each party's local leakage channel outputs a leaked qubit—was previously unexplored. The authors aim to understand whether Shamir's scheme remains secure under quantum leakage, both without preshared entanglement and when leakage devices share entanglement with each other or the adversary.
AI.method: The authors consider a quantum analogue of the single-bit local leakage model, where each party's local leakage channel takes the share as input and outputs a leaked qubit. They analyze distinguishing advantage under various settings: (1) no preshared entanglement, (2) disjoint entangled blocks of fixed maximum size with no inter-block or adversary entanglement, each block emitting a fixed number of qubits, and (3) a specified set of devices sharing entanglement with the adversary, including a linear number of devices sharing entanglement with each other and the adversary. They also construct a negative result using a GHZ state shared by exactly t leakage devices to break classical one-bit leakage security.
AI.result: Without preshared entanglement, the distinguishing advantage is 2^{-Ω(n)} when the threshold rate t/n=τ exceeds τ_*≈0.73339 by a fixed positive margin. For disjoint entangled blocks of fixed maximum size, security holds when the threshold rate is sufficiently close to one. With a linear number of devices (αn for small α>0) sharing entanglement with each other and the adversary, security holds for a large enough threshold rate. As a negative result, a GHZ state shared by exactly t leakage devices makes even classical one-bit leakage insecure without adversary entanglement; each device emits one classical bit, and their joint parity distinguishes any chosen pair of secrets with constant advantage.
AI.conclusion: For fixed threshold rates above τ_*, the maximum number of devices that may share arbitrary entanglement with one another and with the adversary while preserving security is linear in n up to constant factors, though the optimal support fraction remains open.

title: Parametric DRAG for leakage-suppressed exchange gates in superconducting qubits
summary: Programmable exchange interactions support quantum gates and many-body simulation in superconducting circuits. Fast excitation transfer, however, opens two leakage pathways in weakly anharmonic transmons, degrading gates and driving simulated dynamics outside the encoded state space. We introduce parametric derivative removal by adiabatic gate (PDRAG) to suppress both pathways while preserving the target exchange. Their conjugate structure determines first- and second-derivative corrections implemented through one real frequency command. At $g/2π=100$ MHz, calibrated PDRAG achieves a geometric-mean leakage reduction of $5.27\times10^5$ relative to the base pulse across 12.5--35 ns in Duffing simulations. At 13 ns, endpoint leakage reaches $1.98\times10^{-7}$ for the calibrated full-exchange pulse. Transferring the derivative coefficients to a charge Hamiltonian gives a mean 893-fold reduction over 12.5--22 ns after amplitude and carrier recalibration. Floquet return interference and charge-induced gap shifts explain the calibration and transfer gains, connecting compact pulse design to leakage-suppressed programmable interactions.

AI.tldr: PDRAG suppresses the two leakage pathways of fast exchange in weakly anharmonic transmons via adiabatic derivative removal, achieving strong leakage reduction and transferable to charge Hamiltonians.
AI.motivation: Programmable exchange interactions enable quantum gates and many-body simulation in superconducting circuits, but fast excitation transfer in weakly anharmonic transmons opens two leakage pathways. These degrade gate fidelity and drive simulated dynamics outside the encoded state space, motivating a compact pulse scheme that suppresses leakage while preserving the target exchange.

Exploiting the conjugate structure of the two leakage pathways, they derive first- and second-derivative corrections implemented through a single real frequency command. Validation uses Duffing simulations at g/2π = 100 MHz across pulse durations of 12.5–35 ns, with pulse durations down to 13 ns, and transfer of the derivative coefficients to a charge Hamiltonian after amplitude and carrier recalibration.
AI.result: Calibrated PDRAG achieves a geometric-mean leakage reduction of 5.27×10^5 relative to the base pulse across 12.5–35 ns in Duffing simulations. At 13 ns, endpoint leakage reaches 1.98×10^-7 for the calibrated full-exchange pulse. Transferring derivative coefficients to a charge Hamiltonian yields a mean 893-fold reduction over 12.5–22 ns after amplitude and carrier recalibration.
AI.conclusion: Floquet return interference and charge-induced gap shifts explain the calibration and transfer gains, linking compact pulse design to leakage-suppressed programmable interactions. PDRAG provides a practical route to high-fidelity exchange-based gates and simulation in superconducting circuits.

title: A magnetic-field insensitive gate set for trapped-ion nuclear spin qubits
summary: We outline a complete set of operations for manipulating nuclear spin qubits of trapped-ions stored in high magnetic fields such as required for Penning trapping, where the nuclear and electron spins are largely decoupled due to the dominance of the external field Hamiltonian. The reduced nuclear magnetic moment results in insensitivity to external magnetic fields compared to the use of an electron spin, but also makes the nuclear spin hard to manipulate on fast timescales. To maintain speed, we propose a two-qubit phase gate technique which utilizes the electron spin, but for which the qubit remains protected from magnetic fields through retaining the nuclear encoding. This method works for magnetic-field insensitive qubits at lower fields as well as for both microwave and laser field gradients.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a complete set of operations for manipulating nuclear spin qubits of trapped ions in high magnetic fields (e.g., for Penning traps), and proposes a two-qubit phase gate that uses the electron spin for speed while retaining nuclear encoding for magnetic-field protection.
AI.motivation: Nuclear spins in high magnetic fields are largely decoupled from electron spins due to the dominant external field Hamiltonian. While this reduced nuclear magnetic moment gives insensitivity to external magnetic fields (an advantage over electron spins), it also makes nuclear spins slow and hard to manipulate on fast timescales—creating a trade-off between coherence protection and gate speed that needs to be resolved.
AI.method: The authors outline a complete set of operations for manipulating nuclear spin qubits of trapped ions in high magnetic fields required for Penning trapping. They propose a two-qubit phase gate technique that utilizes the electron spin to maintain speed, while the qubit remains protected from magnetic fields through retaining the nuclear encoding.
AI.result: The proposed method works for magnetic-field-insensitive qubits at lower fields as well as for both microwave and laser field gradients.
AI.conclusion: The approach enables fast two-qubit phase gates on nuclear spin qubits while preserving their intrinsic magnetic-field insensitivity, with applicability across different field regimes and gradient types (microwave and laser).

title: A Memory-Magic Exchange Law in Streaming Clifford+T Compilation
summary: A phase that reaches a fault-tolerant processor in additive pieces can be remembered until the last piece arrives, or executed on arrival: the first option costs classical memory carried across rounds, the second costs magic states committed before the phase is known. We determine the exchange rate $α$, committed $T$ gates per bit of memory forgone, for ancilla-free coordinatewise Clifford+$T$ compilation. The Ramanujan bound for the Clifford+$T$ lattice gives $α\ge2$ with explicit constants, the square-root barrier of the spectral method. An elementary determinant method, using that quaternion numerators are lattice points on spheres in both real embeddings of $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2)$, counts words near an arbitrary rotation coset below that barrier and gives $α\ge11/5$ asymptotically and unconditionally, and a height dichotomy for the resulting sphere sections raises this to $α\ge17/7$. At Clifford-framed cosets the volume law holds up to subexponential factors: all but a vanishing fraction of $z$-rotations need $T$-count $(3-o(1))\log_2(1/\varepsilon)$, and processes whose committed pieces are close to Clifford-framed $z$-rotations, including per-rotation pipelines, have $α\ge3-o(1)$, which a fractional-passthrough family attains under the Ross-Selinger typical-cost hypothesis. Under an equidistribution conjecture supported by exhaustive enumeration to $T$-count 22, $α=3$ in general and memory should be shed in whole rotations. The bounds hold even when the phases cancel to the identity; side information enters through a conditional entropy; probabilistic mixing halves the costs but not the rate. With clean ancillas and a phase-gradient catalyst, table lookups batched across coordinates drive the rate to $O(1/\log\log(1/\varepsilon))$, so the constant-rate law is specific to coordinatewise synthesis.

AI.tldr: This paper determines the exchange rate α between committed T gates and bits of classical memory foregone in ancilla-free coordinatewise Clifford+T compilation, proving α≥11/5 asymptotically (raised to α≥17/7 via a height dichotomy), with α=3 conjectured in general under an equidistribution hypothesis.
AI.motivation: A phase arriving piecewise at a fault-tolerant processor can either be stored until complete (costing classical memory across rounds) or executed on arrival (costing magic states committed before the phase is known). Quantifying this trade-off requires knowing the exchange rate α of committed T gates per bit of memory forgone.
AI.method: For ancilla-free coordinatewise Clifford+T compilation, the Ramanujan bound for the Clifford+T lattice yields α≥2 with explicit constants (the spectral square-root barrier). An elementary determinant method exploits the fact that quaternion numerators are lattice points on spheres in both real embeddings of Q(√2), counting words near an arbitrary rotation coset below the barrier. A height dichotomy on the resulting sphere sections tightens the bound. Side information is handled via conditional entropy, and probabilistic mixing is analyzed. Table lookups batched across coordinates with clean ancillas and a phase-gradient catalyst are also studied.
AI.result: The determinant method gives α≥11/5 asymptotically and unconditionally, raised to α≥17/7 by the height dichotomy. At Clifford-framed cosets the volume law holds up to subexponential factors: all but a vanishing fraction of z-rotations need T-count (3−o(1))log₂(1/ε), and processes with committed pieces close to Clifford-framed z-rotations (including per-rotation pipelines) have α≥3−o(1), attained by a fractional-passthrough family under the Ross-Selinger typical-cost hypothesis. Under an equidistribution conjecture supported by exhaustive enumeration to T-count 22, α=3 in general and memory should be shed in whole rotations. Bounds hold even when phases cancel to identity; probabilistic mixing halves costs but not the rate. With clean ancillas and a phase-gradient catalyst, batched table lookups drive the rate to O(1/log log(1/ε)).
AI.conclusion: The constant-rate law is specific to coordinatewise synthesis; alternative architectures (e.g., batched table lookups with ancillas and a catalyst) break it, achieving a vanishing rate O(1/log log(1/ε)). Memory should optimally be shed in whole rotations, and the general exchange rate is conjectured to be α=3.

title: Consistent histories and the ultrametric on infinite tensor products
summary: The consistent histories formulation of quantum mechanics assigns classical probabilities to sequences of coarse-grained events when the corresponding interference terms vanish. In finite models these terms generically need not vanish exactly, and their smallness alone supplies no asymptotic geometry on the space of histories. We construct such a geometry for histories that accumulate quantum records. When the normalized Dowker - Halliwell interference between two histories factorizes as the cumulative fidelity of their records, its decay is controlled by the accumulated squared Bures distance. In the infinite registration limit, the Kakutani - von Neumann dichotomy gives a sharp sector alternative: summable Bures defect yields weakly equivalent record sequences, whereas nonsummable defect produces orthogonal superselection sectors and vanishing normalized interference. The convergence exponent of the Bures defect defines a pseudo-ultrametric on histories. After quotienting its zero distance degeneracy, it becomes a complete ultrametric, requiring neither compactness of the outcome space nor continuity of the record family, and coincides with the gauge invariant sector metric $\tilde d$ introduced in \cite{LesTP}. Its value, the \emph{consistency rate}, has three equivalent interpretations: it is the sector separation metric, the polynomial growth exponent of the negative logarithm of normalized interference, and, by the Helstrom formula, the corresponding exponent of the negative logarithm of the minimum error probability for discriminating the cumulative records. Classical separation profiles determine the rate: positive long time mean defect gives the maximal value $δ=1$, while the borderline profile $d_m^2\asymp m^{-1}$ produces distinct superselection sectors at zero polynomial rate, $δ=0$.

AI.tldr: The paper constructs an asymptotic geometry on the space of coarse-grained quantum histories based on accumulated Bures distance between records, showing that the convergence exponent of the Bures defect yields a complete ultrametric (the "consistency rate") that unifies sector separation, decay of normalized interference, and minimum error probability for record discrimination.

title: Succinct Arguments for QMA in the Quantum Random Oracle Model
summary:
Succinct arguments are a fundamental cryptographic primitive for verifying computational claims with small communication. In the classical setting, succinct arguments for NP can be constructed from unstructured hardness alone (e.g., hash functions) by compiling probabilistically checkable proofs (PCPs) or interactive oracle proofs (IOPs) for NP via the commit-and-open paradigm. In contrast, known succinct arguments for QMA rely on ``structured'' cryptographic primitives, or on the quantum PCP conjecture.
  We construct the first succinct argument for QMA in the quantum random oracle model (QROM) without relying on additional cryptographic assumptions or unproven conjectures. This yields succinct arguments for QMA from unstructured hardness alone, showing that ideal hash functions not only suffice for succinct arguments for NP but also for QMA.
  Underlying our result is an efficiency-preserving transformation that compiles quantum interactive oracle proofs (QIOPs), a recently introduced interactive generalization of quantum PCPs, into quantum arguments for the same language, via a natural quantum commit-and-open paradigm. Our transformation applies to every QIOP with public-query soundness, a notion that we formalize to capture a natural requirement of the commit-and-open paradigm and is satisfied by a known QIOP for QMA. As a key ingredient in our transformation, we formalize and construct extractable vector commitments for quantum states with local openings in the QROM, which may be of independent interest.

AI.tldr: The paper constructs the first succinct argument for QMA in the quantum random oracle model from unstructured hardness alone, by compiling quantum interactive oracle proofs (QIOPs) into quantum arguments via a quantum commit-and-open paradigm.
AI.motivation: Classical succinct arguments for NP can be built from unstructured hardness alone (e.g., hash functions) via PCP/IOP commit-and-open compilers. However, known succinct arguments for QMA either rely on structured cryptographic primitives or on the unproven quantum PCP conjecture, leaving open whether ideal hash functions alone suffice for QMA.
AI.method: The authors introduce an efficiency-preserving transformation that compiles QIOPs with public-query soundness—a notion they formalize—into quantum arguments for the same language using a quantum commit-and-open paradigm. A key ingredient is the formalization and construction of extractable vector commitments for quantum states with local openings in the QROM.
AI.result: The work yields the first succinct argument for QMA in the QROM without additional cryptographic assumptions or unproven conjectures, establishing succinct arguments for QMA from unstructured hardness alone. The transformation applies to every QIOP with public-query soundness, a condition satisfied by a known QIOP for QMA.
AI.conclusion: Ideal hash functions suffice not only for succinct arguments for NP but also for QMA. Extractable vector commitments for quantum states with local openings in the QROM may be of independent interest.

title: Experimental certification of multipartite Bell correlations using only few-body symmetric correlations
summary: Certifying Bell correlations in increasingly larger multipartite quantum systems is challenging because conventional Bell inequalities rely on many-body correlations, which become experimentally demanding to estimate as system size grows. Here we demonstrate that multipartite Bell correlations can be certified using few-body permutation-invariant (PI) correlations with a fixed maximal correlation order. We experimentally test few-body PI Bell correlation witnesses tailored for six- and eight-photon postselected Dicke states. The addition of a few four-body correlators is found to significantly enhance the noise tolerance compared with previously studied two-body witnesses: for instance, for six qubits, the selected witness tolerates a white-noise fraction of $p_c\approx0.301$, compared with $p_c\approx0.048$ for the best two-body PI inequality with the same two settings per party. For six and eight photons respectively, we observe violations of the witness bounds by $32$ and $8.9$ standard deviations, arising from postselected polarisation states with fidelities of $0.933(4)$ and $0.916(11)$ to the corresponding half-excitation Dicke states. The witnesses for the six- and eight-photon cases use the same symmetric two- and four-body correlators, just with different coefficients. These results demonstrate an experimentally accessible approach for certifying multipartite Bell correlations in larger systems without requiring full-body correlation measurements.

AI.tldr: Multipartite Bell correlations can be certified using few-body permutation-invariant correlations of fixed maximal order, demonstrated experimentally on six- and eight-photon Dicke states.
AI.motivation: Certifying Bell correlations in larger multipartite quantum systems is hard because conventional Bell inequalities rely on many-body correlations whose experimental estimation becomes increasingly demanding as system size grows. A scalable certification approach using only few-body correlations is needed.
AI.method: The authors develop few-body permutation-invariant (PI) Bell correlation witnesses with a fixed maximal correlation order, tailored for six- and eight-photon postselected Dicke states. The witnesses combine symmetric two- and four-body correlators with different coefficients for the two system sizes, and are tested experimentally using postselected polarisation states.
AI.result: Adding a few four-body correlators significantly improves noise tolerance over two-body witnesses: for six qubits the witness tolerates a white-noise fraction of p_c≈0.301 versus p_c≈0.048 for the best two-body PI inequality with two settings per party. Violations of the witness bounds by 32σ (six photons) and 8.9σ (eight photons) were observed, with fidelities of 0.933(4) and 0.916(11) to the respective half-excitation Dicke states.
AI.conclusion: The results establish an experimentally accessible route to certifying multipartite Bell correlations in larger systems without requiring full-body correlation measurements, using the same few-body correlators across different system sizes.

title: An Operator-Norm Approach to Security with Quantum Advice
summary:
Non-uniform security allows an adversary to receive bounded advice about an oracle before attempting a fresh challenge. This captures the most realistic attacks and has already been studied extensively in prior work. In this work, we introduce an operator-norm approach for non-uniform security in the quantum random oracle and random permutation models. This new approach yields a unified reduction for both search success probability and distinguishing advantage. Previously, the reduction only worked with success probability even in the decision games, yielding a worse bound.
  Our framework enables tight bounds for Yao's box, both with and without salting, and improved bounds for pseudorandom generators. We also prove an optimal generic salting theorem for decision games. By defining a property of a game, which separates the contributions of the existing queries in the offline stage and subsequent online queries, we obtain stronger bounds for specific salted constructions. These include salted permutation inversion, tight up to logarithmic factors, and salted random-function inversion, tight up to logarithmic factors and the gap already present in classical function inversion.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces an operator-norm approach to non-uniform security in the quantum random oracle and random permutation models, yielding a unified reduction for search success probability and distinguishing advantage, with tight bounds for Yao's box, generic salting, and improved pseudorandom generator bounds.
AI.motivation: Non-uniform security models the most realistic attacks, where an adversary receives bounded advice about an oracle before a fresh challenge; prior work studied this extensively but its reduction only handled success probability even in decision games, giving worse bounds.
AI.method: The authors develop an operator-norm approach for non-uniform security in the quantum random oracle and random permutation models, providing a unified reduction covering both search success probability and distinguishing advantage. They define a game property separating offline-stage query contributions from subsequent online queries.
AI.result: The framework yields tight bounds for Yao's box with and without salting, improved bounds for pseudorandom generators, an optimal generic salting theorem for decision games, and stronger bounds for specific salted constructions: salted permutation inversion tight up to logarithmic factors, and salted random-function inversion tight up to logarithmic factors plus the classical function-inversion gap.
AI.conclusion: The operator-norm approach unifies and strengthens non-uniform security analyses in quantum oracle models, delivering tight or near-tight bounds across several cryptographic primitives and salting constructions.

title: Asymptotic Pseudospectra in Dissipative Floquet Quantum Systems: Geometric Structures and Observable Dynamics
summary: In periodically driven open quantum systems, nonnormality renders the Floquet spectrum insufficient as the system approaches the thermodynamic limit, so that pseudospectra are needed to characterize the dynamics accurately. While conventional approaches mainly focus on the local dynamics of isolated pseudospectra, their global connections and the resulting physical consequences for observables have remained largely unexplored. Here, we uncover this collective behavior by classifying the unit disk into distinct domains of exponential, algebraic, and bounded accuracy according to the asymptotic size-scaling laws of pseudospectral residuals, yielding an underlying geometric structure. We demonstrate the physical implications of this structure through two exactly solvable models. First, in a dissipative shift chain, parameter tuning drives geometric transitions that are detectable via spin-wave observables. Second, in a chiral XY model, we use this geometric structure to explain the origin of a measurable phenomenon: two correlation signals exchange their retention order under continuous parameter tuning. Our findings not only establish a new theoretical paradigm for understanding dissipative Floquet quantum systems, but also predict geometry-driven observables for quantum computing experiments.

AI.tldr: This work classifies the unit disk into geometric domains of exponential, algebraic, and bounded accuracy based on pseudospectral residual scaling, revealing global connections among pseudospectra in periodically driven open quantum systems and linking them to measurable observables.
AI.motivation: In periodically driven open quantum systems, nonnormality makes the Floquet spectrum inadequate near the thermodynamic limit, necessitating pseudospectra for accurate dynamical characterization. However, prior studies focused on local dynamics of isolated pseudospectra, leaving their global connections and observable consequences unexplored.
AI.method: The authors classify the unit disk into distinct domains of exponential, algebraic, and bounded accuracy according to the asymptotic size-scaling laws of pseudospectral residuals, uncovering an underlying geometric structure. They validate this framework using two exactly solvable models: a dissipative shift chain and a chiral XY model.
AI.result: In the dissipative shift chain, parameter tuning induces geometric transitions detectable via spin-wave observables. In the chiral XY model, the geometric structure explains a measurable phenomenon where two correlation signals exchange their retention order under continuous parameter tuning.
AI.conclusion: The findings establish a new theoretical paradigm for dissipative Floquet quantum systems and predict geometry-driven observables for quantum computing experiments.

title: Digital quantum state preparation by nucleation
summary: Quantum state preparation is crucial for quantum algorithms, and improved state preparation methods can reduce resource requirements by orders of magnitude. In this work, we introduce a state preparation method for lattice Hamiltonians on digital quantum computers inspired by nucleation. In our method, the exact ground state of a small lattice Hamiltonian is prepared in a quantum circuit, then a series of growth stages are performed via Trotterized adiabatic evolution to increase the size of the lattice to the desired model. Using the adiabatic theorem and Trotter error bounds, we provide sufficient conditions on the total evolution time and number of Trotter steps required for nucleation to prepare an initial state with desired fidelity. In addition, we introduce optimized nucleation which considers variational optimization on top of the nucleation structure. For a two-dimensional Ising model, we show that optimized nucleation can outperform a current leading method for state preparation on digital quantum computers.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a nucleation-inspired quantum state preparation method for lattice Hamiltonians, using Trotterized adiabatic evolution to grow a small exact ground state into a larger lattice, with rigorous error bounds and a variational extension that outperforms a leading digital quantum state preparation method on a 2D Ising model.
AI.motivation: Quantum state preparation is critical for quantum algorithms, and improved methods can reduce resource requirements by orders of magnitude. Existing state preparation methods on digital quantum computers are resource-intensive, motivating the search for more efficient approaches.
AI.method: The method is inspired by nucleation: first, the exact ground state of a small lattice Hamiltonian is prepared in a quantum circuit, then a series of growth stages are performed via Trotterized adiabatic evolution to expand the lattice to the desired size. Sufficient conditions on total evolution time and number of Trotter steps are derived using the adiabatic theorem and Trotter error bounds. An optimized nucleation variant adds variational optimization on top of the nucleation structure.
AI.result: For a two-dimensional Ising model, optimized nucleation is shown to outperform a current leading method for state preparation on digital quantum computers.
AI.conclusion: Nucleation offers a resource-efficient, theoretically grounded approach to lattice Hamiltonian state preparation, and its optimized variant surpasses a leading existing digital quantum method, indicating practical promise for quantum algorithms.

title: Semiclassical spin-bath calculation of the nitrogen-isotope effect on NV$^-$ ensemble coherence in diamond
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures, 1 table; Supplementary Material (6 pages, 2 figures, 1 table) included
summary: The ratio $T_2$/$T_2^*$ of the Hahn-echo and Ramsey times of nitrogen-vacancy (NV$^-$) ensembles is independent of the nitrogen concentration [N] and is $\approx$ 16 in diamond of natural isotopic abundance ($^{14}$N), yet a recent $^{15}$N-doped ensemble magnetometer gives only 8.05 $\pm$ 0.18 in the single-quantum convention. We ask whether the nitrogen nuclear isotope alone can cause such a reduction. Using a semiclassical spin-bath model with the Jahn-Teller-resolved P1 hyperfine tensor, we show that the fraction of P1 pairs that are hyperfine-degenerate, and hence free to flip-flop, is 1/4 for $^{14}$N (I = 1) but 5/16 for $^{15}$N (I = 1/2). Simulations over [N] = 0.1--100 ppm confirm that this shortens $T_2$ while leaving $T_2^*$ exactly unchanged: $T_2$($^{14}$N)/$T_2$($^{15}$N) = 1.118 $\pm$ 0.011, independent of [N] and 11$σ$ above unity. The measured contrast, 2.07 $\pm$ 0.25, is 3.8$σ$ larger, identifying resonant-channel counting as a real but partial contribution and setting a quantitative benchmark for many-body calculations.

AI.tldr: The nitrogen nuclear isotope alone reduces the Hahn-echo/Ramsey ratio in NV ensembles: hyperfine-degenerate P1 flip-flop fractions are 1/4 for ¹⁴N vs 5/16 for ¹⁵N, eliminating T₂ by ~12% while leaving T₂* unchanged.
AI.motivation: The T₂/T₂* ratio of NV⁻ ensembles is ~16 in natural-abundance (¹⁴N) diamond and independent of [N], yet a ¹⁵N-doped ensemble magnetometer yields only 8.05 ± 0.18 in the single-quantum convention. The authors ask whether the nuclear isotope alone can account for such a reduction, isolating isotope identity from nitrogen concentration as the controlling variable.
AI.method: A semiclassical spin-bath model is used together with the Jahn-Teller-resolved P1 hyperfine tensor. The hyperfine-degenerate (flip-flop-active) fraction of P1 pairs is counted for each isotope, and simulations are run over [N] = 0.1–100 ppm to track T₂ and T₂*.
AI.result: The hyperfine-degenerate P1-pair fraction is 1/4 for ¹⁴N (I = 1) and 5/16 for ¹⁵N (I = 1/2). Simulations confirm that T₂ is shortened while T₂* is exactly unchanged, giving T₂(¹⁴N)/T₂(¹⁵N) = 1.118 ± 0.011, independent of [N] and 11σ above unity. The measured contrast is 2.07 ± 0.25, i.e. 3.8σ larger than predicted.
AI.conclusion: Resonant-channel counting via hyperfine degeneracy is identified as a real but partial contribution to the isotope-dependent T₂/T₂* reduction; the discrepancy with the measured contrast sets a quantitative benchmark for many-body calculations of NV spin-bath dynamics.

title: Optimal interferometric certification of multi-photon indistinguishability
summary: Multiphoton indistinguishability is a key resource for photonic quantum technologies, yet its characterization typically relies on resource-intensive methods. In this work, we develop two efficient and experimentally friendly protocols to estimate or bound the fidelity $F_{\mathrm{ind}}$ of an $N$-photon state to the closest perfectly indistinguishable state. The first protocol applies to sources preparing separable states, uses a single Fourier interferometer together with photon-number-resolving detection, and yields tight two-sided bounds on $F_{\mathrm{ind}}$. The second protocol combines randomized implementations of linear-optical interferometers with photon counting, enabling direct estimation of $F_{\mathrm{ind}}$ for arbitrary $N$-photon states. Both protocols can certify $F_{\mathrm{ind}} = 1 - \mathcal{O}(ε)$ using provably optimal $\mathcal{O}(1/ε)$ samples, in contrast to previous approaches which required prior assumptions on the model of partial distinguishability. Our methods, based on a multiphoton generalization of the Hong-Ou-Mandel test, bring the rigorous and operationally meaningful certification of multiphoton indistinguishability within reach of current photonic technologies.

AI.tldr: Two efficient, experimentally friendly protocols estimate or bound the fidelity of an N-photon state to the closest perfectly indistinguishable state, certifying F_ind = 1 − O(ε) with provably optimal O(1/ε) samples.
AI.motivation: Multiphoton indistinguishability is a key resource for photonic quantum technologies, but its characterization typically relies on resource-intensive methods and prior model assumptions on partial distinguishability.
AI.method: Protocol 1 targets sources preparing separable states, using a single Fourier interferometer with photon-number-resolving detection to yield tight two-sided bounds on F_ind. Protocol 2 combines randomized linear-optical interferometers with photon counting to directly estimate F_ind for arbitrary N-photon states. Both are based on a multiphoton generalization of the Hong-Ou-Mandel test.
AI.result: Protocol 1 provides tight two-sided bounds on F_ind for separable states; Protocol 2 enables direct estimation of F_ind for arbitrary N-photon states. Both certify F_ind = 1 − O(ε) using provably optimal O(1/ε) samples, unlike previous approaches requiring prior partial-distinguishability models.
AI.conclusion: The protocols bring rigorous, operationally meaningful certification of multiphoton indistinguishability within reach of current photonic technologies.

title: Operational theory for photonic circuits: generalizing linear optics beyond quantum theory
summary: We use the analogy between the quadrature operators in quantum optics and the phase-space coordinates in a mechanical harmonic oscillator to generalise the theory of linear optics beyond quantum theory. For this, we introduce a framework for analysing photonic circuits within generalised probabilistic theories based on quadrature operators. Using this framework, we ask whether phenomena like the Hong-Ou-Mandel effect, Mach-Zehnder interferometry are specific to quantum theory or also occur across a broader class of theories. We find the latter: the vanishing photon coincidences at the output of a beam splitter also occur for classical light and for a modified version of quantised light. Similarly, for Mach-Zehnder interferometry we find that there is no qualitative difference between quantum theory and these alternative theories. Our framework can serve as a foundation to study generalised theories of complex photonic set-ups and photonic quantum computers.

AI.tldr: The paper generalises linear optics beyond quantum theory by building a framework for photonic circuits in generalised probabilistic theories (GPTs) based on quadrature operators, and shows that phenomena like Hong-Ou-Mandel and Mach-Zehnder interferometry are not unique to quantum theory.
AI.motivation: The authors are motivated by the analogy between quantum-optics quadrature operators and phase-space coordinates of a mechanical harmonic oscillator, seeking to determine whether celebrated photonic phenomena are specifically quantum or whether they persist in a broader class of physical theories.
AI.method: A framework for analysing photonic circuits within generalised probabilistic theories is introduced, formulated in terms of quadrature operators. This framework is then applied to canonical set-ups—a beam splitter (Hong-Ou-Mandel) and Mach-Zehnder interferometry—across quantum theory, classical light, and a modified version of quantised light.
AI.result: Vanishing photon coincidences at the output of a beam splitter also occur for classical light and for the modified quantised light, and Mach-Zehnder interferometry shows no qualitative difference between quantum theory and these alternative theories.
AI.conclusion: The Hong-Ou-Mandel effect and Mach-Zehnder interferometry are not exclusive to quantum theory; they arise across a wider class of theories. The framework offers a foundation for studying generalised theories of complex photonic set-ups and photonic quantum computers.

title: Adaptive decoding of quantum LDPC codes through decoder disagreement
summary: Accurate decoding of quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes often relies on expensive post-processing search, although decoding difficulty varies strongly between syndromes. We find that the benefit of deeper post-processing search is highly concentrated in a small subset of decoding instances, and that these instances can be identified directly from the decoder itself. To this end, we introduce an adaptive decoder based on belief propagation (BP) and ordered-statistics decoding (OSD), using the disagreement between the BP hard decision and the syndrome-consistent order-zero OSD solution as an internal risk signal to determine where deeper search is required. On a $[[144,12,12]]$ bivariate bicycle code under circuit-level depolarising noise, encoding $12$ logical qubits in $144$ data qubits with distance $12$, escalating only the highest-risk $20\%$ of instances recovers $85\%$ to $92\%$ of the improvement in logical error rate available from a full one-free-variable sweep, while reducing the mean serial decoding cost by a factor of $3.6$ relative to applying the same truncated search to every instance. At matched budget, disagreement-guided routing also outperforms routing based on the BP syndrome residual, syndrome weight and random selection. The same behaviour reappears on a structurally distinct radial qLDPC code obtained from a lifted-product construction, where escalating $20\%$ of instances recovers $87\%$ to $94\%$ of the available gain. A $Z$-memory experiment on the Quantinuum H2 trapped-ion processor, implementing both $X$-type and $Z$-type checks, further shows that the signal remains predictive under device noise. These results show that decoder-internal disagreement can expose where additional decoding effort is valuable, allowing classical computation to be concentrated on the instances most likely to benefit from it.

AI.tldr: An adaptive BP+OSD quantum LDPC decoder uses the disagreement between BP hard decisions and order-zero OSD solutions as an internal risk signal to selectively apply deeper post-processing search only to high-risk decoding instances, achieving most of the accuracy gain at a fraction of the cost.
AI.motivation: Decoding qLDPC codes typically relies on expensive post-processing search, but decoding difficulty varies strongly between syndromes. Since deeper search benefits are concentrated in a small subset of instances, uniform expensive search wastes classical computation; the goal is to identify which instances genuinely need deeper search.
AI.method: Introduce an adaptive decoder combining belief propagation (BP) and ordered-statistics decoding (OSD). The disagreement between the BP hard decision and the syndrome-consistent order-zero OSD solution serves as an internal risk signal to route only high-risk instances to deeper search. Evaluated on a [[144,12,12]] bivariate bicycle code under circuit-level depolarising noise, a structurally distinct radial qLDPC code from a lifted-product construction, and a Z-memory experiment on the Quantinuum H2 trapped-ion processor.
AI.result: Escalating only the highest-risk 20% of instances recovers 85%–92% of the logical error rate improvement from a full one-free-variable sweep on the [[144,12,12]] code, while cutting mean serial decoding cost by 3.6x versus applying the same truncated search to all instances. Disagreement-guided routing outperforms routing based on BP syndrome residual, syndrome weight, and random selection at matched budget. On the radial qLDPC code, escalating 20% of instances recovers 87%–94% of the available gain. The H2 experiment shows the signal remains predictive under device noise.
AI.conclusion: Decoder-internal disagreement exposes where additional decoding effort is valuable, enabling classical computation to be concentrated on the instances most likely to benefit, generalizing across code families and holding under real device noise.

title: Resonance Breaking in Noisy Shor's Algorithm
summary: We argue that the exponential quantum advantage in Shor's algorithm is broken under one-layer depolarizing noise of arbitrary small error rate, by analyzing a resonance breaking phenomenon in noisy quantum circuits. First, we express the distribution of measurements on $n$-qubit strings as the superposition of the $4^n$ wave functions in the Pauli path integral. In the noiseless case, the bit-strings achieving resonant peaks guaranteed a constant rate of successful measurements to factor a large number. Secondly, when the middle layer of the quantum circuit has independent depolarizing noise of rate $λ$, for any Hamming weight $d$, we obtain corresponding measurement rate bounded by $2(1-λ)^d$ for higher frequency terms and by $O(n^d)/2^{n/2}$ for low frequency terms. The rate approaches to zero as $n$ and $d$ approaches to infinity. Resonance breaking destroys the exponential quantum advantage. Furthermore, we design a classical factoring algorithm in polynomial time $O(n^d)$ to substitute the low frequency contribution.

AI.tldr: One-layer depolarizing noise of arbitrarily small rate breaks the exponential quantum advantage of Shor's algorithm via a resonance-breaking phenomenon, and a polynomial-time classical algorithm is designed to substitute the low-frequency contribution.
AI.motivation: To examine whether the exponential quantum advantage of Shor's algorithm is robust under realistic noise, specifically a single middle layer of independent depolarizing noise of arbitrary small rate.
AI.method: The measurement distribution over n-qubit strings is expressed as a superposition of 4^n wave functions via the Pauli path integral. The noiseless case is compared against the noisy case where the middle layer has independent depolarizing noise of rate λ. Measurement rates are bounded for higher-frequency terms by 2(1-λ)^d and for low-frequency terms by O(n^d)/2^(n/2), for any Hamming weight d.
AI.result: Under noise, the measurement rate approaches zero as n and d go to infinity, so resonance breaking destroys the exponential quantum advantage. The high-frequency terms decay as 2(1-λ)^d and low-frequency terms as O(n^d)/2^(n/2).
AI.conclusion: Even arbitrarily small one-layer depolarizing noise eliminates the exponential quantum advantage of Shor's algorithm through resonance breaking; a polynomial-time O(n^d) classical factoring algorithm is designed to replace the low-frequency contribution.

title: Integrated balanced homodyne detector using CMOS capacitive-feedback TIA for quantum measurements

summary: A low-noise, high-speed balanced homodyne detector is demonstrated, combining a capacitive-feedback transimpedance amplifier implemented in 28 nm CMOS with a custom photonic integrated circuit fabricated in imec's iSiPP200 silicon photonics platform. The receiver achieves a 3-dB bandwidth of 7.6 GHz, a maximum shot noise clearance of 27 dB, a shot noise-limited bandwidth of 13.7 GHz and a common-mode rejection ratio up to 54.8 dB. AI.motivation: Demanding quantum and coherent optical sensing applications—such as continuous-variable quantum key distribution, quantum random number generation, and optical coherence tomography—require low-noise, high-speed balanced homodyne detection, motivating a receiver that integrates a CMOS capacitive-feedback transimpedance amplifier with a photonic integrated circuit.

title: Constant-rate quantum codes with low-weight stabilizers and full logical Clifford actions via transversal and fold-transversal gates
summary: Low-space-overhead fault-tolerant quantum computation requires not only high-rate quantum error-correcting codes but also space-efficient implementations of logical operations. Transversal and fold-transversal gates are promising since they limit error propagation and require no additional qubits. However, the logical operations they enable are typically restricted, and a central challenge is to construct codes that combine a complete set of logical Clifford gates with favorable code parameters. In this work, we introduce a family of quantum codes with an asymptotically constant encoding rate and sublogarithmically growing stabilizer weight, while supporting the entire logical Clifford group using only transversal and fold-transversal gates. Our construction is based on classical codes whose code spaces are absolutely irreducible Steinberg modules of their Tanner-graph automorphism groups. Taking hypergraph products of these classical codes yields quantum codes for which all logical Clifford operations can be synthesized from a fixed set of transversal and fold-transversal gates. Moreover, the slow growth of the stabilizer weight enables a high error-correcting performance in small instances. These results provide a path toward fault-tolerant quantum computation with low space overhead using transversal and fold-transversal gates.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a family of quantum codes with asymptotically constant encoding rate and sublogarithmic stabilizer weight that support the full logical Clifford group using only transversal and fold-transversal gates, based on classical codes arising as Steinberg modules of Tanner-graph automorphism groups combined via hypergraph products.
AI.motivation: Low-space-overhead fault-tolerant quantum computation needs both high-rate quantum error-correcting codes and space-efficient logical operations. Transversal and fold-transversal gates are attractive because they limit error propagation and need no extra qubits, but the logical operations they enable are typically restricted. A central challenge is to construct codes combining a complete logical Clifford gate set with favorable code parameters.
AI.method: The authors construct a code family based on classical codes whose code spaces are absolutely irreducible Steinberg modules of their Tanner-graph automorphism groups. They then take hypergraph products of these classical codes to obtain quantum codes in which all logical Clifford operations are synthesized from a fixed set of transversal and fold-transversal gates.
AI.result: The resulting quantum codes have asymptotically constant encoding rate and sublogarithmically growing stabilizer weight while supporting the entire logical Clifford group via only transversal and fold-transversal gates. The slow growth of the stabilizer weight also yields high error-correcting performance in small instances.
AI.conclusion: These results offer a path toward fault-tolerant quantum computation with low space overhead using transversal and fold-transversal gates.

title: Optimal single-copy estimation of quantum state moments: why $\operatorname{Tr}(ρ^3)$ and $\operatorname{Tr}(ρ^4)$ are equally hard
summary: Estimating nonlinear properties of an unknown quantum state with restrictive experimental accessibility is a fundamental problem in quantum learning. We study the sample complexity of estimating the state moments $\operatorname{Tr}(ρ^t)$, allowing arbitrary adaptive single-copy measurements. While purity estimation has optimal sample complexity $Θ(\sqrt d)$ at constant additive error, the optimal dimension dependence for higher moments has remained unclear. We resolve this question for every fixed integer $t\ge 2$: for any sufficiently small constant additive error, the optimal sample complexity is \[ Θ\!\left(d^{\frac{\lceil\log_2 t\rceil}{1+\lceil\log_2 t\rceil}}\right) \] with constant success probability. The complexity thus follows a dyadic hierarchy: for each integer $h\geq1$, all moment orders $2^{h-1}<t\leq2^h$ share the same exponent. In particular, the third and fourth moments both require $Θ(d^{2/3})$ copies. We also establish an $Ω(d^{1-1/t})$ lower bound for arbitrary nonadaptive single-copy protocols, matching the known upper bound and demonstrating an advantage from adaptivity for every $t\geq4$. Our upper bound uses adaptive state filtering to reduce higher-order moment estimation to lower-order moment estimation in a smaller state space. For the lower bound, we directly compare moment-matched ensembles through a smooth interpolation, bypassing the maximally mixed state as an intermediate hypothesis and yielding matching bounds beyond $\sqrt d$.

AI.tldr: This paper determines the exact sample complexity of estimating state moments Tr(ρ^t) under adaptive single-copy measurements, proving a dyadic hierarchy Θ(d^{⌈log₂t⌉/(1+⌈log₂t⌉)}) for every fixed integer t≥2, and shows adaptivity strictly helps for t≥4.
AI.motivation: Estimating nonlinear properties of an unknown quantum state under restrictive experimental accessibility (single-copy measurements) is a fundamental problem in quantum learning. AI.result: For every fixed integer t≥2 and sufficiently small constant additive error, the optimal sample complexity is Θ(d^{⌈log₂t⌉/(1+⌈log₂t⌉)}) at constant success probability, following a dyadic hierarchy where all orders 2^{h-1}<t≤2^h share one exponent (e.g., third and fourth moments both need Θ(d^{2/3})). AI.conclusion: The sample complexity of estimating Tr(ρ^t) with adaptive single-copy measurements follows a precise dyadic hierarchy governed by ⌈log₂t⌉, resolving the dimension dependence for all fixed t≥2. Adaptivity strictly outperforms nonadaptive strategies for t≥4, with third and fourth moments requiring Θ(d^{2/3}) copies. The technical innovations—adaptive state filtering and smooth moment-matched ensemble interpolation—provide matching bounds beyond the √d regime.

title: Quantum Complexity of Ancilla-Free Unitary Embeddings for Nonlinear Dynamics via Generalized State-Dependent Double-Bracket Flows
summary: Simulating nonlinear dynamics with quantum computers has gained increasing attention. In general, such simulations require additional quantum resources because unitary quantum evolution is linear. A fundamental question is how nonlinear dynamics can be embedded into fully coherent, ancilla-free unitary circuits and how the complexity of the dynamics governs the required quantum resources. In this work, we generalize the ancilla-free double-bracket quantum algorithm for imaginary-time evolution by replacing its state-independent Hamiltonian with a state-dependent Hermitian operator. Our framework recursively calls an initial state preparation oracle and its inverse, and prepares the target solution to any prescribed accuracy using a fully coherent, ancilla-free unitary embedding. We relate the query cost to the complexity of the nonlinear dynamics, specifically their sensitivity to initial conditions. We obtain query upper bounds of $\exp(O(T))$, $\exp(O(T^2))$, and $\exp(\exp(O(T)))$ when the distance between solutions contracts at least exponentially (contractive), does not increase (nonexpansive), or grows at most exponentially (expansive), respectively, where $T$ is the target evolution time. For the discrete Gross--Pitaevskii equation, our ancilla-free double-bracket circuit achieves optimal worst-case query complexity $Θ(e^{gT/2})$ over a specified family of single-qubit initial states, where $g>0$ is the nonlinearity strength. These results connect the complexity of nonlinear dynamics to the query cost of coherent quantum simulation and provide a foundation for designing ancilla-free unitary embeddings with optimal query complexity.

title: Measuring the spin of a spin-1/2 and getting a result of 7
summary: The weak value of an operator is the average result of measuring that operator on a quantum system given specified initial and final states. The overlap between these states appears in the denominator of the weak value, and thus if that overlap is small, the weak value can be arbitrarily large. In 1988, Albert, Aharonov, and Vaidman proposed a weak Stern-Gerlach experiment which would be able to measure a so-called anomalous weak value, a measurement result which lies out- side of the eigenvalue spectrum of the operator being measured. Though anomalous weak values have been measured in numerous optical systems, here we present the first such realization of this experiment as originally proposed. By placing a Bose-Einstein condensate of 87Rb in a magnetic gradient and performing an unlikely postselection, we measure an effective magnification of a weak magnetic momentum kick (~ 8 $μ$m/s) by a factor of 14. We also demonstrate that increasing the momentum kick decreases the "weakness" of the measurement and reduces the amplification.

AI.tldr: First realization of the original weak Stern-Gerlach experiment using a 87Rb Bose-Einstein condensate, demonstrating anomalous weak values via a 14x magnification of an ~8 μm/s magnetic momentum kick.
AI.motivation: The weak value of an operator, defined by specified initial and final states, can become arbitrarily large when the overlap of these states (appearing in the denominator) is small. Albert, Aharonov, and Vaidman proposed in 1988 a weak Stern-Gerlach experiment capable of measuring an anomalous weak value—a result outside the eigenvalue spectrum. While such values have been observed in various optical systems, the experiment exactly as originally proposed had not been realized.
AI.method: A Bose-Einstein condensate of 87Rb was placed in a magnetic gradient and subjected to an unlikely (small-overlap) postselection, constituting the originally proposed weak Stern-Gerlach configuration.
AI.result: An effective magnification of a weak magnetic momentum kick (~8 μm/s) by a factor of 14 was measured. Increasing the momentum kick was shown to decrease the "weakness" of the measurement and reduce the amplification.
AI.conclusion: This work provides the first realization of the weak Stern-Gerlach experiment as originally proposed, confirming anomalous weak-value amplification in a matter-wave system and reproducing the expected trade-off between kick magnitude and amplification.

title: Towards verifiable quantum advantage with random circuits: Observables that survive concentration
summary: Demonstrating quantum advantage on current quantum hardware is a central goal of quantum computing, and random quantum circuits underpin many leading proposals. Yet sampling-based demonstrations are often difficult to verify, while observable-based approaches face a different challenge: concentration can suppress differences between circuit instances. Recent experiments have put forward the estimation of out-of-time-order correlators (OTOCs) in random circuits as a promising task for verifiable quantum advantage, yet whether their circuit-to-circuit fluctuations survive concentration as system size grows has remained open. Here we show that they do. For broad classes of local random circuits in any fixed spatial dimension, we prove inverse-polynomial fluctuations of fixed-order OTOCs at system-scale depths. In one-dimensional Haar-random brickwork circuits, we further show that macroscopically many gates contribute to these fluctuations, yet in each layer they remain confined to a sublinear-width region. As a byproduct, we develop a classical algorithm exhibiting the first rigorous improvement over brute-force classical simulation of OTOCs in 1D. Although classical hardness remains open, our results rule out strong concentration as an obstruction to OTOC-based proposals for verifiable quantum advantage.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that fixed-order out-of-time-order correlators (OTOCs) in local random circuits exhibit inverse-polynomial circuit-to-circuit fluctuations at system-scale depths in any fixed dimension, ruling out strong concentration as an obstruction to OTOC-based verifiable quantum advantage.
AI.motivation: Sampling-based quantum advantage demonstrations are hard to verify, while observable-based approaches suffer from concentration that suppresses differences between circuit instances. OTOC estimation in random circuits was recently proposed as a verifiable alternative, but it was unknown whether OTOC fluctuations survive concentration as system size grows.
AI.method: The authors analytically prove fluctuation lower bounds for fixed-order OTOCs in broad classes of local random circuits in any fixed spatial dimension at system-scale depths. For 1D Haar-random brickwork circuits, they additionally analyze the spatial structure of contributions to the fluctuations and develop a classical algorithm for OTOC simulation.

In 1D Haar-random brickwork circuits, macroscopically many gates contribute to the fluctuations, yet within each layer they are confined to a sublinear-width region. The authors also obtain the first rigorous improvement over brute-force classical OTOC simulation in 1D.

title: A Neutral Atom-Based Hybrid Classical-Quantum Approach for the Entanglement Routing Problem
summary: Efficient end-to-end entanglement distribution in quantum information networks requires routing under limited resources and fidelity constraints. We study entanglement routing as a fidelity-constrained unsplittable multicommodity flow problem that maximizes the number of admitted requests. As a proof of concept, we integrate neutral-atom quantum optimization into a hybrid classical--quantum column-generation framework. A classical restricted master problem selects routes, while a pricing problem generates fidelity-feasible paths. We formulate this NP-hard constrained shortest-path pricing problem as a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problem and address it with hardware-aware register embedding and instance-driven pulse shaping. To our knowledge, this is the first study of neutral-atom quantum optimization as a pricing oracle for fidelity-constrained entanglement routing. On small benchmark instances evaluated with neutral-atom processor emulators, the method, combined with warm-start and post-processing, achieves an optimality gap below 1% across all tested sizes; the selected simulated-annealing route-generation baseline exhibits gaps of up to 6%. These results indicate that the generated bitstrings can provide useful candidate routes for classical refinement within column generation. This proof of concept does not establish quantum utility or scalability; further evaluation on larger instances, against stronger classical baselines, and on quantum hardware is needed.

AI.tldr: This proof-of-concept integrates neutral-atom quantum optimization as a pricing oracle within a hybrid classical-quantum column-generation framework for fidelity-constrained entanglement routing, achieving <1% optimality gap on small emulated instances versus up to 6% for a simulated-annealing baseline.
AI.motivation: Efficient end-to-end entanglement distribution in quantum information networks requires routing under limited resources and fidelity constraints, motivating a fidelity-constrained unsplittable multicommodity flow formulation that maximizes admitted requests.
AI.method: A hybrid classical-quantum column-generation framework is used: a classical restricted master problem selects routes, while a pricing problem generates fidelity-feasible paths. The NP-hard constrained shortest-path pricing problem is cast as a QUBO and solved via neutral-atom quantum optimization with hardware-aware register embedding and instance-driven pulse shaping, plus warm-start and post-processing.
AI.result: On small benchmark instances evaluated with neutral-atom processor emulators, the method achieves an optimality gap below 1% across all tested sizes, whereas the simulated-annealing route-generation baseline shows gaps of up to 6%.
AI.conclusion: The generated bitstrings can supply useful candidate routes for classical refinement within column generation, but this proof of concept does not establish quantum utility or scalability; further evaluation on larger instances, stronger classical baselines, and quantum hardware is required.

title: Optimal Quantum Junta Testing without Inverse Queries
summary: We study the query complexity of testing quantum juntas. Given an unknown $n$-qubit unitary or quantum channel, the goal is to decide whether it acts nontrivially on at most $k$ qubits or is $\varepsilon$-far from every such operation. For unitaries, we consider the forward-only model, where the tester has access to $U$, but not to $U^\dagger$ or controlled-$U$. We give tight bounds for both unitary and channel junta testing. For sufficiently large $k$, $n \ge 2k$, and a broad range of $\varepsilon$, both problems have query complexity $Θ\left(k/(\varepsilon^2\log k)\right)$. Our upper bounds are achieved by simple nonadaptive testers using product inputs and single-qubit measurements. For junta channels, this closes the gap by Bao and Yao (COLT 23, TPAMI 2025) between an $\widetilde{O}(k)$ upper bound and a $\widetildeΩ(\sqrt{k})$ lower bound at constant $\varepsilon$, establishing the optimal $Θ(k/\log k)$ query complexity. At the heart of both bounds is a strong connection between quantum junta testing and classical support-size testing. For the upper bounds, we reduce quantum junta testing to a generalized support-size problem for distributions over random subsets, and develop a new tester with improved sample complexity. For the lower bounds, we proceed in the reverse direction, reducing classical support-size testing to quantum junta testing through a phase-masked hard ensemble and showing that forward quantum queries can be exactly classicalized on average. Together, these reductions identify support-size testing as the classical core of quantum junta testing and yield matching lower bounds. At constant $\varepsilon$, they also give a separation between $Θ(k/\log k)$ forward queries and $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{k})$ queries with inverse access.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes tight query complexity bounds for testing quantum juntas, showing both unitary and channel junta testing require Θ(k/(ε² log k)) queries, resolving an open gap for channels.
AI.motivation: Quantum junta testing—deciding whether an unknown n-qubit unitary or channel acts nontrivially on at most k qubits—had a significant gap between upper and lower bounds, particularly for channels where an Õ(k) upper bound and an Ω̃(√k) lower bound left the true complexity unresolved. The paper aims to settle these bounds and uncover the structural nature of the problem.
AI.method: For unitaries, the forward-only model (access to U but not U† or controlled-U) is used. Upper bounds are obtained by reducing quantum junta testing to a generalized support-size testing problem for distributions over random subsets, with a new tester of improved sample complexity using nonadaptive product inputs and single-qubit measurements. Lower bounds reverse the reduction: classical support-size testing is reduced to quantum junta testing via a phase-masked hard ensemble, showing forward quantum queries can be exactly classicalized on average.

At constant ε, this closes the gap by Bao and Yao, establishing the optimal Θ(k/log k) query complexity for junta channels. It also yields a separation between Θ(k/log k) forward queries and Õ(√k) queries with inverse access at constant ε.
